Is a Criminal Matter Judicially Reviewable?

293. We are not, however, abdicating jurisdiction to act in matters with criminal overtures under Writ jurisdiction-far from that. We have no hesitation to say that in appropriate cases, we are duty bound to intervene by engaging Article 102 even in criminal matters. We do, in this respect note that the history of the evolution of the doctrine of judicial review reveals that the egg of judicial review was incubated in the womb of criminal matters, even before the Tudor period, as certiorari were issued by the King's Bench to quash judgments or orders passed by the 'Justices of the Peace'(Henderson, Foundation of English Administrative Law: de Smith, Judicial Review of Administrative Action 4th Edition 584: de Smith Wolf and Jowel 14-001:

Holdsworth, History of English Law, 228, 658: Caenegern, Royal Writs in England from the con- quest to Glanville: R vs Lowle 1759 2Bnm 834 )and, even today that trend persists. So in In R vs Hereford Magistrate Court ex-parte Rowlands (1998 Q13 110) the Queens Bench Division quashed an irregular conviction on judicial review not with- standing the petitioner's right of appeal to the Crown Court.

294. In R vs Wandsworth JJ ex-parte Read (1942 1 KB 281, in which Chief Justice Lord (Viscount) Caldecott in refuting the argument that judicial review would not lie as it was open to the petitioner to challenge the criminal conviction by lodging an appeal or by resorting to the device known as 'Case Stated', (similar to our section 561 A CrPC. procedure), observed, "It remains to consider the argument that the remedy of certiorari is not open to the appellant because others were available. It would be ludicrous in such a case, as the present, for the convicted person to ask for a case to be stated. It would mean asking the Court to consider as a question of law whether the justices were right in convicting a man without hearing his evidence. This is so extravagant an argument as not to merit a moment's consideration".

295. The House of Lords decision in Leech vs Deputy Governor of Parkhurst Prison (1988 AC 533) also provides strong, persuasive though, authority to lend support to this contention. In R vs Reading Crown Court, ex p. Hutcbinson (1988 QB 384), RV Devizes Justices, ex p. lee(1988 QB 384, DPP vs Head (1959 AC 83), R vs Smith (Thomas George ) (1984 CrLR 630) and in R vs Oxford Crown Court ex p Smith (1989 2 Admin Law Report), the various English Courts, inclusive of the House of Lords, judicially reviewed Magistrate Court's and Crown Court's decision to ignore the plea raised by the accused that the criminal Courts concerned were obliged to examine the validity of the by-laws, validity /applicability of the orders, under which the accused persons were prosecuted. In Boddington vs British Transport Police (1998 2 DLR 639 ) the House of Lords judicially reviewed a Magistrate Court's decision to refuse to examine the vires of a bye-law, though, at the end held that the by-law was valid.

296. True it is that unlike ours, in Britain there is no written constitution to dictate that the High Court Division may interfere, "if satisfied that no other equally efficacious remedy is provided by law". But it is equally true that the area of the Common Law principle, upon which the English doctrine of judicial review is founded, is no way different from our written Constitutional mandate. It is also very much an English Common Law requirement that judicial review may not normally be available where alternative, effective, statutory remedies are in hands. In any event, when fundamental right is invoked, question of alternative remedy becomes a matter of discretion only because unlike Article 102(2), Article 102(1)does not speak of efficacious alternative remedy.

297. The Indian Supreme Court in State of Hariana vs Bhajan lal, (AIR 1992 SC 604), vigilantly discarding the idea that writ jurisdiction cannot be invoked in a criminal matter, expostulated seven types of situation, not exhaustive though, where the High Courts may review a criminal matter under writ jurisdiction.

298. Even our Appellate Division did not find any reason to debase itself from the above disclosed principles. So in Government of the Peoples Republic of Bangladesh vs Iqbal Hasan Mahmood Tuku, (60 DLR (AD) 147) the Appellate Division declined to endorse the contention that a criminal matter cannot be agitated through writ jurisdiction because of the existence of alternative remedy under section 561 A of the CrPC.

299. The Appellate Division in MA Hai vs TCB [40 DLR (AD) 206] arrived at similar conclusion.

Reasons for Our Disinclination to interfere with the Petitioner's Conviction and Sentence

300. Our above observation notwithstanding we are still not inclined to interfere with the conviction, with the reckoning that this is not the proper forum because of the following reasons:

Firstly, although the conviction was handed by a void forum, a military Court, original cognizance was, nevertheless, taken by a properly constituted Court viz, a Court of Session, and hence, the notion of justice will be frustrated if, through a writ of certiorari the conviction is completely set aside, because in that event he will go scot free without facing a fresh trial de-novo. Secondly other complicated issues are also blended with this case, such as whether a second FIR is recognised by the CrPC., and what consequences would flow if it is not recognised, which issues are not apposite for a writ Bench, and, thirdly, question of bail is also involved. Had it been a straight forward case of setting a conviction aside, by issuing a writ of certiorari, we could have explored that possibility without hesitation. Our refusal to intervene also means cessation of the petitioner's bail privilege.

How to Take Ershad and other Perpetrator(s) to Task?

<u>301. Now, how about the perpetrator, General Ershad, who dared to unleash illegal and outrageous impingement on our Sacrosanct entity, our hard earned Constitution? Can he be reprieved, after committing such a heinous felony as putting the Constitution in abeyance for years together, plundering the divine rights of the people, thereby plunging them to grave predicament? History will impeach us should we fail to address this question in conduciveness with desire of the people-people want to see him tried and that is what it ought to be. Not only General Ershad, but all his accomplices, as well as such perpetrators of 1975 martial law, who may still be alive, Mushtaque-Zia-Sayem having already had died, must face the wrath of ultimate justice. In this respect we note with wholehearted approbation the Pakistan Supreme Court's observation in the Sindh High Court Bar Association case, supra, which reads as follows: "We lay it down firmly that the assumption of power would be unconstitutional not to be recognised by any Court including the Supreme Court. Henceforth, a Judge playing any role in future in recognition of such assumption of power would be guilty of misconduct Within the ambit of Article 209." We also remind ourselves that Oliver Cromwell was notionally tried, his skeleton heading been exhumed, years after he was buried, and that was done only to transmit an undistorted message to possible adventurists. So, we do endorse the view Mis. M. Arnir-ul-Islam, AFM Mesbah Uddin learned senior Advocate, advanced. We are, simultaneously, in all four with the suggestion the learned Attorney General, Mr. Mahbubey Alam and Mr. Murad Reza, Additional Attorney General, put forward to the effect that the question as to how General Ershad should be dealt with should best left with the government. We subscribe to the overriding view that booking the perpetrators will act as a deterrent against future adventurers and that is why it is all the more essential that all the Martial Law perpetrators and those who were 'pardelictum' with them should be thrown to the long arms of justice. The Appellate Division, in the Fifth Amendment case, has quite discernibly expressed that the government and the Parliament should come up with infallible legislation to ensure appropriate punishment for such disgruntled people, and we are in no doubt, in order to protect the Constitution from future vultures, which must be the prime obligation of the government as well as of the representatives of the people, such move shall be forthcoming. The government may also explore whether there are sufficient evidence to indict the perpetrator(s) under any existing provision of the Penal Code, particularly sections 121 A and section 124 and 124A, or under any provision of any other special law. Our memory must not betray us in reminiscing that usurpers like Suharto, Pinochet, Gortiary, Idi Amin had to face the harsh music of law, while destiny steered Hitler, Mussolini, Franco, Mirza, Ayub, Yahya, Ziaul Haque and Musharraf to dire eventualities. There exists no reason why those who dared to play with the fate and the destiny of our people should not face same obnoxious consequences-no crime should go unpunished.</u>

Bangalee Nationalism

302. During the hearing of this petition Mr. M Amir-ul-lslam, who is one of the framers of the Constitution, submitting that one of the most ruthless casualty of successive Martial Law usurpation was the guillotining of the aspiration of our liberation war, pointed out that General Zia disparagingly throttled, after illegally assuming power, the word 'Bangalee Nationalism' from our Constitution, ostensibly with communal afterthought, although, said Mr. Islam, the Liberation War was fought to secure the recognition of 'Bangalee Nationalism' and an independent country for Bangalee Nation.Mr. Islam further contended that the phrase Bangalee Nationalism was figured in Article 6 of the original Constitution of 1972, because the entire population of the country wanted the victory to 'Bangalee Nationalism' and as such, scripting of this phrase in their Sacred Constitution reflected the overwhelming will of the people. Mr. Islam contended that although it was Zia who ejected this phrases from our Constitution, General Ershad is no less to blame as he continued with it,

303. We could not agree more. The whole world knows that we fought our War of Liberation to hold the flag of ' Bang alee Nationalism' high. It is also true that everyone in Bangladesh, including people of all ethnicity are also Bengalees too. They also speak in, Bangla, fought valiantly for the liberation of Bangladesh. Mr. Islam thought a clear message should be beaconed from this Court in this respect.

304. This question found a place for consideration in the Appellate Division at the time the Fifth Amendment Case was before their Lordships. Reproduced verbatim, the Appellate Division's modifying order, stands like' this; "Regarding Nationalism though express the view that being political issue, Parliament is to take decision in this regard, but if in place of 'Bangladeshi' the 'Bangalee' is substituted, in term of the judgment and the order of the High Court Division, then all passports, identity cards, nationality certificates issued by the Government ..... will have to be changed, reprinted or re-issued ..... Bangladeshi nationals will who will return to Bangladesh as well as those travelling abroad, will also face serious complications with immigration authorities abroad. Apart from the above this change of nationality will also cost millions from the public exchequer. So for wider public interest the substituted Article 6 is retained."

305. What is abundantly clear from the Appellate Division's modification is that the retention of substituted Article 6 was not meant to be perennial, or ad-infinitum, and not absolute but flexible, and was meant to be for a finite duration subject to the political decision of the government, and the decision to modify was taken considering the questions of the problems that would spring from what are presently scripted in our passports and other documents etc, as well as considering the question of expenses.

<u>306. So, the government should take steps to remove the countervailing factors the Appellate Division cited, which stand as hurdles on our way to restore unimpaired Article 6, with a view to eventually restore unimpaired Article 6, which reflected sovereign will of the people and of Bangabandhu.</u>

<u>307. There is no doubt, and keeping in mind the question of expenses and the necessity of the changes that are to be brought about, as viewed by the Appellate Division, and the Appellate Division's ruling, we can gradually proceed to eventually restore uninflected Article 6 and bring back 'Bangalee Nationalism' in our Constitution, which was the commitment of the historic War of Liberation and the cherished desire of the people and Bangabandhu himself. The government should take the initiative to make that happen without delay by commencing the process forthwith.</u>

308. Mr. Khasru, with all earnestness supplied copies of Argentine and Mexican Constitution to depict the measures these countries have taken in order to insulate their Constitution. This would definitely be a commendable action on the part our legislators to follow such move. Pakistan has also taken similar steps. After all, nobody wants to see any more martial law. This outlaw and abhorrent demon must find a perpetual exit from our land.

The Ultimate Summing Up

309. Our judgment may be summed up in following terms;

1) Martial Law is totally alien a concept to our Constitution and hence, what Dicey commented about it, is squarely applicable to us as well.

2) A fortiori, usurpation of power by General Mohammad Ershad, flexing his arms, was void ab-initio, as was the authoritarian rule by Mushtaque-Zia duo, before Ershad, and shall remain so through eternity. All Martial Law instruments were void ab-initio. As a corollary, action purportedly shedding validity through the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act 1986, constituted a stale, moribund attempt, having no effect through the vision of law, to grant credibility to the frenzied concept, and the same must be cremated without delay.

3) The killing of the Father of the Nation, which was followed by successive military rules, with a few years of intermission, was not an spontaneous act-it resulted from a well intrigued plot, harboured over a long period of time which was aimed not only to kill the Father of the Nation and his family, but also to wipe out the principles on which the Liberation War was fought.

4) During the autocratic rule of Khandaker Mushtaque and General Ziaur Rahman, every efforts were undertaken to erase the memory of the Liberation War against Pakistan,

5) Two military regimes, the first being with effect from 15th August, 1975, and the second one being between 24th March 1982, and 10th November 1986, put the country miles backward. Both the martial laws devastated the democratic fabric, as well as the patriotic aspiration of the country. During Ziaur Rahman's martial law, the slogan of the Liberation War, "Joy Bangla" was hacked to death. Many other Bengal i words such as Bangladesh Betar, Bangladesh Biman were also erased from our vocabulary. Suharwardy Uddyan, which stands as a relic of Bangabandhu's 7th March Declaration as well as that of Pakistani troops' surrender, was converted into a children's park. Top Pakistani collaborator Shah Azizur Rahman was given the second highest pnli: ical post of the Republic while other reprehensible collaborators like Col. Mustafiz (10 in Agarlate conspiracy case). ASM Suleiman.Abdul Alim etc were installed in Zia's cabinet. Many collaborators.who fled the country towards the end of the Liberation War, were allowed, not only to return to Bangladesh. butwere also greeted with safe haven, were deployed in important national positions. Self- confessed killers of Bangabandhu were given immunity from indictment through a notorious piece or purported legislation. They were also honoured with prestigious and tempting diplomatic assignments abroad, The original Constitution of the Republic of 1972 was mercilessly ravaged by General Ziaur Rahman who erased from it one of the basic features. Secularism and allowed communal politics proscribed by Bangabandhu, to stage a comeback.

6) During General Ershads Martial Law also democracy suffered devastating havoc. The Constitution was kept in abeyance. Doors or communal politics, wide opened by General Zia, were remained so during his period. Substitution of Bengali Nationalism by communally oriented concept or Bangladeshi Nationalism was also allowed longevity during Ershad's Martial Law period.

7) By the judgment in the Fifth Amendment Case all the misdeeds perpetrated by Mushiaque-Zia duo have been eradicated and the Constitution has been restored to its original position as it was framed in 1912.

8) It is about time that the relicsleft behind by Martial Law perpetrators be completely swept away for good.

9) Steps should be taken by the government to remove the impeding factors the Appellate Division cited, in order to restore original Article 6, i.e, Banga Ice Nationalism.

10) Those who advised Ershad, including his law minister and Attorney General during his Martial Law period to keep the Constitution suspended, should also be tried.

Rule made absolute in part

310. For the reasons assigned above, the Rule is made absolute in part. The Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act 1986 is hereby declared to be thoroughly illegal, without lawful authority, void ab-initio and the same is, hence invalidated forthwith through this judgment, subject however, to the con- donation catalogued above, where they would apply.

311. Paragraph 19 of Fourth Schedule to the Constitution, is herby declared extinct where for the same must be effaced from the Constitution without delay.

312. The Respondents are further directed, having regard to the Appellate Division's modifying Order in the Fifth Amendment case, to take steps to clear the impediments, cited by the Appellate Division, with a view to eventual restoration of original Article 6.

313. The Respondents No.1 is directed to reflect this judgment by re-printing the Constitution.

314. No Order, however, is made to interfere with the petitioner's conviction or the sentence for the reasons stated above and hence he must surrender to his bail.

315. The learned Counsel for the petitioner applied for a certificate under Article 103(2)(a) of the Constitution and, as the case raises a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, we have no hesitation to issue the certificate asked for, which is hereby issued.

There is however, no Order as to cost.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Abu Zafor Siddique J: On an application filed under Article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution a Rule Nisi was issued in the following terms:

"Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Order No. 55 dated 22-6-2010 passed by the respondent No.2, the Artha Rin Adalat No.4, Dhaka in Artha Rin Case No. 153 of 2009 should not be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper."

2. By the Rule issuing order the proceeding of the Artha Execution Case No. 153 of 2010 arising out of Artha Rin case No. 153 of 2009 was stayed initially for 3 (three) months and subsequently extended for further period of 3 (three) months by order dated 6-4-2011.

3. Material facts necessary for disposal of the Rule, in short, are as under:

Respondent No.3, the Mercantile Bank filed the above noted Artha Rin Case stating that the petitioner No.1, Md Enayetur Rahman (defendant No. 1) as a businessman opened a SOD (FO) Account on 29-1-2004 with the Mercantile Bank Limited, Kowranbazar Branch, Dhaka (shortly the plaintiff- Bank). The petitioner obtained an SOD limit of Taka 65,00,000 (sixty five lakh) in terms of a sanction letter dated 29-1-2004. The loan was enhanced from time to time and lastly it was enhanced to Taka 4,85,00,000 (four crore eighty five lakh) only by sanction letter dated 8-7-2004. The credit facility was secured in two modes. The first mode of security was by getting lien of 8 FDRs issued by the Sonali Bank, Goran Branch, Dhaka (shortly, the Sonali Bank) in the names of the petitioner No.2, Mrs Khurshid Jahan and deceased Dr Abdul Kadir, being defendant Nos. 2 and 3 respectively of the Artha Rin Case. On the death of Dr Abdul Kadir, the present petitioners as, the heirs have been substituted as defendants. The order mode of security was the personal guarantee of defendants Nos. 2-8 of the said Artha Rin Case including deceased Dr Abdul Kadir, (defendant No.2). Thus the present petitioners Nos. 2-8 furnished personal guarantee for Taka 5,00,00,000 (five crore) by issuing letters of guarantee against the said FDRs issued by the Sonali Bank.

4. The plaintiff-Bank (respondent) before sanctioning the loan, requested the Manager of Sonali Bank to mark a lien on the FDRs. Accordingly, the then Manager, Sonali Bank, Mr Khandaker Hadi Imran confirmed by various letters that lien against each of the FDRs has been duly marked. The said manager also verified the signatures of the mentioned FDRs holders. After some time, the plaintiff-Bank (respondent) sent a letter to the Manager of the Sonali Bank to know the current value of the said FDRs, and the Manager of Sonali Bank working at that time informed by his letter dated 30-8-2004 that the total value of the FDRs was Taka 26,000 only.

5. So the plaintiff Bank lodged an FIR with the Tejgaon Police Station, being Case No. 91(8) 2004 against the defendant Nos. 1, 2, 3 and Mr Khandaker Hadi Imam, the Ex Manager of Sonali Bank, Goran Branch, Dhaka under sections 406, 420, 467, 468, 471 and 109 of the Penal Code. Thereafter the petitioner Nos. 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 on 2-10-2004 executed an undertaking in favour of the plaintiff Bank to the effect that they would pay the entire loan liabilities. But they failed to repay the loan. So the plaintiff Bank filed Artha Rin Suit No. 182 of 2006 in the Court of Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No.2, Dhaka for recovery of an amount of Taka 5,90,40,000 with interest. Subsequently, the suit was transferred to the 4th Artha Rin Adalat, (shortly, the Adalat) Dhaka and renumbered as Artha Rin Case No. 153 of 2009. Eventually, the suit was decreed ex-parte for an amount of Taka 5,90,40,000 (five crore ninety lakh forty thousand).

6. Pending hearing of Artha Rin Case, the petitioner Nos. 1 and 6, as defendant Nos. 1 and 7 respectively, filed two written statements, and the other petitioners as defendant Nos. 2-5 and 8 filed another joint written statement. All these defendants denied the material allegations of the plaintiff Bank. At the stage of pre-emptory hearing on 22-6-2010, the petitioner Nos. 1 to 7 filed an application under section 21 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (shortly, the Ain, 2003) before the Adalat for disposal of the case by settlement conference. The said application was rejected by the Adalat on the ground that section 21 of the Ain 2003 had already been repealed, and by the same order the case was taken up by the Adalat for ex-parte hearing and it was decreed ex-parte by the impugned Order No. 55 dated 22-6-2010.

7. Being aggrieved by the said order dated 22-6-2010 the petitioners have filed the present writ petition and obtained the Rule and stay order as stated above.

8. At the time of hearing the petitioners filed an application for modification of the cause title of the Writ Petition and for issuing a fresh Rule on the ground that the Rule issuing order dated 6-1-2011 does not contain any reference to the ex parte decree passed on the basis of the impugned order dated 22-6-2010 by which the Artha Rin Case was disposed of ex-parte.

9. We have considered the application in the light of the materials on record. It appears that the order impugned in this Writ Petition has been sufficiently narrated in the Rule issuing order dated 6-1-2011 as quoted earlier. So the reference to the exparte decree will not serve any purpose. Accordingly, we hold that the Rule issuing order need not be modified.

10. Md Ashrafuddin Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, supports the Rule and submits that the impugned order dated 22-6-2010 is illegal and arbitrary, because exposition of any witness of the plaintiff bank was not recorded and that the written statements along with the affidavits of the defendant-petitioners were not considered.

11. In this regards Mr Khan, the learned Advocate, drew our attention to section 6(4) of the Ain, 2003.

12. Mr Khan, the learned Advocate next sub- mitted that the expression কেবল এইরুপ হলফনামা-যুক্ত আরজি বা লিখিত জবাব ও সংশ্লিষ্ট দালিলিক প্রমানাদি বিশ্লেষণ করিয়া রায় বা আদেশ প্রদান করিবে” occurring in the section 6 (4) means that the Adalat should have considered both the plaint and written statements and that the words  আরজি বা লিখিত জনাব” are to be read conjunctively. In this connection the learned Advocate refers to the following comments of Mr Mahmudul Islam made in the book "Interpretation of Statutes and Documents" First Published February, 2009 page-83.

"Conjunctive and disjunctive words Ordinarily the word and is conjunctive and the word 'or' is disjunctive, but to give effect to the manifest intention of the legislature 'and' can be construed as 'or' and vice versa. If the literal reading of the words produces an unintelligible or absurd result 'and' may be read for 'or' and 'or' for 'and' even though the result so modifying the words is less favorable to the subject provided that the intention of the legislature is quite clear, but if such reading produces grammatical distortion and makes no sense 'and' cannot be read for 'or' and 'or' cannot be read for 'and'. Such reading of one for the other is not possible where the meaning of the relevant provision is clear or if such construction would operate to charge the law."

13. Mr Khan, the learned Advocate, next submits that the petitioners deposited Taka 2,67,16,500 on various dates and lastly they deposited a further amount of Taka 4,10,000. But without adjusting those amounts the plaintiff Bank made untrue statements and filed the Artha Rin Case.

14. Mr Khan further submitted that on 22-6- 2010 the petitioners were present in the Adalat by filing an application under section 21 of the Ain, 2000 and after hearing the Adalat rejected the same and, without complying with the requirement of section 19 (1) by way of calling out (ডাকিয়া)  the defendants, the Adalat took up the case for exparte disposal and decided it on the basis of the plaint and affidavit of the plaintiff, and thus violated sections 6 (4) and 19 (1) of the Ain, 2003.

15. Mr Khan lastly submitted that since the defendants in their written statements denied claims of the plaintiff bank, the Adalat is required to frame issues under section 13 in view of the pleadings and affidavits of both sides, even if they are absent, and therefore the exparte decree was without jurisdiction. But the Adalat neither framed issues nor considered the written statements of the defendants and therefore such a decree may be challenged in Writ Jurisdiction of this Court.

16. In support of his submission. Mr Khan referred to the unreported judgment dated 23-3-2010 passed by a Division Bench of this Court and thereby disposing of Writ Petition Nos. 6501 of 2009,6502 of 2009, 6503 of 2009 and 6504 of 2009. The learned Advocate drew our attention to the following observations made in that judgment:

"We have examined section 13 of Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. This section has conferried power or jurisdiction upon the Artha Rin Adalat to dispose of the suit without holding trial only when the defendants admit the claim of the plaintiff financial institution. When the borrower defendant does not admit the claim of the plaintiff financial institution, the Artha Rin Adalat does not have or cannot have any power to dispose of that suit under section 13 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. Where the defendant borrower denies the claim of the plaintiff financial institution, the Artha Rin Adalat has no power or jurisdiction to dispose of the suit under section 13 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 without holding trial. If the Artha Rin Adalat disposes of any suit under section 13 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 where the claim of the plaintiff is not admitted that will be beyond jurisdiction of the Adalat."

17. Mr Khan the learned Advocate also referred to the case of Md Arfan Uddin Akhand with Mr Kamal Uddin Akhand vs Joint District Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Gazipur and another, reported in 15 BLT 2007, 343 wherein a similar view was taken as quoted above.

18. Mr Khan, the learned Advocate also drew our attention to the following observations of their lordships of the Appellate Division in the case of Tafijul Huq Sarker vs Bangladesh, reported in 4 MLR (AD) 19 = 3 BLC (AD) 135:

"Thus the consistent view of our Courts is that an alternative remedy by way of appeal under a statute will not be a bar to a writ petition under Article. 102(2) of the Constitution (which corresponds to Article 98(2) of 1962 Constitution) if there is a non relatable precondition for bringing the appeal .

19. In support of the principle enunciated in the above noted cases, Mr Khan the learned Advocate further referred the case of Collector of Customs, Custom House Chittagong vs M Hannan, reported in 10 BLD (AD) 216 = 42 DLR (AD) 167 and the case of Government of the People s Republic of Bangladesh vs Iqbal Hasan Mahmud alias Iqbal Hasan Mahmud Tuku, reported in 60 DLR (AD) 147 wherein similar view was expressed with regard to the manner of exparte disposal of an Artha Rin Case.

20. In reply, Mr Zaforullah Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr Nafiz Ahamed Chowdhury for the decree-holder Bank, with reference to the affidavit-in-opposition, submitted that the Bank allowed the petitioners (defendants) ample time to repay their outstanding loan liabilities, but they willfully resorted to delaying tactics.

21. Mr Chowdhury, the learned Advocate further submitted that the learned Judge of the Adalat duly applied his judicial mind and lawfully decreed the suit exparte.

22. Mr Chowdhury, the learned Advocate next submitted that the present writ petition is not maintainable as the petitioners neither preferred any appeal against the impugned exparte order and decree under section 41 nor did they take any step to set aside the exparte order and decree under section 19 of the Ain, 2003.

23. Mr Chowdhury, the learned Advocate particularly drew our attention to the legislative intent as reflected in section 19 (1) of the Ain, 2003.

24. He argued that the petitioners were physically present at the time of passing the ex-parte order. Because after hearing the petitioners, the Adalat rejected their application under section 21 of the Ain, and then by the same order took up the case for ex-parte hearing and it was disposed of ex-parte decreeing the suit in terms of the impugned Order No. 55 dated 22-6-2010. In such circumstances calling out the petitioners would be a farcical and unnecessary exercise and accordingly the Adalat did not record the word ডাকিয়া in that order.

25. He further drew our attention to section 6 (4) of the Ain, 2003 as quoted earlier and submits that a decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat can be challenged in a Writ Petition on the ground of fraud and lack of jurisdiction. But in this case there is no allegation that fraud was practiced upon the Adalat by the Bank or that the Adalat had no jurisdiction to pass the exparte order and decree, and therefore the instant writ petition is not maintainable.

26. In support of his submission Mr Chowdhury referred to two unreported decisions of a Division Bench of this Court in (1) the case of Ms Farhad Banu vs Artha Rin Adalat No.4, Dhaka and others, and (2) GM Saleh Ahamed and others vs Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka and others.

27. In respect of non-maintainability of writ petition against a decree passed by an Artha Rin Adalat, Mr Chowdhury submitted that an appeal is the proper and efficacious remedy and that the condition of deposit of 50% or 10% of the decreetal amount is not a legal ground for filing a Writ Petition under Article 102 of the Constitution.

28. In support of such submission Mr Chowdhury referred to the decision in the case of Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) vs Artha Rin Adalat, reported in 59 DLR (AD) 6, in which their lordships observed as follows:

"In view of the decisions quoted above we are led to irresponsible conclusion that there being specific remedy in the statute for filing appeal against the judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain in the present case the defendant not availing of the aforesaid remedy cannot maintain the writ petition. Since we find that the writ petition was not maintainable we do not like to embark upon other submissions made on behalf of the defendant petitioner touching the merits of the cases."

29. Mr Chowdhury also referred to the case of Gazi M Towfic vs Agrani Bank, reported in 54 DLR (AD) 6 wherein similar view as taken.

30. We have examined the writ petition, the affidavit-in-opposition, and other materials on record as well as the impugned order and considered the submission of the learned Advocates of both the sides.

31. It appears that the following legal issues need to be considered in this case:

(1) Whether the ex-parte decree was passed by the Adalat without jurisdiction, by way of not considering the written statements and the related affidavits of the defendants, and whether the Adalat should have framed and considered issues based on the pleadings.

(2) Whether impugned order was passed illegally, because of the fact that the Adalat did not record any finding as to whether the defendants were found absent after calling as required by section 6 (4) of the Ain, 2003.

(3) Whether the writ petition is maintain- able in view of the fact that an appeal could have been preferred or a separate proceeding could have been initiated for setting aside the ex parte decree, under section 41 or 19(2) respectively of the Ain, 2003.

32. For consideration of the above issues we may first look into the order-sheet of the Adalat (Annex-D to the writ petition). It appears that after filing of the several written statements by the different set of defendants, the Adalat framed issues by order dated 30-9-2008. So it cannot be said that the Adalat failed to exercise its jurisdiction on this aspect.

33. Next comes the question of the legal responsibility of the Adalat to consider the issues so framed, and the written statements supported by affidavits filed by the defendant. For considering this aspect of the case we firstly need to look into exparte order dated 22-6-2010 which is quoted below:

৫৫

২২-৬-১০

অদ্য PH এর জন্য দিন ধার্য্য আছে। বাদীপক্ষ হাজির।

১-৫/৮ নং বিবাদী পক্ষ এক দরখাস্ত দায়ের করিয়া বর্নিত কারণে অর্থঋণ আদালত আইন ২০০৩ এর ২১ ধারা মোতাবেক মিমাংসা সভায় মাধ্যমে মোকাদ্দমা নিষ্পত্তিকরার প্রর্থনা করিয়াছে। শুনিলাম বিাদী পক্ষ অর্থ ঋণ আদালত আইনের ২১ ধারাতে ২১ ধারা মতে দরখাস্ত সহ দাখিল করেছে। কিন্তু ২১ ধারা বর্তমানে নেই সে জন্য দরখাস্তটি না মনজুর করা গেল। (VOP)

বাদীপক্ষ ফিরিস্তি দ্বারা কাগজ পত্রের ফটোকপিও সইমোহর নকল দাখিল করিয়াছেন। নথি পেশ করা হইল।

পরে বিবাদীপক্ষ আর কোন পদক্ষেপ গ্রহন করেনি। সে জন্য মামলাটি একতরফা শুনানীর জন্য গ্রহন করা হলো।

বিজ্ঞ কৌশুলীর বক্তব্য শুনলাম। উল্লেখ্য যে, অর্থঋণ আদালত আইন, ২০০৩ এর ৬(৪) ধারার বিধানে বাদীপক্ষ মোকদ্দমা দায়েকালে আরজি ও কাগজাদির সাথে এফিডেভিট দাখিল করলে মোকত্তমা একতরফা বা তাৎক্ষনিক নিষ্পত্তির ক্ষেত্রে কোন সাক্ষীকে পরীক্ষা ব্যতিরেকে হলফনামাযুক্ত আরজি ওদালিলিক প্রমানদি বিশ্লেষন করে রায় বা আদেশ প্রদান করা যায়।

নথি, বাদীপক্ষ তাদের দীবির সমর্থনে দাখিলকৃত ঋণ আবেদন পত্র, মঞ্জুরীপত্র সহ অন্যন্য চার্জড ডকুমেন্ট এবং ব্যাংক হিসাব পত্র পর্যালোচনা করলাম। উক্ত কাগজাদি পর্যালোচনায় বাদী ব্যাংকে দাবী প্রমানিত হওয়ায় বাদী ব্যাংক গত ৩০-০৯-২০০৬ ইং তারিখ পর্যন্ত ৫,৯০,৪০,০০০ (পাঁচ কোটি নব্বই লক্ষ চল্লিশ হাজার টাকা) বিবাদীগণের নিকট প্রাপ্য হয়। যা বিবাদীগন পরিশোধে বাধ্য প্রদত্ত কোর্ট ফি সঠিক।

অতএব আদেশ হল যে,

এ মোকদ্দমা একতরফাসূত্রে বিবাদীগনের বিরুদ্ধে খরচসহ ডিক্রী হয়। বিবাদীগনকে গত ৩০-৯-২০০৬ ইং তারিখপর্যন্ত ৫,৯০,৪০,০০০ (পাঁচ কোটি নব্বই লক্ষ চল্লিশ হাজার) টাকা এবং উক্ত তারিখের পর হতে ডিক্রী কৃত টকা আদায় না হওয়া পর্যন্ত অর্থঋণ আদালত আইন,২০০৩ এর ৫০(২) ধারা মতে নির্ধারিত সুদ বা ক্ষেত্রে মতে শুনাফাসহ মুদয় টাকা আগমী ৬০ (ষাট) দিবসের মধ্যে ডিক্রীদার ব্যাংক বরাবরে পরিশোধ করতে নির্দেশ প্রদান করা হল। ব্যর্থতায় ডিক্রীদার ব্যাংক আইনানুগ পস্থায় ডিক্রীকৃত টাকা আদায় করে নিতে পারবে।”

34. It is evident from the impugned order as quoted above that the learned Judge of the Adalat heard the defendant side on the application for settlement-conference under section 21 of the Ain, 2003 and rejected it on the ground that the said section 21 has already been repealed. Then the Adalat disposed of the case on consideration of the plaint and the affidavits filed therewith. Evidently the Adalat did not consider the written statements. In doing so he relied on section 6 (4) of the Ain, 2003.

35. The legal issue is whether the Adalat was under a legal duty to consider the written statements of the defendant petitioners, when they did not participate in the hearing of the case or as the Adalat stated পরে বিবাদীপক্ষ আর কোন পদক্ষেপ গ্রহন করেনি।”

36. Section 6 (4) of the Ain, 2003 needs to be examined and it is quoted below (underlines added):

৬। বিচার পদ্ধতি-(১),(২),(৩)

(৪) এই আইনের অদীন অর্থঋণ আদালতে মামলা নিষ্পত্তির ক্ষেত্রে উপ-ধারা (২) ও(৩) এর বিধান অনুযায়ী সংযুক্ত হলফনামা (Affidavit) মৌখিক সাক্ষ্য (substantive evidence) হিসাবে গন্য হইবে, এবং আদালত কোন মামলার একতরফা বা তাৎক্ষনিক নিষ্পত্তি ক্ষেত্রে কোন সাক্ষীকে পরীক্ষা ব্যতিরেকে, কেবল এইরুপ হলফনামা-যুক্তি আরজি বা লিখিত বাব ও সংক্ষিপ্ত দালিলিক প্রমাণাদি বিশ্লেষণ করিয়া রায় বা আদেশ প্রদান করিবে।

37. In our view section 6 (4) generally employees the Court to dispose of a case by way of considering the plaint along with affidavit and writ- ten statement, and by treating the concerned affidavits and the documents filed therewith as substantive evidence. The emphasis of this provision is clearly on the pleadings, and the affidavits and the documents filed, without formal examination of witnesses. But section 6 (4) does not prescribe the procedure to be followed in a situation requiring exparte disposal. This is regulated by section 19 as quoted below :

ধারা -১৯। একতরফা ডিক্রী সম্পর্কিত বিধান।-

(১) মামলার শুনানীর জন্য ধার্য কোন তারিখে বিবাদী আদালতে অনুপস্থিত থাকিলে, কিংবা মামলা শুনানীর জন্য গৃহীত হইবার পর ডাকিয়া বিবাদীকে উপস্থিত পাওয়া না গেলে, আদালতে মামলা একতরফা সূত্রে নিষ্পত্তি করিবে।

(২) কোন মামলা একতরফা সূত্রে ডিক্রী হইলে, বিবাদী উক্ত একতরফা ডিক্রীর তারিখের অথবা উক্ত একতরফা ডিক্রী সম্পর্কে অবগত হইবার ৩০ (ত্রিশ) দিবসের মধ্যে, উপ-ধারা (৩) এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, উক্ত একতরফা ডিক্রী রদের জন্য দরখাস্ত করিতে পারিবেন। (৩) উপ-ধারা (২) এর বিধান অনুযায়ী দরাখাস্ত দাখিলের ক্ষেত্রে বিবাদীকে উক্ত দরখাস্ত দাখিলের তারিখের পরবর্তী ১৫ (পনের) দিবসের মধ্যে ডিক্রীকৃত অর্থের ১০% এর সমপরিমান টাকা বাদীর বাদীর সেই পরিমাণের জন্য স্বীকৃতিস্বরুপ নগদ সংশ্লিষ্ট আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানে, অথবা জামানত-স্বরুপ ব্যাংক ড্রাফট, পে-অর্ডার বা অন্য কোন প্রকার নগদায়নযোগ্য বিনিময়ে দলিল (Negotiable Instrument) আকারে জামানত হিসাবে আদালতে জমাদান করিতে হইবে।

(৪) .......................................................

(৫) .........................................................

(৬) অর্থ-ঋণ আদালতে বিচারাধীন কোন মামলা, বাদীর অনুপস্থি বা ব্যর্থতা হেতু খারিজ করা যাইবে না, এবং এইরুপ ক্ষেত্রে আদালত, নথিতে উপস্থাপিত কাগজাদি পরীক্ষা করিয়া শুনাগুন বিশ্লেষণে মামলা নিষ্পত্তি করিবে।”

38. The language employed in section 19(1) requires that on the date of hearing, the Adalat can proceed to dispose of the case exparte if the defendant is found absent (ডাকিয়া পাওয়া না গেলে)

39. The impugned order shows that the defendant side participated in the hearing of their application which was rejected and by the same order the Adalat took up the case tor hearing, but the defendant side did not participate in the hearing of the case.

40. From the course of events, as expressed in the impugned order particularly the words আর কোন পদক্ষেপ গ্রহন করেনি” it appears that the defendant neither prayed for time nor otherwise marked their presence for the purpose of hearing of the case.

41. In such a situation the physical act of calling ডাকিয়া”, of the defendants would be a fruitless exercise. So non-recording of a finding about absence of the defendant-with any expression such as  ডাকিয়া” in the impugned order does not render the impugned order as being violative of section 19(1).

42. The other aspect of the case is whether the Adalat should have considered the written statements and the issues framed. In our view, when the defendant side did not participate in the hearing, it means that they were not agitating their claims in the written statements. The word একতরফাসূত্রে” in section 19 (1) clearly indicates that the Adalat was not required to consider the case of the defendants as made out in the written statements or the issues earlier framed, based on the plaint and the written statements.

43. The point raised by the learned Advocate for the petitioners (defendant) with regard to the import of the expression হলফনামাযুক্ত আরজী বা জবাব” is not acceptable to us. His point is that the word "বা" is to be read as a conjunctive expression and thereby indicating that even if the defendant is absent his written statement and affidavit are to be considered by the Adalat.

44. It is noted that the said expression হলফনামাযুক্ত আরজী বা জবাব” has been used in the context of কোন মামলা একতরফাসূত্রে বা তাৎক্ষনিক নিষ্পত্তির ক্ষেত্রে” So the question is, whether. the expression হলফনামাযুক্ত আরজী বা জবাব relates only to a situation of exparte disposal or only to a situation of instant disposal.

45. In case of an exparte disposal situation, if the word বা is taken in the disjunctive sense, then the expression আরজী বা জবাব would mean that the Adalat must consider either the plaint only or the written statement only. That is clearly absurd. Because that would render the section 19(6) nugatory, because this provision requires consideration of the plaintiff's case on merit even in the absence of plaintiff.

46. Again if the word "বা" is taken in the conjunctive sense in an exparte disposal situation, it will mean that even if the defendant is absent, the Adalat must consider both the plaint and written statement. This would clearly render section 19(1) nugatory, as this section requires ex-parte disposal (একতরফাসূত্রে) in the absence of defendant.

47. The other situation is তাৎক্ষনিক নিষ্পত্তির ক্ষেত্রে” | This expression does not clearly indicate the presence or absence of any of the parties. It may mean presence of anyone of the parties or of both parties. In anyone of such situations the expression হলফনামাযুক্ত আরজী বা জবাব and consideration thereof would render section 19(1) and 19(6) nugatory as discussed above.

48. In our view the intention of the expression হলফনামাযুক্ত আরজী বা জবাব occurring in section 6(4) is that the plaint along with affidavit, is to be considered and, where necessary the written statement and affidavit, if any, are also to be considered. So the proper expression in Bangla might be হলফনামাযুক্ত আরজী এবং যথাযথ ক্ষেত্রে বিবাদীর হলফনামাযুক্ত জবাব”।

49. The intent of section 6(4) is not to exempt the defendant from remaining present, but to give the parties an opportunity not to produce witnesses for the purpose of proving their case by way of formally stating it on the witness dock and to prove their documents, as in an ordinary Civil Case.

50. The above view taken by us is supported by the language of sub-section 19(6), which provides that when plaintiff is absent the Adalat cannot dismiss the suit. In such a situation, the Court is under a legal responsibility to consider the merit of the plaint and affidavit and also the documents filed.

51. It is noticeable that section 19(6) speaks of a situation where only the plaintiff is absent as reflected in the words  বাদীর অনুপস্থিতি বা ব্যর্থতার হেতু।” The provision further speaks of  গুনাগুন বিশ্লেষণে মামলা নিষ্পত্তি করিবে”।

52. In reality, if the plaintiff is absent or fails to appear, there may be two situations-namely-(1) plaintiff is absent but defendant is present, or (2) both the parties are absent. However section 19(6) is silent about presence or absence of the defendant. So what is the real intention of section 19(6)?

53. In our view, in both situations the case of the plaintiff must be considered on merit, even if he is absent. For such consideration, section 6(4) comes in aid of the Court enabling it to consider the plaint, affidavit and the documents. However if the defendant is present his case is also to be considered in the either of the two modes of disposal; namely? by way of production of formal evidence through witness, or under section 6(4) i.e. without examination of witnesses.

54. But if the defendant is also absent, it would be unfair to consider only the case of the absentee plaintiff and not of the absentee defendant. In our view, the case of both the parties should be considered, and not of the plaintiff alone.

55. A question follows that, if the rule of fairness requires the Adalat to consider the merit of the case of the absentee defendant under section 19(6) when plaintiff is absent, then why the same rule of fairness will not be followed under section 19(1) when the plaintiff is present, but defendant is absent.

<u>56. In our view, section 19(1), puts a clear bar to consider the case of defendant as evident from the word  একতরফাসূত্রে” This bar may appear to be unfair compared to the advantage given to the plaintiff under section 19(6). But the legislative intent as reflected in section 19(1) cannot be interpreted otherwise than by applying the literal rule of interpretation, which requires that when language is clear, it has be followed unless it results in an absurdity. Undoubtedly 'unfair' and 'absurd' do not bear the same meaning or consequence.</u>

57. The facts of the case show that the Adalat has exercised its jurisdiction as a competent Court, so far the framing of issues and the passing of the exparte decree in the absence of defendant are concerned.

58. Again as interpreted by us, the Adalat is not under a legal responsibility to consider the written statement, affidavit and documents of the defendant when he is absent but plaintiff is present. There was no breach of section 6(4) or section 19(6) of the Ain, 2003 in passing the exparte decree.

59. So the principles laid down in the case reported in 15 BLT 343 and the unreported decision referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner are not applicable to the present case. Accordingly we hold that the Adalat was within its jurisdiction in passing the impugned order and exparte decree.

60. What is more important the defendant petitioners had an alternative forum for the purpose of filing an application under section 19(2) of the Ain for setting aside the ex-parte order and decree. The petitioners have another remedy in the form of preferring an appeal under section 41 of the Ain, 2003 of course subject to limitation. But they have not yet availed themselves of any of those remedies. Section 41 runs as follows:

ধারা-৪১। আপীল দায়ের ও নিষ্পত্তি সম্পর্কিত বিশেষ বিধান।-(১) মামলার কোন পক্ষ, কোন অর্থঋণ আদালতের আদেশ বা ডিক্রী দ্বারা সংক্ষুব্ধ হইলে, যদি ডিক্রীকৃত টাকার পরিমান ৫০ (পঞ্চাশ) লক্ষ টাকা অপেক্ষা অধিক হয়, তাহা হইল উপ-ধারা (২) এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, পরবর্তী ৩০ (ত্রিশ) দিবসের মধ্য হাইকোর্ট বিভাগে, এবং যদি ডিক্রীকৃত টাকার পরিমাণ ৫০ (পঞ্চাশ) লক্ষ অথবা তদঅপেক্ষা কম হয়, তাহা হইলে জেলা জজ আদালতে আপীল করিতে পারিবেন।

(২) আপীলকারী, ডিক্রীকৃত টাকার পরিমাণের ৫০% এর সমপরিমান টাকা বাদীর দাবীর আংশিক স্বীকৃতিস্বরুপ নগদ ডিক্রীদার আর্তিক প্রতিষ্ঠানে অথবা বাদীর দাবী স্বীকার না করিলে জামানতস্বরুপ ডিক্রী প্রদানকারী আদালতে জমা করিয়া উক্তরুপ জমার প্রমাণ দরখাস্ত বা আপীল মেমোর সহিত আদালতে দাখিল না করিলে, উপ-ধারা (১) এর অদীন কোন আপীল কার্যার্থে গৃহীত হইবে না।

(৩) উপ-ধারা (২) এর বিধান সত্ত্বেও, বিবাদী-দায়িক ইতিমধ্যে ১৯ (৩) ধারার বিধান মতে ১০% (দশ মংতাশ) পরিশান টাকা নগদ অথবা জামানত হিসাবে জমা করিয়া থাকিলে, অত্র ধারার অধীনে আপীল দায়েরের ক্ষেত্রে উক্ত ১০% (দশ শতাংশ) টাকা উপরি-উল্লিখিত ৫০% (পঞ্চাশ শতাংশ) টাকা হইতে বাদ হইবে।

61. So, we agree with Mr Zaforullah Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the Respondent No. 3 being the plaintiff Bank, that the writ petition is not maintainable in view of the fact that there are alternative and efficacious remedy available to the petitioners. The principles laid down in the 59 DLR and 54 DLR Cases as referred to by Chowdhury and earlier quoted are applicable to the present case.

62. The petitioners have resorted to a wrong forum by invoking the writ jurisdiction of this Court. They can still avail the remedy at least under section 41, of course subject to the limitation issue.

63. In view of the discussion made above we hold that the present writ petition is not maintain- able.

64. We find no merit in this Rule

65. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

66. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

Communicate the judgment to respondent No. 2 at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Sheikh Abdul Awal J : As common question of facts and law are involved in these writ petitions they are heard together and are being disposed of by this common judgment which will govern all the writ petitions.

2. In all these Rules the respondents were called upon to show cause as to why the section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments (amendment) Act, 2006 putting an embargo in filing of appeal against the order of conviction and sentence under sub-section (1) of section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act unless an amount of money not less than 50% of the cheque amount is deposited in the Court shall not be declared to be void as it conflicts with the right of appeal as enshrined in section 410 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

3. Writ Petition No. 3058 of 2008 is from judgment and order dated 12-2-2008 passed by the respondent No.3, Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong in Sessions Case No. 64 of 2007 arising out of CR Case No. 150 of 2006 (Bandor Zone) convicting the petitioner under section 138(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act and sentencing him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 6(six) months and to pay a fine of Taka 12,30,600.

4. Writ Petition No. 6720 of 2008 is from the judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 16-10-2006 passed by the respondent No.3, Metropolitan Assistant Sessions Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Metropolitan Sessions Case No. 426 of 2006 arising out of CR Case No. 384 of 2005 convicting the petitioner under section 138(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and sentencing him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for a period of 1 (one) month and to pay a fine of Taka 3,00,000.

5. Writ Petition No. 6721 of 2008 is from judgment and order dated 16-10-2006 passed by the respondent No.3, Metropolitan Assistant Sessions Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Metropolitan Session Case No. 355 of 2006 arising out of CR Case No. 385 of 2005 convicting the petitioner under section 138(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act and sentencing him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 1(one) months with a fine of Taka 1,50,000.

6. Writ Petition No. 5530 of 2008 is from judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 16-3-2008 passed by the respondent No. 2, Joint Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Metropolitan Sessions Case No. 474 of 2006 arising out of CR Case No. 2398 of2005 convicting the petitioner under section 138(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act and sentencing him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for, 1(one) year and to pay a fine of Taka 8,00,000.

7. Writ Petition No. 8333 of 2008 is from judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 23-10-2008 passed by the respondent No. 3, Additional Sessions Judge, 1st Court, Comilla in Sessions Case No. 181 of 2008 arising out of CR Case No. 105 of 2007 convicting the petitioner under section 138(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act and sentencing him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 1 (one) year and to pay a fine of Taka 13,50,000.

8. Writ Petition No. 2463 of 2008 is from judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 6-3-2008 passed by the respondent No.4, Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong in Sessions Case No. 300 of 2007 arising out of CR Case No. 391 of 2006 (Double Mooring Zone) convicting the petitioner under section 138(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act and sentencing him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 6(six) months and to pay a fine of Taka 2,35,20,000.

9. Writ Petition No. 2461 of 2008 is from judgment and order dated 6-3-2008 passed by the respondent No.4, Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong in Sessions Case No. 438 of 2007 arising out of CR Case No. 1564 of 2004 convicting the petitioner under section 138 (1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act and sentencing him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 6(six) months and to pay a fine of Taka 1,00,20,000.

10. Writ Petition No. 5716 of 2008 is from judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 9-3-2008 passed by the respondent No.2, Additional Sessions Judge, 2nd Court, Narayanganj in Sessions Case No. 342 of 2006 arising out of CR Case No.6 of 2006 convicting the petitioner under section 138(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act and sentencing him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 1 (one) year with a fine of Taka 60,00,000.

11. Writ Petition No. 3524 of 2008 is from judgment and order dated 13-11-2007 passed by the respondent No.2, Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong in Sessions Case No. 522 of 2007 arising out of CR Case No. 76 of 2007 convicting the petitioner under section 138(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act and sentencing him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 6(six) months and to pay a fine of Taka 33,74,337.

12. In all these writ petitions the learned Advocates on behalf of the petitioners after placing their respective cases asserted the provisions of section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act (as amended on 9-2-2006) mainly on 3 (three) counts.

Firstly, that the statutory law must be comprehensive in its nature and should provide adequate provision in respect of trial and appeal but the provisions of section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act is harsh, unreasonable, oppressive and arbitrary.

Secondly, that the petitioners were tried by Sessions Judge/Additional Sessions Judge/Joint District Judge/Assistant Sessions Judge under the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure and section 410 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides appeal against judgment and order of conviction as a matter of right but section 138A of the Act provides a restriction in filing of appeal in case of any order of conviction and sentence under section 138(1) of the Negotiables Instrument Act unless an amount of money not less than 50% of the cheque amount is deposited in the Court which awarded the sentence which is not only unconstitutional and also curtailment of the statutory right of appeal of the petitioners and it causes hardship to the petitioner/s and, as such, the provisions of section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Act, 2006 is liable to be declared null and void.

Thirdly, that the provisions of section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act was promulgated on 9-2-2006 and the cases were filed prior to insertion of the said section, in those cases the provisions of section 138A of the Act cannot be applicable retrospectively.

13. Mr M Faruque, the learned Advocate appearing for the complainant-respondent No.3 in Writ Petition No. 3524 of 2008 submits that the provision of section 138A of the Act is not ultra vires to the Constitution or contrary to Articles 27, 31, 40, and 42 of the Constitution inasmuch as the right to file appeal is not a fundamental right but it is a statutory right and therefore, it cannot be said that the petitioner's right has been curtailed by provision of section 138A of the Act. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Metropolitan Additional Sessions Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong on consideration of the entire materials on record rightly found the petitioner guilty under section 138 of the Act and sentenced him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 6(six) months and to pay a fine of Taka 33,74,337. He finally adds that by now it has been well settled specially in Artha Rin Adalat Ain that the provision for depositing 50% of the decretal amount at the time of preferring appeal is well maintained and it cannot be said that the defaulters have lost their fundamental right as guaranteed by the Constitution.

14. Mr M Faruque in support of his submission has relied on the decisions reported in 2 BLC (AD) 87, 2006 BLD (AD) 172 = 59 DLR (AD) 26, 59 DLR (AD) 26, 13 BLC 686, 1997 BLD (AD) 35 = 2 BLC (AD) 35, 1 MLR (AD) 66 = 48 DLR (AD) 6, 48 DLR (AD) 6, 12 BLC 22, 2 BLC 49, 52 DLR4 and 52 DLR (AD) 122.

15. Mr AJ Mohammad AIi, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No.5 in Writ Petition No. 2461 of 2008 and Writ Petition No. 2463 of 2008 at the very outset referring a decision reported in 13 BLC 686 opposes the Rule.

16. Mr Kamruzzaman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No.4 in Writ Petition No. 3058 of 2008 submits that right to file appeal is not a fundamental right, but it is a statutory right. The petitioner's right has not been curtailed for such pre-condition provided in section 138A of the Act to deposit 50% of the cheque amount at the time preferring appeal in the Court and moreover, the said deposited amount is refundable. Mr Kamruzzaman, the learned Advocate in support of his submission relied on the decisions reported in 44 DLR (AD) 260,1990 BLD (AD) 190 = 42 DLR (AD) 219 and 2006 BLD (AD) 250 = 59 DLR (AD) 6.

17. In order to appreciate the legal aspects involved in this case it would be useful, if we trace that scheme and purpose of the amendment of Negotiable Instruments Act on 9-2-2006. Section 138 of the Act provides for special forum for realisation of dishonoured/unpaid cheque money from the drawer by special method. The law is by now well settled that the appeal is a continuation of the suit/case and there is no dispute that in the society a class of borrowers or drawers in taking shelter of this principles of law deliberately used to drag the appeal for an indefinite period in order to hang the process of realisation of loan money or unpaid cheque's money for an indefinite period in which the payee or the holder of the cheque not only suffers a lot also the process of realisation of cheque amount or loan money falls into dark Keeping the said view in mind the legislature in applying their wisdom made amendment in section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act providing to deposit not less than 50% of the dishonoured cheque at the time of tiling an appeal in the Court which awarded the sentence.

18. We have in this connection gone through the section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments (amendment) Act, 2006 which runs as follows:

138A. Restriction in respect of appeal- Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, no appeal against any order of sentence under sub-section (1) of section 138 shall lie, unless an amount of not less than fifty percent of the amount of the dishonourd cheque is deposited before filing the appeal in the Court which awarded the sentence.

19. A similar precondition has been provided in Artha Rin Adalat Ain. The Legislature in applying their wisdom put similar type of restriction in section 7 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 and later on in section 41 (2) of the new Ain namely, the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003.

20. Section 7 of the Artha Rin AdalatAin, 1990 is reproduced herein below:

(৩) অর্থ ঋন আদালতের কোন রায় বা ডিক্রির বিরুদ্ধে কোন বিবাদী আপীল দায়ের করিতে ইচ্ছুক হইলে এবং তিনি উক্ত রায় বা ডিক্রির বিরুদ্ধে-

(অ) ধারা ৬(২) এর অধীন দরখাস্ত এবং উপ-ধারা (২) (ক) এর অধীন আপীল করিয়া থাকিলে, উক্ত দ্বারা ৬(২) এবং উপ-ধারা (২) (ক) এর অধীন জমাকৃত অর্থ বাদ দিয়া মূল মামলায় ডিক্রিকৃত অবশিষ্ট অর্থের অন্ততঃ অর্ধেক অর্থ ডিক্রি প্রদানকারী আদালতে জমা করিয়া উপধারা (১) এ নির্ধারিত সময়ের মধ্যে হাইকোর্ট বিভাগে আপীল দায়ের করিতে পারিবেন।

(৪) কোন বিবাদী উপ-ধারা (২) এবং এ নির্ধারিত অর্থ ডিক্রি প্রদানকারী আদালতে জমা না করিলে বিবাদীর আপীল গ্রহনযোগ্য হইবে না।

21. Section 41(2) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 is reproduced herein bellow:

আপিলকারী, ডিক্রীকৃত টাকার পরিমানের ৫০% এর সমপরিমান টাকা বাদীর দাবীর আংশিক স্বীকৃতিস্বরুপ নগদ ডিক্রীদার আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠানে, অথবা বাদীর দাবী স্বীকার না করিলে, জামানতস্বরুপ ডিক্রী প্রদানকারী আদালতে জমা করিয়া উক্তরুপ জমার প্রমাণ দরখাস্ত বা আপীলের মেমোর সহিত আদালতে দাখিল না করিলে, উপ-ধারা (১) এর অধীন কোন আপীল কার্যার্থে গৃহীত হইবে না।

22. The provisions of those sections were challenged up to the Appellate Division unsuccessfully.

23. In the case of Md Nur Islam vs Agrani Bank reported in 1 MLR (AD) 373, it has been decided that deposit of 50% decretal amount as a precondition is mandatory both in the case of an appeal or an application for setting aside an ex parte decree.

24. In the case of Anisur Rahman vs Bangladesh reported in 12 BLC 22, it has been held as follows:

"We are of the view that the provision of section 41 (2) of the Ain or any part of the same is not violative of Articles 27, 31, 40 or 42 of the Constitution. Similar view has been taken in the case of Chandpur Jute Supplier reported in 2 BLC 49 and in other cases decided by this Court."

25. In the case of AHN Kabir vs Bangladesh reported in 13 BLC 686, it has been held as follows:

"Therefore, depositing 50% of the face value of the dishonoured cheque cannot be said to be illegal in case of a pending case ended up in conviction and sentence."

26. Negotiable Instruments Act is a special law. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act provided certain pre-condition for bringing prosecution against the drawer of the unpaid cheque. Under section 138(c) of the Act, 30 days' time is given for payment of the amount due under the cheque from the date of receipt of notice regarding dishonour of cheque issued by the payee. The payee has to wait for 30 days anticipating payment of the amount by the drawer. After the expiry of 30 days, if the drawer does not pay the amount, the cause of action starts 31st day onwards. The limitation to file a complaint as prescribed under section 142(b) of the Act is one month. On trial, both the parties are entitled to adduce evidence both oral and documentary. The trial Judge in deciding the case under the Act has to consider first, whether the cheque in question was dishonoured and whether after fulfilling the legal requirement of section 138 (b) and (c) of the Negotiable Instruments Act the case was filed or not. In that view of the matter, there is little chance of success in the appeal on the part of the drawer of the unpaid cheque, although, the appeal takes much more time for disposal. We have already noticed that the convict-appellant on various pretexts used to take adjournment in order to hang the process of realisation of cheque amount. In order to meet such situation the legislature in applying their wisdom inserted section 138A providing the provision for depositing not less than 50% of the unpaid cheque amount as pre-condition in the case of an appeal.

27. On the face of the foregoing facts and circumstances vis-a-vis the above quoted decisions, Dr Rafiqur Rahman in his usual frankness finds it difficult to submit that the provisions of section 138A of the Act is ultra vires to the Constitution rather he concedes this patent position of law.

28. Mr Rehan Husain, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 5530 of 2008 and Writ Petition No. 5716 of 2008 however, argued that the requirement of 50% deposit of cheque amount prior to filing an appeal in the Court as laid down in section 138A of the Act is contrary to the petitioner's substantive right to prefer appeal against any such order of conviction under section 138(1) of Act and it causes hardship to the petitioner. There is, however, other side of the coin. Admittedly, the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 5530 of 2008 took Taka 4,00,000 from the respondent No. 4 as loan and later on, the complainant Md Delwar Hossain-respondent No.4, demanded the money when the petitioner gave post-dated cheque amounting to Taka 4,00,000 in favour of the respondent No.4 on 20-12-2004 and thereafter, on presentation of the said cheque was dishonoured on 18-6-2005, 19-6-2005 and lastly on 20-6-2005. In such background after fulfilling the legal requirements of section 138(b) and (c) of the Act the complainant- respondent No.4, filed the case in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, Eventually, the petitioner was put on trial in the Court of Joint Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka to answer a charge under section 138(1) of the Act. The learned trial Judge on consideration of the evidence and materials on record by judgment and order dated 16-3-2008 convicted the petitioner under section 138(1) of the Act and sentenced him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 1 (one) year and also to pay a fine of Taka 60,00,000. It also appears that the petitioner in Writ Petition No.5 716 of 2008 took Taka 30,00,000 on 14-3-2005 as loan and later on, the complainant (respondent No.4), demanded the money when the petitioner issued a cheque of Taka 30,00,000 vide Cheque No. CDEB- 1365713 dated 30-6-2005 of Eastern Bank Limited, Sonargaon Road Branch, Dhaka. On presentation, the said cheque was returned as unpaid since there was no sufficient fund in the account and ultimately, after fulfilling the legal requirement of section 138(b) and (c) of the Act the complainant (respondent No.4) filed the case. On trial, the petitioner was convicted under section 138(1) of the Act and sentenced thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for 1 (one) year and also to pay a fine of Taka 60,00,000 vide judgment and order of conviction dated 9-3-2008. Moreover, on going through the materials on record it seems to us that the complainants of those cases in order to recover their earned money have been running after the petitioners more than 5 years and in such view of the matter, we do not find any logic to say the petitioner's right is taken away by the provision of section 138A of the Act. It is not right that the strong should be allowed to push the weak to the wall. Therefore, we are unable to see eye to eye to such submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners.

<u>29. So, our considered view is that, the requirement of 50% deposit of cheque amount at the time of filing an appeal in the Court under the provisions of section 138A of the Act is not unconstitutional or violative of the provisions of the Constitution.</u>

30. Let us, now, consider another aspect of law. At the fag end of the hearing Mr Rehan Husain, the learned Advocate relying on a Single Bench decision namely, in the case of Akhter Hossain vs Hasmat Ali reported in 60 DLR 368 submitted that the provisions of section 138A of the Negotiable Instruments Act was promulgated on 9-2-2006 and the same cannot be applicable retrospectively as those cases were filed prior to the said law came into force.

31. In reply Mr Deputy Attorney-General relying on the decisions reported in 2 BLC (AD) 87, 8 MLR 404 = 56 DLR 31 and 13 BLC 686 has submitted that the Negotiable Instruments Act is a special law, the amendment in question is procedural in nature and by now it is well settled that a procedural law always would apply retrospectively even to pending proceedings.

32. On perusal of section 138A of the Act as amended on 9-2-2006 and on consideration of the whole enactment, it appears to us that the Negotiable Instruments Act being a procedural law, there is no bar in giving its effect retrospectively and more so by the Act there is no difference in awarding sentence if any upon the accused. Furthermore, the right of appeal accrues on the date of pronouncement of judgment.

33. Similar question arose while the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 came into force. In the case of Md Mofiz Mia vs Artha Rin Adalat reported in 16 BLT 476 and so many other cases, it has been consistently held that all cases relating to recovery of loan including execution cases pending in those Adalats established under Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 stood transferred by operation of law to the Artha Rin Adalats established under section 4 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 and the trial of those cases shall be resumed from its previous position as far as practicable.

34. It is the established principle of law that "Special Law always prevails over the general law."

35. On consideration of the matter vis-a-vis the cited decisions, we find no possible reason to hold that the provisions of section 138A of the Act will not apply in those cases which were filed before the said section came into force.

36. Be that as it may, it has been long standing practice of this Court that where there is a conflict between the decisions of Single Bench and Division Bench of this Court the decision of the Division Bench shall prevail. So, on this score also we are led to hold that there is no legal bar in giving its effect retrospectively in respect of all cases filed prior to section 138A of the Act came into force.

37. Mr Md Belayet Hossain, the learned Advocate on behalf of the petitioner in writ petition No. 3058 of 2008 submits that the petitioner's statutory right to prefer an appeal against the judgment and order of conviction but the embargo to prefer appeal as laid down in section 138A of the Act which, in fact, taken away the vested right of the petitioner to prefer appeal.

38. We have already indicated that the pre-condition of depositing 50% of decretal amount at the time of preferring appeal was first introduced in Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 which has also been challenged in various writ petitions unsuccessfully. The proposition of law is clear that if the appellant succeeds in the appeal he will get back his entire deposited amount and in that view of the matter, we find no merit in such argument that deposit of 50% cheque amount at the time of preferring appeal after losing the case is one kind of punishment or taken away the statutory right of the convict-petitioner to prefer appeal as canvassed by Mr Belayet Hossain. Moreover, the provision of section 138A of the Act does not debar the petitioners to file appeal under section 410, CrPC. Hence, question of violation of the right as guaranteed under Articles 27, 31, 40 and 42 of the Constitution does not arise at all.

39. Mr Momtazuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 8333 of 2008 has submitted that the learned Additional Sessions Judge miserably failed to consider the defence case that the blank cheque and other goods were forcibly taken away from the accused about 2(two) months before filing of the petition of complaint under section 138 of the Act and, as such, the judgment and order of conviction cannot be sustained in law.

40. The disputed questions of fact such as the blank cheque and other goods were forcibly taken away by the complainant from the accused before filing of the petition of complaint under section 138 of the Act cannot be decided in the writ jurisdiction. This venture under the writ jurisdiction is not permissible.

41. Mr Abu Taleb, the learned Advocate, how- ever submitted that due to certain embargo as laid down in section 138A of the Act the poor petitioner could not prefer appeal against the impugned judgment and order of conviction under section 138A of the Act although the petitioner has every chance of success in appeal. However, it is to be observed that a convict may invoke the inherent jurisdiction of the Court under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure if he can make out a case of coram non judice of the trial Court or that the facts alleged do not constitute any offence or that the conviction has been based on no legal evidence or otherwise for securing the ends of justice. Hence, this bunch of argument also fails.

42. Mere allegation of violation of provisions of law cannot give rise to any cause of action for filing a writ petition when there is forum for seeking remedy against the impugned order/judgment.

43. In view of the above provisions of law and our discussions made in the foregoing paragraphs vis-a-vis the decisions as cited above, we have no hesitation to hold that the provision of section l38A of the Act is not violative of Articles 27, 31, 40 and 42 of the Constitution.

44. No other points urged, all the points having failed, we find no substance in these Rules.

45. In the result, all these Rules are discharged without any order as to costs. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated. The petitioners are directed to surrender their respective bail bond within 2(two) months from date.

Communicate this judgment at once.

End.
