59. On the question of limitation, Mr. Sheikh Fazle Noor Tapash, learned Advocate on reference to the Fatal Accident Act, 1955 and Section 22 of Limitation Act 1908, i.e. effect of substituting or adding new plaintiff or defendant and Article 22 i.e. the period of limitation for compensation for any other injury to the person, submits that, the appellant having been impleaded long after the period of limitation so the suit is not maintainable against the plaintiffs.

60. The learned Advocate for the appellant submits that, the suit was instituted after the period of limitation as prescribed under section 22 and Article 22 of the Limitation Act Section 22 of the Limitation Act speaks that:

"22. Effect of Substituting or adding new plaintiff or defendant :-

(i) Where, after the institution of a suit, a new plaintiff or defendant is substituted or added, the suit shall, as regards him, be deemed to have been instituted when he was so made a party.

(ii) Nothing in sub-section (1) shall apply to a case where a party is added or substituted owning to an assignment or devolution of any interest during the pendency of a suit or where a plaintiff is made a defendant or a defendant is made a plaintiff."

61. The learned Advocate submits that, under this law the appellant may be allowed to be added as a party if the same is made within the period prescribed under Article 22 of the Limitation Act. Let us quote Article 22 of the Limitation Act. Article 22 prescribed compensation for any other injury to the person and the period prescribed is one year and it started from the date when the injury took place.

62. Mr. Md Khalilur Rahman on the other hand submits that, the appellant did not raise this question of limitation at the time of filing of written statement rather in written statement he contested the suit ratifying the action of the driver as such, at this moment he cannot raised such question. Learned Advocate submits that, Article 22 of the Limitation Act is not applicable on the facts of the given case as the instant suit for compensation was filed for life not for injury. Learned Advocate submits that, the suit was filed on re-opening day on 3-12-1990 and last date was 3-12-1989 as such, as per section 4 of the Limitation Act the suit was within time. Since the suit was filed within time the appellant was added under order rule 10 read with Order XXII of the Code of Civil Procedure as such, the question of limitation does not arise.

63. In the instant suit, the original suit was filed against the driver, was filed on 1-1-1991. The accident took place on 3-12-1989. The District Judiciary was completely on holidays from first December to 31st December. Section 4 of the Limitation Act prescribed when Court is closed and period expires, the suit, appeal or application may be instituted, preferred or made on the day the Court re-opens. It appears that the period for limitation expired (one year prescribed under Article 22) on 3-12-1990, the last date filing suit having fallen during the vacation of the Court, as such, filing of the suit on 1st January, 1991 i.e. on reopening day, was perfectly within time. Since the suit was filed within time, the appellant was impleaded as defendant No. 1 on 4-3-2003 by an application filed under Order 1Rule 10 by amendment of the plaint under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the said application was allowed on 4-3-2003. Apparently after 13 years of institution of the suit, but there is no period of addition of party and also for amendment of the pleadings as it can be done at any point of time during continuation of the suit and appeal and while addition was made and plaint was amended, it relates back to the date of institution of the suit, as such, plea of limitation as raised by the appellant is not sustainable. Moreover, defendant- appellant did not challenge the order dated 4-3-2003 in any forum. Defendant No. 1 appellant only contested the suit and filed written statement on 2-9- 2003 and adduced evidence in support of the case made out in the written statement but no where this defendant-appellant challenged his implication in the suit.

64. We have gone through the law of tort and we do not find law of tort itself prescribe for any limitation. It is the acts under which occurrence took place, the legal proceeding is guided by that law. The parties agreed that the instant occurrence is tortuous liability and according to me, tortuous liability is a continuous compensatory liability can be brought within a reasonable time as there is no limitation prescribed under law of Tort, as such, Article 120 of the Limitation Act i.e. where there is no prescribed limitation, action can be brought within six years from the date of occurrence is applicable. Similar question was called to answer by the Appellate Division in the case of Jamila Khatun vs Rustom Ali, 48 DLR (AD) 110 wherein the Appellate Division held as 'No such corresponding provisions exists in respect of suits filed by a Muslim for a core responding relief. In our opinion, residuary Article 120 of the First Schedule, providing for a period of limitation of 6 years from the time when the right to suit accrues in respect of a suit for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere in the first schedule will be applicable to a suit for maintenance under Ordinance of 1985. As such, we are of the view that the submission of Mr. Sheikh Fazle Noor Tapash, learned Advocate is of no substance. This is not a case either under Motor Vehicle Act or under Fatal Accident Act, as such, Article 22 of the Limitation Act has no manner of application on the facts of the given case. The appellant was impleaded in the suit as per law.

65. Mr. Sheikh Fazle Noor Tapash, learned Advocate for the appellant, accepted claim No. 1 and 4 candidly, claim No. 1 and 4 are:

১/ বাদিনীর স্বামী দৈনিক সংবাদ পত্রিকা হইতে বার্তা সম্পাদক হিসেবে অবসর গ্রহণ অবধি যে বেতন পাইতেন সেই ক্ষতির পরিমাণ ১৯,০৭,০০৮/- টাকা৷

৮/ বাদিনীর স্বামী অবসর জীবনে ১৮ বৎসরে গ্র্যাচুইটি যে আয় করিতেন সে ক্ষতির পরিমাণ ৩২,৪০,০০০/- সে ক্ষতির পরিমাণ৷

66. But submits that these claims ought to be substantiated by proper accountancy and ought to be based on, service book and other papers relating to service condition. It appears from exhibit 1 kha, the Service Book of the Sangbad Limited that if ill fated Mozammel Hossain lived up to his retirement, then what would be his monthly salary together with house rent, medical allowance, conveyance, charge allowance and additional allowance etc.

67. Mr. Sheikh Fazle Noor Tapash, learned Advocate does not totally disputed these two items and submits these may be allowed, as, if the deceased alive then he would be in service for further 13 years and drawn salary at the rate of Taka 5,988 per month and he is entitled of Taka 19,07,008 and for the retirement benefit he may be entitled for Taka 32,40,000. Relying on the decision of Serajul Islam Chowdhury vs Md Jainal Abedin,49 DLR (AD) 164, we are of the view that these two items are calculable one. The claim of compensation of these two items as we see, are not without any material and we find, these two claims are calculable. Since it is calculable we are of the view that the decree passed on these two claims/items are maintainable.

68. Mr. Sheikh Fazle Nom Tapash, learned Advocate, totally disagree with the claim made in item 2, 3, 5 and 6. In claim Nos. 2 and 3, plaintiffs claimed Taka three crore for compensation for damages caused to the infants and the widow for not getting father's and husband's affection, care and nursing for the untimely death of the deceased at the hand of defendant and claim Nos. 5 and 6 are for using "goodwill" of the deceased by the sons and damages caused to the other members of the family members who suffered shock for premature death of the deceased. In our considered view item Nos. 5 and 6 of the claims are totally vogue and cannot be substantiated.

69. In respect of item Nos. 2 and 3 i.e. for suffering of pain by untimely loss of the father of two minor sons and husband of wife, lump sum amount of Taka 3 crore have been claimed by the plaintiffs. Mr. Sheikh Fazle Noor Tapash, learned Advocate, here, objected that no money which is not calculable can be awarded and relied again on the decisions of Serajul Islam Chowdhury vs Md Jainal Abedin, 49 DLR (AD) 164, Government of the People s Republic of Bangladesh, 49 DLR (AD) 127, Smt. Kamla Devi vs Kishanch and, AIR (MP) 168 and CK Subramonia Iyer vs Kunhikuttan Nair, AIR 1970 (SC)376. In these decisions we are of the view that the occurrence happened and money claimed are calculable but pain, anguish and suffering of the sons and wife of the death of deceased cannot be calculable. There is no known method of calculating the money value of these sufferings and also loss of expectation of life. Calculation can be made when the money claimed is calculable but there is certain phenomenon of human life which is beyond calculation. It is not denied that deceased met untimely death at the hand of the driver of the appellant and pain, sufferings, privation, destitution of the surviving family member will continue title their death. In the decision of PS Bhatnagar vs State of Punjab, AIR 1978, Punjab and Haryana 166, wherein it has been held that, there can be no gainsaying that money cannot renew a shattered human frame. Still, the law was said that paid and suffering is a head of damage for which monetary compensation can be awarded and so the Court must do the best it can to be of assistance to it.

70. In the case of N Sivammal vs The Managing Director, Pandian Roadways Corpn., AIR 1985 (SC) 106, it has been held that, the claimants are entitled to compensation for continuous pain and suffering. In the decision of Sri Manmath Nath Kuri vs Mvi Md Mokhlesur Rahman, 22 DLR (SC) 51, it has been held that, it was not necessary specific compensation aspect. So if it is found that anyone died due to the irresponsible act of anyone his surviving formal member can claim compensation for continuing pain and suffering both physical and mental against the wrong doer

71. On consideration of these decisions together with the facts of the case in hand we are of the view that the plaintiffs are entitled to the compensation under item 2 and 3. These two items are not be fully covered under tort as submitted by the learned Advocate for the appellant but the case of N Rakshit vs Bhadreswar Municipality, 73 CWN 88, empower judges to create new tort. The pain, agony anguish, suffering and loss of expectation of life as claim in item No.2 and 3 are tortuous liability and can be awarded.

72. Question is whether the damages that will be awarded would be calculable one or in lump sum. In respect of claim Nos. 2 and 3 it is our view that love, affection, paid, suffering, mental agony, physical in capability, emotions are not calculable and if he Court satisfied that the plaintiffs be paid any compensation that can be only in lump sum not on calculation.

73. In the case of Ehsan Ali vs Karachi Road Transport Corporation, 20 DLR (WP) 226 where in the fact that in railway crossing at Karimabad a railway engine hit the bus and causing injury to several bus passengers, it has been held that :-

"On this evidence, I have no hesitation to hold that the plaintiff went though serious physical and mental suffering on account of the accident in question, and these injuries he received have caused permanent disabilities to him, in addition to reducing his enjoyment and expectancy of life and impairing his earning capacity. The question, therefore, arises, as to what compensation the plaintiff should consequently receive from the defendants. In this connection, I would refer to the decisions cited by Kemp & Kemp in "The Quantum of Damages", (Vol.1, Second Edition). In the case of Boyle vs Conselt Iron Co Ltd cited at page 413, the Court of Appeal awarded £800 as damages for fracture of pelvis, damage to right hip and the base of the left lung. The Athevictor, cited at page 458, £3,500 were awarded for permanent injury to one arm. In the Supplement to the Second Edition, there is reference, at page 17, to the case of Chambers vs British Railway Board where the plaintiff was awarded £ 11,000 as general damages on account of injuries to right shoulder and right and left ankles, left hip and kidneys. In this case the claimant remained unconscious for three weeks, and as a result of the injuries he was liable to periodical attacks of dizziness, head-aches, defective speech and weakness in the right arm and right leg. In Suit No.8 of the 1960 decided by this Court by judgment dated 16th February 1967, the plaintiff, Suraya Hafeez, was given Rs 15,000 as compensation for injuries which included confusion 2" x 1" on right forearm, lacerated wound 2" x 1/4" muscle deep on left leg, abrasion 1/4" in diameter on right elbow, abrasion 1-1/2" diameter on right shoulder, The judgment given by this Court in Letters Patent Appeal No. 99 of 1960 upheld the finding of a learned single judge giving to the claimant Rs 10,000 as damages for future loss resulting from reduced efficiency and earning capacity and diminution in the enjoyment of life, and Rs 5,000 for shortened expectancy of life, pain and bodily suffering.

74. The decision I have referred to above do give guidance in the assessment of compensation in the present case. The plaintiff received serious physical injuries and remained in a state of unconsciousness for 7 or 8 days. For more than 9 months the plaintiffs remained confined to bed. Due to the nervous shock caused by the accident, the plaintiffs has lost sexual appetite, the correctness of which statement I have to reason to doubt. The plaintiff still suffers from limp and pain in his foot, pain in pelvis and restricted movements of his left arm, and is subject to distress whenever he makes any mental efforts. I should say that not only the plaintiff's enjoyment of life has been reduced but his life expectancy also has been shortened. The plaintiff has also suffered impairment of physical and mental efficiency, which would effect his future earnings".

75. It the case of Kayumraz vs Messrs Mohammadi Tramway Company, Karachi, PLD 1968 Karachi 376 it has been held that:

" The next point is, what compensation should be awarded to the plaintiff on account of general damages. Under issue No.3 it has been noticed that the plaintiff sustained serious injuries in the accident "***** I am further of the view that the injuries received by the plaintiff were of such a nature that it can be reasonably said that his expectation of life had been shortened. The plaintiff, accordingly, is entitled to compensation for pain and suffering caused to him by these injuries and the consequent shortened expectation, and diminution in enjoyment of life and prospective loss in earning capacity. I would fix this compensation at Rs 16,849. In my opinion the plaintiff is entitled to much more substantial amount in this connection, but I am unable to grant him anything more, as the plaintiff's suit is only for Rs. 70,000."

76. In the case of Amin Yousuf Nizami vs Rashid Rayon Mills, Karachi, PLD1971 (Karachi) 505, it has been held that :-

" No doubt it is correct that the permanent incapacity suffered by the plaintiff in his right hand index finger is such as would interfere with the ordinary vocation of weaving master for the reasons mentioned above. But the question is whether the reduction in salary from Rs 1,500 to Rs 1,000 per month is due only to this incapacity, or due to other economic factors like supply and demand of skilled workers such as weaving masters. It is possible that the reduction in the monthly remuneration of the plaintiffs may partly be attributed to availability now of more skilled workers like weaving masters than when the plaintiffs was in the employment of the defendants. These economic factors should be taken into consideration. Now, in the present case, as I have stated, economic factors have also to be taken into consideration. It cannot be said with certainty, as there is no evidence on this point, that the reduction in the plaintiff's earning from Rs 1500 to Rs 1,000 per month is only due to the injury in his right hand index finger. In the present case, the reduction in income can safely and reasonably be based on Rs 1,500 per month. On this basis the general damages may either be awarded to the plaintiff according to the method of capitalization on annuity basis, or by capitalizing the reduction in income for a number of years, or a third alternative method may be adopted, that is, damages may be assessed according to the extent of the permanent incapacity suffered by the plaintiff."

77. In the case of Sri Manmath Nath vs Moklesur Rahman 22 DLR (SC) 57. it has been held:-

" What is recoverable is pecuniary loss resulting to the estate of the deceased not from his death or as a consequence of his death but from the wrongful act, neglect or default itself and as a consequence of such act or default. The action for the former is to be brought by the representatives of the deceased not for the benefit of the estate but as trustees for the persons named in the statute. For the latter, namely; the loss caused to the estate the action may be brought by quite different persons such as creditors, legatees other beneficiaries although ordinarily the dependants of the deceased will also be the persons interested in the assets of the deceased. In such event both the causes of action may well be combined in the same suit."

78. If this distinction is kept in mind, it will not be difficult to appreciate that under section I the pecuniary loss will be loss resulting to the parties beneficially entitled as a consequence of the death. Act itself does not, however, lay down any principle for calculating the measure of such loss but an estimate has still to be made by the Court which has also to apportion the sum so determined between the beneficiaries proportionately, according to the nears as of their relationship and the interest which each of them had in the life of the deceased. Under this head legal liability alone is not the test of the loss. But even the reasonable expectation of pecuniary advantage which might have been derived from the deceased had he remained alive, may be taken into account, and damages given in respect of that expectation.

79. Assessment of damages in such a case must, therefore, necessarily be to some extent of a rough and approximate nature based more or less on guess work, for, it may well be impossible to accurately determine the loss which has been sustained by the death of a husband, wife, parent or child.

80. No definite or hard and fast rule can, as such, be laid down as to the matters which should be taken into account. But this much can be said that only such damages can be given as can be shown to have been financially suffered by those who bring the action. In estimating such damages the Court will, no doubt, take into account the age of the deceased, his or her health, earning capacity and even the changes of advancement. There must however, be evidence of "reasonable expectation of pecuniary advantage" and not of a "mere speculative possibility". Thus parents may recover for the loss of the probability that the deceased child would have contributed towards their maintenance and children may recover for the loss of education, comfort and position in society which they would have enjoyed if the father had lived and maintained the income which had died with him. The basis of the assessment is not the requirement of plaintiff but the money value of the assistance which the deceased might probably have given had he continued to live".

81. In the case of Phool Chand vs Jai Devi. AIR 1966 All 527, where the respondent was dragged by the appellant for committing sexual assault, it has been held-

"where a man drags a woman for the purpose of committing sexual intercourse, the amount of damages has to be assessed at the discretion of the Court which of course must be judicially exercised. The damages awarded to the wronged woman are not as compensation for any injury as there is no injury, but for mental pain and shock. There is no known method of calculating the money value of the pain and anguish caused to a woman who is dragged by a ruffian for the purpose" of assaulting her."

82. In the case of Satya Wati vs Union of India AIR 1967 Delhi 98, it has been held :-

"There are some other factors which have to be taken into consideration-(i) the hazards to which the deceased would have been subjected; and (ii) the plaintiff will earn interest for the next five years, being the expected age, on the lump sum awarded which, having regard to the present market conditions, should be anywhere between 6 to 8 percent. She will further have the advantage of immediately having a lump sum amount in hand. The damages, are to be based on the reasonable expectation of pecuniary benefit or benefit reducible to money value in the hands of the plaintiff. No doubt, in such like cases, which are of frequent occurrence these days, certain rules relating to the measure or assessment of damages have gradually been evolved, yet, in general, there is no specific rule upon the matter and it is always left to be good sense of the Court to assess as best as it can what it considers to be an adequate recompense for the loss suffered by the plaintiff. The assessment may well be a matter of great difficulty, indeed, in some cases, one of guess work but the fact that it cannot be made with mathematical accuracy is no reason for depriving the plaintiff of compensation. Yet that is the mistake into which the trial Court seems to have fallen."

83. In Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Subhag wanti, AIR 1966 SC 1750 the Supreme Court approved the following passage from the judgment of Lord Wright in Davies vs Powel Duffrvn Associated Companied Ltd 1942 AC 601 settling the principle on which damages in cases of fatal accidents should be ascertained-

" It is a hard matter of pounds, shilling and pence, subject to the element of reasonable future probabilities. The starting point is the amount of wage which the deceased was earning, the ascertainment of which to some extent may depend upon the regularity of his employment. Then there is an estimate of how much was required or expended for his own personal and living expenses. The balance will give a datum or basic figure which will generally be turned into a lump sum by taking a certain number of years' purchase, That sum, however, has to be taxed down by having due regard to uncertainties, for instance that the widow night have again married and thus ceased to be dependant, and other like matters of speculation & doubt". The deceased in that case was 28 years old at the time of his death and the Supreme Court approved the assessment of damages by capitalizing for a period of 15 years the monthly sum which was available for the subsistence and education of his dependants at the time of his death. In the present case the amount which was available for the maintenance and education of the plaintiffs from the earning of the deceased was, as held by us above, Rs 125 per month or Rs 1,500 per year. The damages of Rs 30,000 granted by the trial Court would be equal to the capitalization of the above amount for a period of 20 years. The amount awarded may appear to be excessive, but in our opinion it is not. The pay of the deceased was being increased from time to time. It can be safely assumed that in the course of time his earnings would have been higher. Moreover, he died in a period of soaring prices. Like other employees, he would have received higher money wages as a result of a rise in the price level. The real value of the amount of Rs 30,000 awarded by the trial Court is much less today than it was when the amount was claimed by the plaintiffs in the suit. Under the circumstances we are of the view that the damages awarded by the trial Court are proper and that reduction in that amount would not be justified.

The second Issue which relates to reparation is the most difficult of all the issues in the case. It cannot be gainsaid that the Fatal Accidents Act, 1977 (1920 AD) of the State gives a right amongst other persons to parents including grand-parents to claim compensation in case of death caused by actionable wrong. It is, however, the measure of reparation that presents the real difficulty. The principles on which the compensation is to be awarded in our State are the same as those on which it is awardable in England under the English Fatal Accidents Acts 9, and 10 Viet Chapter 93, known as the Lord Campbell's Acts and (The Indian) Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 (Act No. XIII of 1855) Section 1 of the State Fatal Accidents Act 1977 (1920 AD) Act No.XVII of 1977 which is a reproduction of Section I-A of (The Indian) Fatal Accidents Act, 1855 (Act XIII of 1855) provides that the compensation for the loss in case of fatal accidents has to be proportionate to the actual pecuniary benefit which the dependants of the deceased might reasonably expect of enjoy. Reference in this connection may also be usefully made to the decisions reported in AIR 1936 Mad 247, AIR 1959 Punj 297 and AIR 1956 Cal 555."

84. Thus we find all the questions raised in the appeal decided in favor of the plaintiffs.

85. In a discussion as aforesaid it is clear that the claim made under item No.2 and 3, cannot be calculable by applying statistical or actuarial text and it is the discretion of the Court which should be reasonable, not arbitrary in awarding compensation on these two items. The basic for claiming compensation mainly loss of expectation of life according to us is tortuous liability and can be awarded. It also to be noted that deceased was a valiant freedom fighter who sweat of his brow in liberating the country which is also not calculable. But we are, at the same time conscious the amount for his sad demise at the hand of appellant due to untimely death should not be beyond imagination. His untimely death is suffered by his wife as widow as she did not marry again and his two sons who are students, their sufferings as loss of their father and husband will run till their death but, lapse of time may minimize their pain, agony and sufferings. In awarding compensation beside their sufferings, day to day expenses, cost living, educational expenses and economic situation needs to be considered within reasonable estimation. We have already considered that plaintiffs suffered their pain, agony etc as individual as well as a family as such we amalgamate both item 2 and 3 into one. It has already seen that there is no subject value in giving compensation on these two claims i.e item No.2 and 3 and it is the Court who will decide the compensation in lump as such, It needs to be emphasized that the standard for estimating the amount of damages in case of actionable. negligence resulting in death must not be a subjective standard but an objective one and regard in this behalf's to be had to the earnings of the deceased at the time of his death, his future prospects, his life expectancy, the amount he would have spent on himself and on the support of his dependants, the economic condition of the country the property left by him and the like. On this count ends of justice would be met if we award compensation to the tune of Taka 1,50,000 on these two claim/items. This money on the fact of the given case, according to us IS not unreasonable but good.

86. The end, thus stand, the appeal allowed in part. The plaintiffs do get a decree as ;-

i) For item No.1 Taka 	19,07,008

ii) For item No.2 and 3 Taka 	1,50,00,000

iii) For item No.4 Taka 	32,40,000

Total Taka 2,01,47,008

87. Defendant appellant is directed to pay the decreetal amount of Taka 2,01,47,008 within 60 days from the date of receipt of this judgment to the plaintiffs filing which the plaintiff shall realize the amount through process of law.

<u>88. Before parting with the decisions we draw our anxiety over regular accidental death of our country. Life is a bundle of incident. Every child is born with expectation of life and with constitutional guaranteed right of basic requirements for living Death is inevitable but premature death in whatever form is not expected and cannot be consoled. Accidental death also a premature death Government is answerable to all such premature death as Government is to protect the citizen and is responsible for the life of a citizen as such, when anyone of what- ever class, society, place met death by accident, it should be the duty of the Government to mitizate the sufferings of the survivors of the family. We suggest the Government to bring the wrong doers to Court, either by assisting the survivors in their effort to approach the law of Government on behalf the survivors realize such compensation from the wrong doers which may at least console their sufferings as accidental death shattered a family in every aspect. It appears that only making criminally liable by punishing the wrong doers do not at all being any fruitful result to the survivors of the deceased. We also suggest the Government not to issue driving Licence to anybody who has no education and no basic qualification to be a driver but to a person who has at least some education as education makes a man a bit responsible.</u>

Communicate this order at once.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

parties:
Khan Md Firoj Kabir ------ Appellant
Vs.
Rupali Bank Ltd and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 17-8-2000 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2363 of 1998).
full_judgment:
Md Tafazzul Islam J: This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment dated 17.8.2000 of the High Court Division passed in Civil Revision No. 2363 of 1998 discharging the Rule which was obtained against the order dated 14-5-98 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 278 of 1997 rejecting the application filed by the plaintiff/appellant praying for fixing the next date of the suit for ex parte hearing in view of the default of the defendants to file written statement within two months.

2. The appellant, as plaintiff, filed the above suit seeking declaration that the order dated 26-1-1997 placing him under suspension is void and illegal and the notice dated 2-9-97 asking him to show cause as to why he shall not be dismissed from service is also void and illegal contending, inter alia, that he joined Rupali Bank, the defendant No, 1 /respondent, on 23-10-1973 as probationary officer and by dint of merit he was promoted to the rank of Deputy General Manager; because of his outstanding performance and due to his rapid promotions he became an eyesore of his rivals and at their instigation, by order dated 26-1-1997, he was put under suspension on false allegations; then different notices were issued asking him to show cause as to why he should not be dismissed from service and he replied to those notices stating that the allegations made against him have no basis at all; but his explanations were not accepted by defendant No,1 and the final notice to show cause being issued by the same officer who conducted the departmental inquiry against him, he replied to the same stating that he would not get fair trial; then the plaintiff, being compelled to believe that the defendant No. 1, in order to dismiss him from service initiated the so-called departmental proceeding, had no other alternative but to file the suit. The defendants having entered appearance in the suit on 7-10-1997 prayed for time to contest the suit and the Court fixed the next date on 4-11-97 for filing written statement; subsequently, on the prayers of the defendant No.1, the Court fixed 4-1-98, 20-2-98, 16-3-98 and 14-5-98 the next dates for filing written statement and the defendants having not filed the written statement the plaintiff on 14-5-98 filed an application praying that the suit be fixed for ex parte hearing as the defendants did not file any written statement within two months as provided in Order VIII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The defendants, on the same day, also filed an application praying for further time to file written statement. The learned Assistant Judge by the order passed on the same day i.e. 14-5-98, rejected the objection of the plaintiff to the prayer of the defendant and fixed the next date on 18-5-1998 for filing the written statement; Being aggrieved the plaintiff moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 2363 of 1996 but, in the meanwhile, the defendants filed written statement on 18-5-198. The High Court Division, after hearing, relying upon the case of Fazlul Huq vs Md Tahed Ali reported in 47 DLR 326, discharged the Rule holding that the time limit set by Order VIII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directory and not mandatory.

3. Leave was granted on the submissions that the above judgment and order of the High Court Division passed relying upon the principle of law laid down in the case reported in 47 DLR 326 conflicts with the principles as laid down in the case of Messrs Adamjee Jute Mills Ltd vs Chairman 3rd Labour Court and another reported in 39 DLR 11 and also the case of Lal Mamud and others vs Siraj Miah and others reported in 45 DLR 638.

4. The learned Counsel for the appellant submitted that the intention of the legislature for amending Order VIII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure by Ordinance No. XLVIII of 1985 was to expedite the time for disposal of the civil suits and that in 39 DLR 11 the High Court Division held that after amendment of Order VIII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure after the expiry of the stipulated time for filing the written statement, the suit is to proceed for hearing without a written statement and subsequently, in 45 DLR 638 a Single Bench of the High Court Division also took the view that filing of the written statement by the defendant within the prescribed period is a mandatory requirement of law and accordingly, the decision reported in 47 DLR 326 relying on which the High Court Division discharged the Rule by the judgment dated 17.8.2000 conflicts with the decisions reported in 39 DLR 11 and in 45 DLR 638.

5. The learned Counsel for the respondent submitted that Order VIII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure having not provided for any consequence for not filing written statement within the time limit as set out, filing of the written statement within the stipulated time is merely directory and not mandatory as held in 47 DLR 326 and that the decisions reported in 39 DLR 11 and 45 DLR 638 being based on different facts are distinguishable and the High Court Division was not wrong in distinguishing the decisions reported in 39 DLR 11 and 45 DLR 638 and further, the decision reported in 39 DLR 11 does not support the contention of the appellant, inasmuch as in that decision it has been held that the Court cannot fix the case for ex parte hearing even when the defendant did not file written statement and that, in any view of the matter, the defendants having filed the written statement on the next date fixed, ends of justice required that there should have been no ex parte hearing.

6. As it appears before amendment was made by Ordinance No. XLVII of 1983 the provisions of Order VIII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure stood as follows:

" The defendant may, and, if so required by the Court, shall at or before the first hearing or within such time as the Court may permit, present a written statement of his defence.".

After amendment as made in the year 1983 the above Order VIII, rule 1 stands as follows:

"The defendant shall, at or before the first hearing or within such time not exceeding two months as the Court may permit, save as provided in the proviso to sub-section(2) of section 80, present a written statement of his defence".

7. It is also evident that the above Order VIII, rule 1, as amended, was brought in the Code of Civil Procedure to expedite the disposal of civil suit. But the question is, since no consequence is provided in the amended Order VIII, rule 1, in case the defendant fails to file written statement within 2 months after appearance, whether this requirement of filing written statements within two months from the date of appearance is mandatory or directory.

8. As it appears in 39 DLR 11, as cited from the Bar, the High Court Division found that two months having not yet elapsed since the defendant entered appearance and prayed for time to file a written statement and that the defendant filed written statement on 16-6-85, well within two months from the date of his first appearance in Court, and that there was a persistent refusal by the Labour Court to accept the written statement because the defendant failed to pay the adjournment cost and that on 18-6- 85 the defendant filed as many as two applications praying that the earlier order dated 16-6-85 for ex parte hearing be vacated and another date be fixed for hearing in presence of both sides and by another application the defendant also offered the adjournment cost Taka 100 but the Court rejecting the said two applications proceeded to try the case ex parte and, in the background of the above facts, the High Court Division held that under amended Order VIII, rule 1 it is not obligatory upon the defendant to file the written statement within the stated time and the defendant may still file a written statement and that in a large majority of cases the trial Courts invariably fix cases for ex parte hearing if the defendant fails to file written statement and such fixing for ex parte hearing is not proper because a case can be fixed for ex parte hearing only under Order IX, rule 6 and Order VIII, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure and if the defendant fails to file a written statement the, Court shall fix the case for hearing in default of the written statement and on the date so fixed the defendant can still appear and cross examine plaintiff's witness as well as argue his case without the written statement and that under the unamended Order VIII, rule 1 it was not obligatory on the part of the defendant to file a written statement within specified time but under the amended Order VIII, rule 1 the defendant is bound to file a written statement within specified time but however, the consequences for the failure to file a written statement remained the same and the suit still cannot be fixed for ex parte hearing and it can be fixed for hearing only in case of default to file the written statement and the defendant still retains the right to appear on the date of hearing and participate at the trial.

9. In the decision reported 45 DLR 638, as cited from the Bar, the plaintiff filed a partition suit praying for saham in respect of suit land and the written statement filed by the defendant No. 88 on 18-8-84 was rejected on 27-8-84 and then the suit was decreed in preliminary form. On appeal by the defendant Nos. 30, 31, 36 and 61 the lower appellate Court allowed the appeal and remitted the suit to the trial Court for allocating shahams to the defendants; after remand the defendant No. 88 filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for accepting the written statement which was already rejected by the trial Court and after hearing the trial Court rejected the said application. Being aggrieved the defendant No.88 moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule but the High Court Division, after hearing, relying on the decision reported in 39 DLR 11, discharged the Rule holding that although the defendant was not under legal obligation to file a written statement within the prescribed period as contemplated in Order VIII, rule I of the Code of Civil Procedure before amendment, but after amendment it is a mandatory provision of law.

10. In the decision reported in 47 DLR 326, relying on which the High Court Division discharged the present Rule the defendant 1 appeared in the suit on 12-6-90 and filed application for time in order to file written. statement and although by order dated 6-6-90 the Court granted him time upto 10-7-90, the defendant I did not take any steps whatsoever and as a result the suit was fixed on 14-8-1991 for ex parte hearing but on that date the defendant No. 1 again filed an application praying for time to file written statement which being allowed the next date was fixed on 22-9-90 for filing written statement but on 22-9-90 defendant No. 1 again filed an application for filing written statement and the learned Assistant Judge, relying on the provisions of Order VIII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, fixed 21-10-90 for ex-parte hearing of the suit and then on 21-10-90 the defendant No.1 filed written statement with an application showing reasons for delay in filing the written statement and then the next date was fixed on 4-11-90 for ex parte hearing and on 4-11-90 the defendant No.1 filed an application praying for acceptance of the written statement which was rejected; thereafter the defendant No. 1 filed an application under section 151 read with Order XLVII, rule 1 and Order IX. rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for recalling the order dated 4-11-90 and for acceptance of the written statement and the above prayer being rejected the defendant No.1 moved the High Court Division and obtained the Rule and during the hearing of the Rule the learned Advocate for the defendant No. 1 submitted before the High Court Division that the provision in Order VIII, rule 1 regarding filing of written statement within two months may be interpreted as directory and not mandatory although the word "shall" has been incorporated in the amended provision of Order VIII, rule 1, CPC and so the court below ought to have accepted the written statement filed with explanation and in support of the above submission the learned Advocate of the defendant No.1 referred to the case of Afsaruddin Ahmed vs Banque Indosuez 44 DLR (AD) 136 wherein the question of filing document out of time under the new provisions of rules 14 and 18 of Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure came up for interpretation. As it appears the Court in the above decision held that if reasonable grounds are shown for not filing original document at the time of filing of the plaint the Court may accept the original document subsequently upon reasonable explanation and that the word "shall" appearing in the above rule 14 was directory and not mandatory and in the above decision the Court further held that "it is needless to say that if very rigid and literal construction is given to the language of the newly added proviso to rule 18 of the said Order, then in many genuine cases ends of justice will be frustrated"; The High Court Division, relying on the principle as laid down by this Court in the above decision, held that reasonable cause shown and explanation given in not filing written statement within specified time may be accepted in appropriate cases and that the defendant No.1 filed an application showing sufficient cause for acceptance of the written statement on 21-10-90 and that it is a long drawn practice that if written statement cannot be filed within the time fixed by the court the same is generally accepted upon filing of an application explaining the delay.

11. As it appear by Ordinance No. XLVII of 1983 the legislature, while incorporating amended Order VIII, rule 1, also incorporated the amended rules 14 and 18 of Order Vll of the Code of Civil Procedure in order to expedite the disposal of suits but since in the above rules 14 and 18 of Order VII, CPC no consequence was provided in case of non-filing the original document along with the plant, the Appellate Division held that amended provisions are directory and not mandatory. Accordingly, the decision reported in 47 DLR 326, though is in conflict with the decision reported in 39 DLR 11 and 45 DLR 638 but since the decision reported in 47 DLR 326 is based on the decision reported in 44 DLR (AD) 136 and, as such, the decision reported in 47 DLR 326 will have precedence over the decisions reported in 39 DLR 11 and 45 DLR 638.

<u>12. Since in the instant case the High Court Division discharged the Rule holding that the learned Senior Assistant Judge exercised his discretion in granting time to the defendant for filing written statement rejecting the application of the plaintiff for fixing the suit for ex parte hearing and the said discretion does not appear to have been exercised arbitrarily and capriciously and further since in 47 DLR (AD) 136 it has been held that the provisions of amended Order 1, rule 8 is directory and not mandatory and Order VIII, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure allowed the Court to give appropriate relief, we are of the view that the High Court Division did not commit any error in discharging the Rule. Further, since the High Court Division, on proper appreciation of the materials on record and applying the correct principle of law as applicable in present case, arrived at the correct decision, there is no cogent reason to interfere with the same.</u>

Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost.

End.

Md Lutfor Rahman Mandai, with Kohinoor Hossain Khan, &KM Zahid Sarwar, Advocates-----For the Petitioner. 
Md. Mostafa, Advocate-----For Opposite Party No.1.
parties:
Rowshan Haq ----- Plaintiff-Petitioner
Vs.
Abul Hossain and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
SM ZiauI Karim J: This Rule was issued, calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the order dated 11-8-2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 184 of 1999 should not be set aside and or pass such other order or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Short facts leading to this Rule are that on 29-11-1999 the petitioner as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 184 of 1999 in the First Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Gazipur impleading the opposite parties as defendants to enforce an agreement of sale of 77 decimals of land described in the schedule to the plaint.

3. The plaintiff's case, put in a nutshell, is that defendant No.1 at first, proposed to sell his 17 decimals of land at a consideration of Taka 8,25,000; that accordingly, the plaintiff agreed to purchase the same and on 30-11-1997 defendant No.1, on receiving Taka 50,000 executed a bainapatra in favour of the plaintiff; that the plaintiff, on different occasions paid the entire amount for Taka 8,25,000; that again the defendant No. 1 agreed to sell 77 decimals of land including the earlier land at a consideration of Taka 19,30,000 and on 20-3-1999 executed a bainapatra in favour of the plaintiff with a promise to execute kabala deed on 31-7-1999 after receiving the rest of the amount; that after the expiry of the said period defendant No.1 refused to execute the kabala deed rand that later on the plaintiff came to know that on 21-11-1995, the defendant No. 1 mortgaged the suit property and took loan from Janata Bank (herein defendant No.2). Hence, is the suit.

4. The defendant No. 1 appeared in the suit by filing a written statement denying all material allegations made in the plaint, contending inter alia, that the plaintiff created some forged papers and bainapatra to grab the property; that the suit property was mortgaged with the Janata Bank, so the question to execute bainapatra is absurd and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. Subsequently, on an application filed by the plaintiff, the documents relating to mortgage of the suit property was called for, from the Janata Bank.

6. On 11-8-2003, the plaintiff filed an application under sections 45 and 73 of the Evidence Act to examine the disputed signature and initial of the bainapatra with that of the admitted signature appearing in the mortgaged deed. After hearing the learned Judge of trial Court rejected the said application. Hence, is the Rule.

7. Mr Lutfor Rahman Mondal, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the trial Court has committed an error of law in not allowing the petition for examination of the disputed signature of the defendant No. 1 by a handwriting expert and it would have been in a better position in determining the crucial question as to whether the defendant No. 1 has executed the present disputed bainapatra. He adds that the learned Judge of the trial Court did not at all consider that the expert opinion would merely be an aid to the court. He further submits that the disputed signature along with signature appearing in the mortgaged deed is already hefore the trial Court. So according to him, the signature should be examined by the handwriting expert. In support of his contention the learned Counsel refers to the case of Sk Abul Quasem and others vs Mayez Uddin Mondal and others reported in 45 DLR 169, wherein it is held-

"Evidence Act (1 of 1872)

Sections 45 & 73

Examination of LTI- It is true Court itself can compare any signature or LTI of any concerned person himself under section 73, Evidence Act but it is better to have an expert's opinion also, particularly in a case of LTI.

8. He further refers to the case of Serajuddin Ahmed and others vs AKM Saiful Alam and others reported in 56 DLR (AD) 41 wherein it is held- "Evidence Act (1 of 1872) Sections 45 & 73 Since by scientific process or method examination of signature, particularly thumb impression, has developed much, it is safe and sound to leave the matter of such examination to the expert or to the person specialised in the examination.

9. Mr Mondal lastly submits that the learned Judge of the trial Court failed to weigh and sift the materials on record as required by law and evidently fell in an error in coming to his ultimate decision occasioning failure of justice.

10. Mr Md Mustafa, the learned Advocate appearing for opposite party No.1, without filing any counter-affidavit submits that as per provision under section 73 of the Evidence Act the Court is competent to compare the signature of a person and there is no cause of prejudice of the appellant by such comparison. The learned Counsel further submits that the suit was filed on 29-11-1999 and the application was filed on 1l-8-2003 i.e. the application was filed at a very belated stage only to delay the disposal of the suit. Such an application was filed by the plaintiff. In support of his contention, the learned Counsel refers to the case of Ishaque (Md) vs Ekramul Haque Chowdhury and others reported in 54 DLR (AD) 26 wherein it is held-

"Evidence Act (1 of 1872)

Section 73

The section permits the Court to make a comparison of signature or writings and so adoption of such a method chariot be termed as hazardous or dangerous."

He further refers to the case of Aftab Ali (Captain Retired) vs SM Kutubuddin being dead his heirs Nuzhat Banu and others reported in 56 DLR (AD) 117 wherein it is held-

"In view of the provision of section 107(2) of the Code the High Court Division was competent to compare the signature of the defendant in the 'bainapatra' with his available signatures and, as such, was in error in sending back the case for retrial for the said purpose to the trial Court."

The learned Counsel lastly submits that the impugned order is just and proper which calls for no interference by this Court and, as such, the Rule is liable to be discharged,

11. We have gone through the revisional application, the annexure furnished with it, along with the plaint of Title Suit No. 184 of 1999, written statement filed by the defendants, the application under sections 45 and 73 of the Evidence Act, the impugned order, the other materials on record and have given our anxious considerations to the submission advanced by the learned Counsels of both sides.

12. Admittedly the suit property was mortgaged with the Janata Bank ( herein referred to as defendant No.2), and defendant No. 1 executed deed of mortgage in favour of defendant No.2. The said document of mortgage is already before the trial Court. According to the plaintiff, the defendant No.1, after receiving advance money, executed a, bainapatra in favour of him but the defendant No. 1 disowned such facts.

13. Now, the question calls for our consideration is, whether the examination of the disputed signature with that of the admitted signature by a hand writing expert is at all necessary and whether the learned Judge of the trial Court committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of Justice in passing the impugned order.

14. It is well known that the Evidence Act has provided for the following, four modes for proving handwriting or signature of a person in any document, namely.

1. By the opinion of an expert who can examine and compare the handwriting or signature in a scientific process, vide section 45 of the Evidence Act.

2. By a witness who is acquainted with the handwriting or signature of the person by whom the same is supposed to be written and signed, vide section 47 of the Evidence Act.

3. By proof of the signature or handwriting of the person alleged to have signed or written the document by evidence vide section 67 of the Evidence Act.

4. Also by comparison of the signature or handwriting of the person with his other admitted and proved handwriting or signature by the Court itself vide section 73 of the Evidence Act. So, the identity of the handwriting or signature of a person by the opinion of an expert is one of the methods as provided in the Evidence Act.

In the instant case when it is the duty Of the, plaintiffs to prove the identity and genuineness of the signatures of defendant No. 1 on the alleged document, the plaintiff may avail herself of any of the methods as enumerated above. She cannot be forced by the defendants to resort to any particular method in proving the alleged, signature. In this regard, reliance is being placed on the case of Sree Dulal Banerjee @ Moni vs Sree Sharat Chandra Pal and another reported in 1992 BLD 277.

15. It is true that the learned Judge of the trial Court is quite competent under section 73 of the Evidence Act to compare the signature of the executant defendant No. 1, Abul Hossain, in the bainapatra with that of the admitted signature appearing in the mortgage deed available in the record of the suit but in the facts and circumstances of the case, it will be better to have an expert's opinion by the examination and comparison of the disputed signature with that of the admitted signature, particularly when there is a provision under section 45 of the Evidence Act for the examination of the signature by an expert.

16. In the case of Kessarbai vs Jethabai reported in AIR 1928 (PC) 277 wherein it was observed that a mere comparison of the admitted signature without an expert's advice or microscopic examination is dangerous. In the decision reported in 28 DLR 123 it has been observed that an expert's opinion enables the Court to come to a satisfactory conclusion though the said opinion is not binding upon the Court.

<u>17. It is true that the Court itself can compare any signature or LTI of any concerned person under section 73 of The Evidence Act and come to a decision but it is better to have an expert's opinion also, particularly in a case of LTI.</u>

18. In the case of Nurul Huq (Md) @ MN Huq vs Nirmal Chandra Dutta and another reported in 56 DLR (AD) 143 wherein it is held:

"Code of Civil Procedure (V of 1908)

Section 107

In view of the contentious submissions of the parties, it was the duty of the courts below to send the impugned documents to the Hand-writing Expert for opinion. Such opinion being not taken by either of the Courts below, the appeal is allowed, impugned judgment and decree are, set aside. The First Appeal is remanded to the High Court Division with a direction to hear the appeal afresh after obtaining report from the competent Handwriting Expert as to execution of the documents."

19. In the case of Tarak Chandra Majhi vs Atahar Ali Howlader and others reported in 13 BLT (AD) 3= 8 BLC (AD) 67 wherein it is held:

"In case of contentious writing, signature, etc. though provision of section 73 of the Evidence Act permits the court to compare the contentious signature with the admitted signature, the safe and best course, in our view, for the court would be to avoid the practice of comparing the writing or signature, etc and should not stake its judgment on the opinion formed or view taken upon resorting to risky or, in other words, unsatisfactory and dangerous procedure."

20. Having regard to the facts and the principle enunciated in the above cases, we hold that the plaintiff petitioner should be given chance to prove her case to have an expert's opinion by examination and comparison of disputed signature of defendant No. 1 Abul Hossain appearing in bainapatra dated 30-11-1997 and 20-3-1999 with that of the admitted signature appearing in the mortgage deed relating to the suit property.

21. We are in respectful agreement with the principles enunciated in the cases as referred to by the learned Counsel for the opposite party No.1 but the facts leading to those cases are distinguishable from that of the instant case and we therefore are unable to accept his submission. On the contrary, the legal, plea taken by the learned Counsel for the petitioner prevails and appears to have a good deal of force.

22. Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case and foregoing narrative we are led to the conclusion that the impugned order suffers from legal infirmity which calls for interference by this Court. Thus the Rule having merit succeeds.

23. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned order dated 11-8-2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Gazipur, in Title Suit No. 184 of 1999 is hereby set aside. The application dated 11-8-2003 filed by the plaintiff petitioner for examining the disputed signature of defendant No.1 Abul Hossain with that of his admitted signature appearing in the mortgaged deed is allowed.

24, The trial Court will fix up the necessary cost for the purpose and direct the plaintiff-petitioner to deposit the same in the Court within a reasonable time for the purpose of such examination by a handwriting expert and his opinion. The order of stay granted earlier stands vacated.

Communicate the order at once with a copy of the judgment for information and for taking of necessary action.

End.

Mf Farooque with AFM Ashaduzzaman and Nazneen Nahar Advocates-----For Appellants.

Joinal Abedin Jamal and others ----- Appellants
