full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider J : This appeal has been preferred by the 2nd party appellants being aggrieved by Order No.37 dated 2S-3-2006 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 973 of 2002 refusing to set aside the arbitral award dated 11-6-2003 passed by the sole Arbitrator. Facts necessary for the disposal of this appeal in short are that the appellants being owners of, approximately, 18.40 kathas of land, comprising of Dhaka City Corporation holdings No. 80, 80/1, 80/2 and 80/3, Nowabpur, within Sutrapur Police station, fully described in the Agreement (Bainapatra) (subsequently described as the arbitral agreement), executed between the appellants and the present respondent on 4-8-1999 for sale of the said property at a consideration of Taka 3,68,00,000. As per terms of the said agreement, the present respondent was suppose to pay Taka 50,00,000 to the appellants as advance. Accordingly, the respondent paid Taka 2,50,000 in cash, Taka 35,00,000 in cheque dated 4-8-1999 of lslami Bank and the rest of Taka 12,50,000 by another cheque of AI-Baraka Bank (BD) Limited dated 11-8-1999. It was further contemplated in the said agreement that since the sellers(appellants) mortgaged the property in question with Islami Bank (BD) Ltd. prior to the said agreement, sale deed cannot be executed and registered without releasing the property from the said Bank upon repaying the entire loan. But, however, according to the terms of the agreement, possession in a portion of the said property was handed over to the purchaser respondent who was also allowed to put up a signboard in her own name upon expressing willingness to sell/allot different spaces for market/office/apartment/car parking to the interested persons. The purchaser respondent was also allowed to obtain clearance certificate from the RAJUK and get the plan approved and sale/allot the aforementioned spaces to various customers and receive money for the said purpose from the aspirant customers. The seller appellants under the said agreement were bound to assist the purchaser respondent in all respect. In. case the seller appellants would not co-operate with the purchaser in respect of the works mentioned above, the seller would be wholly responsible for the damages arising out of such non- co-operation. Under such circumstances, it is alleged by the respondent, that the seller- appellants, in violation of the terms of the said agreement did not handover the possession of the entire property along with all original documents upon executing the sale deed even upon receiving Taka 37,5.0,000 in advance for which the purchaser respondent, on various occasions requested the seller appellants, through her agent, to hand over the possession of the entire property along with all original papers. But the seller appellants did not comply with the same. Thus the purchaser respondent, on the basis of Clause No.6 of the said agreement gave a notice on 05.08.2002 to the seller appellants for arbitration upon appointing Mr. AFM Mesbahuddin, a former Judge of the High Court Division, as her Arbitrator and requested the seller appellants to appoint their Arbitrator within 30 days from the date of service of the said notice failing which the purchaser respondent would have no alternative but to take shelter of the Court under the existing law. The seller appellants received the said notice on 6-8-2002 but did not comply with the same. Thus the purchaser respondent, on 19-11-2002, filed an application before the learned District Judge, Dhaka, under section 12(3)(1)(ka) of the Arbitration Act 2001 (which came into force upon repealing the earlier Act of 1940), for appointment of Arbitrator.

2. The seller appellants, on 19-1-2003, filed written objection against the said application under section 12 contending, inter alia, that though the consideration money was fixed at Taka 3,68,00,000 but the condition of payment of Taka 50,00,000 as advance was not fully complied with as the cheque amounting to Taka 12,50,000 of AI-Baraka Bank, dated 11-8-1999 was dishonoured by the concerned bank. So the seller appellants having not received the entire advance money, due to the failure of the purchaser respondent, to comply with the condition of paying the entire advance amount within 4-11-1999 and the balance consideration money within the next 12 months, by equal monthly installments to be paid by the 4th day of every month from 4-12-1999, there was no question of handing over possession of the property along with the original documents. However, the seller appellants asserted that as the purchaser respondent violated the terms of agreement, they requested the purchaser and her husband to comply with the terms and conditions of the agreement but having not succeeded in the said effort, they were taking steps for referring the matter to the Arbitrator as per Arbitration Clause. But before they could appoint an Arbitrator the purchaser respondent moved the Court for appointment of Arbitrator. Hence the application for appointment of Arbitrator field by the purchaser should be dis- missed with cost for ends of justice.

3. In course of hearing of the application under section 12 before the learned District Judge, each party submitted list containing 3 names for appointment of Arbitrator. However, upon hearing the parties and on perusal of all the documents the learned District Judge, by his order dated 6-3-2003 appointed Mr. AFM Mesbahuddin as Arbitrator to enter into the reference and arbitrate the matter in accordance with law. Thereafter, the sole Arbitrator entered into the reference and issued notices upon the parties to file their respective claims and objections along with relevant papers by 6-4-2003. Both the parties appeared before the sole Arbitrator and filed their respective claims along with all supporting documents and got the matter heard by the said Arbitrator who, upon perusing all papers and documents placed before him passed an award of Taka 37,50,000 by his order dated 11-6-2003 in favour of the first party (purchaser respondent) along with interest at the rate of 6% per annum, from the date of agreement, till realization. Thereafter, copies of the award were sent to the respective parties and the same was also filed in the Court along with all documents. The seller appellants, on 6-7-2003, filed an application. for cancellation of the award dated 11- 6-2003, under section 42 read with section 43 of the Arbitration Act 2001, without stating any ground for cancellation, and also prayed for passing a fresh award of Taka 6,28,80,000 in their favour. The purchaser respondent, on 11-10-2003, filed written objection against the appellant's application dated 06-7-2003 for cancellation of award. Thereafter the seller appellants filed additional written objection on 18-5-2004 against the award dated 11-6-2003, incorporating the grounds for cancellation of the same which includes, amongst other, that the appointment of the sole Arbitrator was in violation of the Arbitration Agreement dated 4-8-99.

4. Under such circumstances the learned District Judge, by his order No.37 dated 28-3-2006, upon discussing the entire facts and circumstances and considering the various provisions of law, including section 43(1)(K)(D) of the Act, rejected the prayer of the seller appellants for cancellation of the award. Hence this appeal.

5. Mr. MI Farooque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the seller appellants, at the very outset submits that other than the question of appointment of sole Arbitrator, he, under the present law, cannot and shall not make any submission on the award. Thus he submits that section 43 under sub-section (1)(K)(D) clearly gives a right to the aggrieved party to pray for cancellation of the award when appointment/constitution of the Tribunal or the arbitral procedure is not consistent with or in accordance with the agreement. This right being a statutory right the aggrieved party can agitate the same at any time before any forum on the basis of the well settled principle "there is no estoppel against the statute". He next submits that the Arbitration Act 2001 being a special law it is governed by its own procedure, as such, the provisions of the Code of the Civil Procedure or the Evidence Act will not apply automatically, as contemplated in section 24 of the Arbitration Act 2001. So there is no question of applicability of estoppel or waiver as contemplated in the Evidence Act. Since the said section, gives statutory right to the aggrieved party to pray for cancellation of the award, it is immaterial whether any objection, as to appointment, was taken before the Arbitrator.

6. He next submits that although section 17 of the Act, 2001, described the jurisdiction of the arbitral Tribunal and 17(kha) specifically gave authority to the arbitral Tribunal to give decision on the question of its proper constitution/composition/ appointment, yet the aggrieved party can take the said plea for cancellation of the award under section 42 and 43 of the said Act, as the same has given a statutory relief in section 43. Then he submits that although the general principle of law is that the question as to jurisdiction or objection to jurisdiction is to be taken at the earliest stage, even then any party having not taken such objection earlier, can take such objection as a ground for cancellation of the award as provided in section 43(1)(ক)(উ) when such question affects the decision of the Arbitrator. In this respect he referred to section 105 of the Code of Civil Procedure as a principle of statute. Lastly, he submits that the learned District Judge, by appointing the nominee of the respondent as the sole Arbitrator, has committed illegality which is malice in law. As such, the appointment is contrary to the arbitration agreement. Thus the sole Arbitrator being not a neutral person the award passed by him is liable to be cancelled. In support of this submissions he relied on the cases of Hazrat Ali vs Election Commission, reported in 41 DLR 486; Darbari Lal Mudi vs Raneeganj Coal Association Ltd, reported in AIR (31) 1944 (Patna) 30; in Waverly Jute Mills Co. Ltd, vs Raymon and Company India (Pvt) Ltd (and connected appeals), reported in AIR 1963 (SC) 90 = 1963 (3) SCR 209 (judgment delivered on 4-5-1962 in Civil Appeal Nos. 389 to 392 of 1960) and also in the case of Khardah Company Limited vs Raymon and Company (India) Private Limited reported in AIR 1962 (SC) 1810 (Judgment delivered on 4-5-1962 in Civil Appeal Nos. 98 and 99 of 1960).

7. Mr. Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the purchaser respondent submits that the present Arbitration Act, 2001 is a consolidated statute which contains both procedural and substantive law dealing with different subjects at different stages under different chapters. According to him, the well settled principle in the legal arena is "objection as to jurisdiction/ constitution of a Court/ Tribunal is to be taken at the preliminary stage, before the same Court! Tribunal on the earliest possible opportunity." Thus section 6, under chapter II of the Act provides if such objection is not taken at the right time then it will be deemed that the said party has waived his right as to the same. Again chapter -IV (section 11 to 16) deals with appointment of Arbitrator, objection to appointment and appeal against any order as to appointment. Thus in the present case, if the appellants had any objection against the appointment of the sole Arbitrator under section 12 of the Act then they had opportunity to raise such objection against such appointment under section 13 and 14 of the Act. The appellants also had opportunity to raise such objection before the Arbitrator himself, as section 17 provides power to the Arbitrator / Tribunal, itself to decide any question as to its appointment/ constitution/ composition and section 19 provides the right to any party to the arbitration to raise such objection before filing the statement of claim or objection against the same whereupon the Tribunal is to give decision on such objection, raised before it. The Act under section 20, provides forum to challenge the decision of the Arbitrator before the High Court Division. Thus he submits that the appellants had a series of opportunity to challenge the appointment but having not availed any of the aforesaid forums provided under sections, 13, 14, 17, 19 and 20 of the Act it is clear that they have not only waived their right to raise such question, under section 6 but also are estoppel from doing so at a belated stage like after the completion of the arbitration proceedings and passing of the award. Relying on the well settled principle that 'a person cannot take advantage of his own wrong'; meaning a person, who did not avail the opportunity earlier is stopped from taking such objection at subsequent stage, as the appellants waived their right now they cannot take the same plea before any forum after the finality of the proceeding.

8. Referring to the case of Sree Sudhir Chandra Saha vs Matiran Bewa reported in 6 BLD (AD) 182, Mr. Rahman submits that when any party's conduct is in contravention to the well settled principle embodied in the legal maxim that 'no man shall take advantage of his own wrong' the plea of estoppel would be available to bar investigation of a question of fact about which a representation had been made so as to induce the other party to change his position to his prejudice and thus the principle that there being no estoppel against a statute', should only be invoked in such cases, when on the face of it, the contract is shown to be tainted with illegality. He next submits that in the present case the contract being not tainted with any illegality rather there being a valid contract, as the parties admittedly agreed to arbitrate the dispute and the Arbitrator having been appointed by the Court without any objection raised by either party against such appointment and the parties having entered appearance before the said Arbitrator and proceeded with the arbitration without any question as to the constitution/ appointment! jurisdiction of the arbitral Tribunal, the appellant now cannot take advantage of his own wrong upon taking advantage of the principle " there is no estoppel against statute" which cannot be invoked in this case. Lastly, Mr. Rahman submits that the question raised herein is a mere technicality, which will not stand in the way of a decision unless the decision appears to be illegal or apparently the decision is liable to be set aside. He submits that the award has been passed on the basis of admitted facts that the respondent paid and the appellants received Taka 37,50,000 as such the appellants were directed to repay/return the same amount to the respondent of course with 6% interest thereon. Thus, no evidence/paper having been filed by the appellants to show that the award passed is tainted with illegality, there will be no change in the decision, even if, the allegation as to technicality in appointing the Arbitrator is found to be not in accordance with law, is taken into consideration. Thus the decision neither appears to be illegal nor apparently the same is liable to be set aside. Mr. Rahman submits that the aforesaid principle could be invoked only in a case of inherent lack of jurisdiction, when consent or waiver cannot confer jurisdiction, as decided in the case of the Registrar, Supreme Court of Bangladesh vs Md Shafiuddin reported in 10 BLT (AD) 50. But in the present case there is no inherent lack of jurisdiction for which the appellant could take advantage of the said decision.

9. In support of his above contentions apart from the aforesaid decision, Mr. Rahman also relied on the cases of Bangladesh Fisheries Research Institute vs Mr. Bhuiyan Ltd, reported in 61 DLR 400; Bangladesh Water Development Board and others, vs Progati Prakaushali reported in 49 DLR 335; Sree Sudhir Chandra Saha vs Matiran Bewa being dead her heirs Nazmul Rahman Sarker, reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 182; AIR 1945 (Bom) 497 (In re All India Groundnut Syndicate Ltd), Gopal Krishna Das vs Abdul Kader Mia reported in 35 DLR 14; Nagendra Nath Sen Roy vs Saiyad Ali Jamadar, reported in 8 DLR 100; on the case of Abdus Samad Paramanik vs Mosammat Bilkis Khatun reported in BSCD Vol-VI Page 53; The Registrar, Supreme Court of Bangladesh vs Md Shafiuddin reported in 10 BLT (AD) 50; Chief Kwame asante Tredehene vs Chief Kwame Tawia reported in 9 DLR 686; Muhammad Saghir Bhatti and Sons vs Federation of Pakistan, reported in 10 DLR (SC) 169 and in the case of Pubali Bank Ltd vs Contech Ltd. reported in 27 BLD 133. Thus he submits that considering the facts of the case and the principle laid down in the above decisions the appeal is liable to be dismissed with costs.

10. Heard the learned advocates, perused the record and the decisions referred above. On perusal of the record, it appears that the learned District Judge, upon perusing the papers filed by both the parties and upon hearing the parties, appointed Mr. AFM Meshbauddin, the Arbitrator to arbitrate the dispute between the parties in accordance with Arbitration Act 2001 by his order No.5 dated 6-3-2003 and directed the Arbitrator to submit the award in the said Court by 7-5-2003 which was subsequently extended till 11-6-2003 by order dated 5.5.2003 on the prayer of the parties. Thereafter, the said Arbitrator entered into the reference and accordingly, Arbitration Case No. 1 of 2003 was commenced. By Order No. 1 dated 6-4-2003 the Arbitrator, notified the parties and directed them to appear before him and produce all necessary papers and documents, by 10-4-2003. Upon receipt of such notices the parties appeared before the sole Arbitrator and fi led their respective claims, and counter claims along with all supporting papers. It appears from the record that the seller-appellants filed their claim before the Arbitrator on 13-5-2003, without raising any objection as to the appointment or as to the Arbitrator's jurisdiction. Rather it appears that they prayed for passing an award of Taka 6,28,80,000 in their favour. The purchaser respondent on 24-5-2003, filed written objection against the said claim of the seller appellants denying the allegations made therein and on the contrary prayed for an award in her favour claiming Taka 70,00,000 along with interests at the rate of 16% per annum on the said amount till realisation of the same. The learned Arbitrator upon considering the evidences, both oral and documentary, adduced by the parties passed the award dated 11-6-2003, which is under challenge in this appeal. However, since the learned advocate for the appellants admits that he cannot and as such shall not argue on merit of the award but he will simply argue on the appointment and jurisdiction of the Arbitrator so the point, in the instant appeal, for determination is whether the appointment of the sole Arbitrator under section 12 of the Act by the learned District Judge can be called in question after the award is passed upon hearing the parties, without any objection on such question being raised any time before the Tribunal and whether the Arbitrator had jurisdiction to pass the award in question, which has been challenged herein under section 42/43 of the Act.

11. Admittedly, no objection as to the appointment of the Arbitrator, made under section 12 of the Act was ever taken before any forum. The provision of law regarding appointment of Arbitrator, grounds for objection as to appointment, procedure as to raising objection, Arbitrator's competence to rule on its own jurisdiction, objection as to the Arbitrator's jurisdiction and moving the High Court against the objection as to appointment or against any decision of the Arbitrator on the question of its own jurisdiction categorically provided for in sections 12, 13, 14,15, 17,19 and 20 of the Arbitration Act 2001. Section 12 deals with appointment of Arbitrator. The other provisions mentioned above read as follows:

১৩। আপত্তির কারণসমূহ - (১) সালিশকারী হিসাবে নিয়োগের অনুরোধ প্রাপ্ত প্রত্যেক ব্যক্তি প্রথমে তাহার নিরপেকক্ষতা ও স্বাধীনতা সর্ম্পকে সঙ্গত সন্দেহের উদদ্ভব হইতে পারে এইরূপ সকল পরিস্থিতি প্রকাশ করিবেন।

(২) প্রত্যেক সালিসকারী তাহার নিয়োগের সময় হইতে সালিসী কার্যধারা চলাকালীন যে কোন সময়ে উপ-ধারা (১) এ উল্লেখিত পরিস্থিতি অনতিবিলম্বে চুক্তির সকল পক্ষকে এবং অন্য সকল সালিসকারী অবগত করিবেন, যদি ইতোমধ্যে তাহারা তৎসম্পর্কে অবহিত না হইয়া থাকেন।

(৩) কোন সালিসকারীর বিরুদ্ধে আপত্তি উত্থাপন করা যাইবে যদি তাহার নিরপেক্ষতা ও স্বাধীনতা সম্পর্কে সন্দেহ থাকার কোন পরিস্থিতি বিদ্যমান থাকে বা পক্ষগণ কর্তৃক সম্মত যোগ্যতা তাহার না থাকে।

(৪) সালিসকারী নিয়োগদানকারী বা সালিসকারী নিয়োগে সম্মতিদানকারী কোন পক্ষ, উক্ত নিয়োগের পরবর্তী সময়ে তাহার জানা কোন পরিস্থিতির কারণে, উক্ত সালিসকারীর বিরুদ্ধে আপত্তি দিতে পারিবেন।

১৪। আপত্তি দায়ের পদ্ধতি-

(১)	উপ-ধারা (৬) এর বিধান সাপেক্ষে, পক্ষগণ সালিসের বিরুদ্ধে আপত্তি দায়েরের পদ্ধতি নিরূপনের সম্মত হওয়ার ক্ষেত্রে স্বাধীন থাকিবে।

(২)	উপ-ধারা (১) এ উল্লেখিত সম্মতিতে উপনীত হইতে ব্যর্থতার ক্ষেত্রে কোন পক্ষ কোন সালিসকারীর বিরুদ্ধে আপত্তি দায়ের করিতে চাহিলে উক্ত পক্ষ ধারা ১৩ এর উপ-ধারা (৩) এ উল্লিখিত পরিস্থিতি সম্পর্কে অবগত হওয়ার ত্রিশ দিনের মধ্যে লিখিত বিবৃতির মাধ্যমে আপত্তির কারণসমূহ বর্ণনা করিয়া সালিসী ট্রাইব্যুনালের নিকট আপত্তি দায়ের করিবে।

12. On a plain reading of the aforesaid provisions of law it is very clear that any objection as to appointment, jurisdiction or neutrality and independence of the Arbitrator is required to be taken at the earliest opportunity if not before any forum but before the Arbitrator himself prior to filing their respective claims, under section 14(2) and the Arbitrator upon receiving such objection is duty bound to give decision on the same within 30 days from the date of filing of such objection as provided in section 14(3). If any party is aggrieved by such decision he has a right to prefer appeal before the High Court Division under section 14(4) within 30 days of the date of such decision and the High Court Division will give decision on the matter within 90 days of filing of the appeal as provided in section 14(5). Section 15 also provides right to the parties to apply for removal of the Arbitrator through Court. Moreover, under section 17 the arbitral Tribunal has the power to decide any question, including its own jurisdiction and also to decide whether the constitution has been made is accordance with law. Again section 19(1) clearly provides that any objection as to jurisdiction/appointment is to be raised before the arbitral Tribunal before filing of the written objection and section 19(2) provides for raising objection as to exceeding his authority to be taken immediately during the course of continuation of the proceeding. Section 19(3) provides for condonation of delay in filing the aforesaid objections and under section 19(4) the Tribunal is duly bound to give decision on such objections. Section 20 provides for moving the High Court Division for remedy in case any party is aggrieved by the decision given under section 19.

13. So from the aforesaid provisions of law it is clear that where any party submits to the arbitral Tribunal and continues with the proceedings without raising any objection, at any stage, as to any particular issue, not to speak of any technicality like its constitution/jurisdiction and thereafter if the Tribunal is allowed to pass an award on contest, such party is deemed to have waived his right of raising such objection in future, under section 6 of the Act, and as such shall not be entitled to take objection as to the validity of the award on the ground of want of the constitution or jurisdiction of the Arbitrator. Section 6 reads as follows:

৬। আপত্তির অধিকার পরিত্যাগ। - কোন পক্ষ-

(ক) পক্ষগণ ব্যত্যয় ঘটাইতে পারে এই আইনের এমন কোন বিধান প্রতিপালিত হয় নাই, বা

(খ) সালিস চুক্তির অধীন কোন আবশ্যকতা প্রতিপালিত হয় নাই-মর্মে অবগত থাকিয়া উক্ত পক্ষ যদি অযৌক্তিক বিলম্ব ব্যতীত বা তদবিষয়ে কোন সময়সীমা থাকিলে অনুররূপ সময়সীমার মধ্যে আপত্তি না করিয়া সালিসে অগ্রসর হয়, তাহা হইলে উক্ত পক্ষ আপত্তির অধিকার পরিত্যাগ করিয়াছে বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে।

14. In the present appeal, since after the appointment of the Arbitrator the appellant got opportunity to raise objection as to appointment and / or jurisdiction of the Arbitrator but did not raise any objection, whatsoever, at the appropriate time nor they availed the opportunity under section 19(3) or before any other forum rather participated in the proceeding resulting in passing of the award, they, under section 6 of the Act, have waived the right to raise such objection by their conduct and acquiescence and as such estoppel in law from challenging the validity of the reference as well as the award. In the case of Fisheries Research Institute vs MR Bhuiyan Ltd., (61 DLR 400) a Division Bench of this Court held that the point of jurisdiction depending upon the determination of this contentions question of fact between the parties which manifests a go-by by the party by joining in the petition to the Court asking it to make a reference to arbitration and further by taking part in the proceedings before the Arbitrator. Thus it is not open to the said party now to turn around and say that the Arbitrator has no jurisdiction. Moreover, objection as to jurisdiction being "technical" in nature, the same is not tenable at a belated stage. This view finds support in the case of Coal Controller vs Ventura Industries Ltd, reported in 45 DLR (AD)183 where the apex Court observed that this objection is a technical objection which the petitioner could have raised before. Thus when the Arbitrator has already entered on the reference and has started issuing notices to the parties the Court held we 'are not inclined to entertain this technical objection at this stage. In the present appeal the appellants did not raise any objection at any stage before any forum and they allowed the Arbitrator to complete the proceeding and pass the award. So having regard to the aforesaid decisions their objection at such belated stage is not at all maintainable in law. Again in the case of Adamjee Sons Ltd. vs Jibon Bima Corporation, reported in 45 DLR 89 it has been held that where the parties submit to the arbitration and making prayer for passing the award, such parties cannot be allowed to take objection as to the validity of the award on the ground of want of jurisdiction of the Arbitrator. In the case of Pakistan Trading Company vs MM Ispahani Ltd, reported in 11 DLR 405 it has been held that when the petitioner submitted to the Arbitrator with his eyes wide open and knowing fully well that the particular Arbitrator is a member of the arbitration, it is not now open to him to say that he has got a reasonable apprehension that he will not get a proper and fair trial before the said Arbitrator. Thus, in the present case, the appellants, admittedly, having not taken any objection, whatsoever, before the Arbitrator and such action of the appellants having led the other side to believe that such right will not be enforced they are now precluded from taking any such objection at a belated stage like after passing of the award on contest. This view finds support in the case of Ocean lndustries Ltd. and another vs Industrial Development Bank, reported in 18 DLR (SC) 354. Again, in the case of Pathumma vs Kuntaklan Kutty, reported in AIR 1981 (SC) 1683 and in the case of Pakistan vs Abdul Kuddus, reported in PLD 1961(Dacca) 616, it has been held that objection as to jurisdiction can be allowed at the appellate stage if three conditions are fulfilled they are: (i) The objection was taken in the Court of first instance (ii) it was taken at the earliest possible opportunity and in case where issues are settled at or before such settlement; and (iii) there has been a consequent failure of justice. But the appellants have miserably failed to show that their case falls within any of the above noted conditions.

15. We have gone through the citations, referred by the learned advocates for both the parties and we have also perused a series of decisions of the subcontinent, including those of our apex Court. Upon considering all the decisions mentioned above we are of the view that the appellants having not availed the opportunity of raising objection as to the appointment or as to the jurisdiction of the sole Arbitrator, at the earliest possible stage at the first instance, they have waived the right to raise such objection and thus now they cannot take advantage of their own wrong and as such their objection for cancellation of the award, under section 43(1)(ক)(উ) is not maintainable, at this belated stage. Section 43(1)(ক)(উ) reads as follows:

“৪৩। সালিস রোয়েদাদ বাতিলের কারণসমুহ- (১) কোন সালিসী রোয়েদাদ বাতিল করা যাইতে পারে, যদি-(ক) কোন পক্ষ আবেদন দাখিল করিয়া এই মর্মে প্রমাণ উপস্থাপন করে যে-

(অ).............................................

(আ).............................................

(ই)..............................................

(ঈ)..............................................

(উ) সালিসী ট্রাইব্যুনালের গঠন সালিসী পদ্ধতি পক্ষগণের চুক্তির সহিত সংগতিপূর্ণ ছিল না অথবা এইরূপ চুক্তির অবর্তমানে এই আইনের বিধানাবলীর সহিত সংগতিপূর্ণ নয়।”

16. From a reading of the aforesaid statutory provision of section 43(1)(ক)(উ) it appears that the appellants are required to make out a case that the constitution/appointment of the arbitral Tribunal or the arbitration proceeding was not consistent with the arbitration agreement. But nothing as such has been made out or proved by the appellants in that manner anywhere at the earliest stage. Though the said provision provides for filing an application for cancellation of the award on the ground of constitution/Jurisdiction but the general principle as settled by the superior Courts categorically say that such objection is required to be taken at the initial stage and then when such objection, raised before the Arbitrator challenging his appointment/jurisdiction, has been failed and/or in case the Arbitrator, proceeded with the arbitration inspite of such objection having been raised before him and rejected, and passed an award, only then the aggrieved party can take such objection as a ground for cancellation of the award under section 43(1)(ক)(উ). Otherwise the provisions of sections 6, 13, 14, 15 and 17 will be redundant. In the present case since the appellants did not avail the opportunity of raising any such objection at the initial stage before the Arbitrator himself which gave an impression to the respondent that they would not avail the right of objection as to appointment/jurisdiction and thereby allowed the proceeding to be completed as such, now, we are of the view, that such objection cannot be taken at a belated stage as a ground for cancellation of the award passed on contest. If that be allowed then the appellants would be given a chance to take advantage of their own wrong done earlier by not taking proper step at proper time as decided by the Appellate Division in the case reported in 6 BLD (AD) 182 referred earlier. It is true that there is no estoppel against statute. But question is whether this principle can be invoked by one to take advantage of his own wrong/ fraud, to the detriment of the other party, who was given a bonafide belief,. by not invoking the right at the proper time, that the right to raise such objection has been waived. The said principle as to "no estoppel against statute," can only be attracted when the statute appears to defeat the public policy not in the present case where a private interest is involved under no circumstances can be attracted to defeat the public policy as appears from the facts and circumstances discussed above. Thus in the instant case the submissions of the learned advocate for the appellants that "there is no estoppel against the statute" is not tenable.

17. Moreover, the award having been passed on the admitted portion of the claim of Taka 37,50,000 only the same appears to be otherwise valid as such we are of the view that there has not been any consequent failure of justice in passing the same. The Court of law cannot and shall not interfere with and/ or review such award or set aside the same on the ground of technicality or that the Arbitrator exceeded his authority or had no jurisdiction to pass such award or to arbitrate the dispute when a party complaining, has not / or did not make any protest at the earliest stage of the hearing, before the Arbitrator or Tribunal. Thus the award being not tainted with illegality, as the same is passed on the admitted facts, there will be no change in the decision even if the technical objection is taken into consideration. Under the facts and circumstances the award cannot be said to have been passed having inherent lack of jurisdiction. Moreover the superior Courts held "Since the party did not raise any objection to the appointment and jurisdiction and the Arbitrator continued with the arbitration, the party is estopped by his conduct from challenging the said Arbitrator's jurisdiction to act as such". (Federation of Pakistan vs Ghulam Mohiuddin, reported in PLD 1960 (Lah) 677); and If the award is otherwise valid the Court of law cannot interfere with and review it and the Court will not set aside the award on the ground that the Arbitrator has exceeded his authority when the parties complaining has made no protest at the hearing before the Arbitrator'. [PLD 1973 (Kar) 413 = 1973 Law Note 376 (DB)). We do not find any reason to accept the contention of the learned advocate for the appellants.

<u>18. For the aforesaid reasons we are of the view that the appointment of the sole Arbitrator made under section 12 of the Act being not objected to by the appellants at any time before any authority at the earliest possible stage, such appointment /jurisdiction of the Arbitrator cannot be called in question after the award is passed. Hence the same cannot be the ground for cancellation of the award under section 43(1)(ক)(উ) as the appellants waived their statutory right of such objection under section 6 of the Act and as such now they cannot take advantage of their own wrong upon changing their earlier stance. Thus we hold that the Arbitrator had jurisdiction to pass the award as from the conduct of the parties, specially the appellants having expressed their consent through their actions in appearing, filing claims and papers before the sole Arbitrator, without raising any objection as to his appointment or challenging his jurisdiction in accordance with law, at any time earlier and took a chance of a favourable decision and when the decision has gone against them, now they cannot be allowed to take advantage of their own wrong and thereby take shelter of section 43(1)(ক)(উ) of the Arbitration Act.</u>

Accordingly we do not find any merit in this appeal. Hence the appeal is dismissed and the connected Rule is also discharged without any order as to cost.

End.

Vs.

full_judgment:
Sheikh Hassan Arif J: Rule was issued calling upon the respondent to show cause as to why their refusal/denial to mutate the property situated at Plot No. N(W)H Block-6, 159 Gulshan Avenue, Gulshan-2, Dhaka in the name of the petitioner upon receiving the transfer fee on the consideration money as directed by the High Court Division in FA No. 585 of 2001 should not be declared to be without lawful authority and is of no legal effect, and why they should not be directed to mutate the said property in the name of the petitioner by receiving the transfer fee.

2. Short fact, as appear from the relevant documents annexed to the writ petition, are that the land and the building thereon at plot No. N(W)H, Block-6, 159 Gulshan Avenue, Gulshan-2, Dhaka (hereinafter called "the said property") originally belonged to one Mrs lnge Flatz (an Austrian Lady) by virtue of a lease deed dated 14-9-1965 executed by the then Dhaka Improvement Trust (DIT) in her favour for 99 years. After Liberation, since the said property became abandoned under the provisions of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 ("PO 16 of 1972"), the said Lady applied to the Government for release of the same on the plea that it was wrongly vested as abandoned property whereupon the government divested the said property, executed a registered sale Deed in her favour on 21-6-1980, and accordingly restored her possession. The said Lady, thereafter, executed an Agreement for Sale on 10-8-1985 through her constituted Attorney, Mr Mohasin Darbar, agreeing to sell the said property in favour of the petitioner upon receiving certain portion of consideration money and put him in possession. However, since she failed to execute the registered sale deed as per the sale agreement, the petitioner filed a spit for specific performance of contract before the First Subordinate Judge, Dhaka which was subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No.279 of 1999 being transferred to the then Additional Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. The suit was contested by RAJUK (defendant No.3) but not by the Government (defendant No. 2). Never the less, the trial Court having dismissed the suit, the petitioner preferred First Appeal No.585 of 2001 before the High Court Division which was contested by Government, but not by RAJUK. The High Court Division, upon hearing the contesting parties, decreed the suit by judgment and Decree dated 15- 12-2005 and, consequently, directed the Government to execute and register a sale deed in favour of the petitioner within 60 days as it transpired, at the time of appeal-hearing, that the said property had in the meantime vested in the Republic in view of Article 143 of the Constitution because of the death of the said Lady intestate and her attorney. In the said decree, the High Court Division further direct- ed respondent RAJUK "to accord necessary permission receiving the legal transfer fee as per consideration money within the date for facilitating the execution and registration of the sale deed in default of which the plaintiff shall be at liberty to get the sale deed executed and registered through Court in accordance with law". RAJUK's belated attempt to have this decree set-aside by the Appellate Division (in Civil petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2027 of 2008) having been failed, the petitioner filed execution case and got the registered sale deed executed on 24-9-2006 in his favour through the executing court. Accordingly, the petitioner submitted application before the RAJUK to have the said property mutated in his name upon payment of transfer fee as per the terms of the said decree, but the RAJUK having refused to do so, he has moved this Court and obtained the Rule.

3. The respondent RAJUK has entered appearance and contested the Rule by filing affidavit-in- opposition contending mainly that the petitioner having failed to pay the transfer fee and submit required papers, they could not mutate the said property. In addition, they contend that since the said property has been included in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned properties through Gazette Notification dated 23-9-1986, no transfer of the said property, as claimed in the write petition, is tenable in law, and, as such, unless the petitioner gets the said property excluded from the Ka list in accordance with the provisions of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. 54 of 1985) ("the said Ordinance") no direction can be given by this Court upon RAJUK as prayed for.

4. Mr Moudud Ahmed, the learned Advocate, has extensively argued in favour of the petitioner. On the other hand, Mr Mahbubey Alam, the learned Attorney General of Bangladesh has appeared on behalf of RAJUK and vigorously argued issued against issuance of any declaration and/or direction as per the terms of the Rule.

5. Mr Moudud Ahmed submits that the property in question admittedly belonged to the said Austrian Lady under a registered leased deed executed by the then DIT. He argues that although the said property once vested in the Government Wrongly, the Government, upon rectifying the mistake, divested the same and accordingly executed a registered sale deed on 21-06-1980 in favour of the said Lady and restored her possession. Referring to several letters of the Government and RAJUK at the relevant time (Annexures- X-1 to X-5 to the petitioner's Affidavit-in-Reply), he submits that after such sale deed and restoration of possession neither the Government nor the RAJUK can now take advantage of the said 'Ka' list merely because the Government mistakenly included the said property in it. He argues that after such sale, the said lady became the absolute lease-hold owner of the said property subject to the terms of the sale deed and after that she executed the said agreement for sale on 10-8-1985. Therefore, he submits, even if the said property is included subsequently in the list published under the said Ordinance, the same is the result I of non-application of mind by the Government official and a mistake on the face of it and, as such, will carry no legal consequence. He alternatively argues that since the possession of the said property was never taken by the Government after he said sale, inclusion of the same in the 'Ka' list is also an act without jurisdiction. According to him since the High Court Division in its judgment passed in First Appeal No. 585 of 2001 directly or indirectly took into consideration all these circumstances and categorically held that the petitioner had been able to prove all relevant documents including the sale deed executed by the Government (Exhibit- 2) and accordingly directed RAJUK to mutate the said property in his favour, the petitioner has acquired a legally enforceable right and, as such, he is entitled to the directions in the form of mandamus from this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

6. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, the learned Attorney General, on the other hand, raised a very basic legal question as to the consequences of inclusion of a building in the 'Ka' list published under section 5(l)(a) of the said Ordinance. He first submits that since the decree in question is a decree for specific performance of contract, it is not a decree as contemplated in proviso (a) to section 5 of the said Ordinance, i.e. Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, and, as such, there was no bar in inclusion of the said property in the list published under section 5(1)(a). In this regard, he refers to the majority decision of our apex Court in CQMH Md Ayub Ali vs Bangladesh reported in 47 DLR (AD) 71 and Mrs Amena Khatun vs Chairman, Court of Statement reported in 15 MLR (AD) 438 = 63 DLR (AD) 1. He further submits that since the said property has been included, rightly or wrongly, in the list published under section 5(1 )(a), in view of sub-section (2) of section 5 of the said Ordinance, it is now a conclusive evidence of the fact that the said property is abandoned property and, as such, vested in the government, and accordingly, the onus is now on the petitioner to prove that the same is not abandoned property, and he can only prove that before a Court of Settlement in view of the provisions of section 7. In this regard he cites some other cases of our apex court, namely the cases of Government of Bangladesh vs Md Jalil 48 DLR (AD) 10; Hazerullah vs Chairman, 1st Court of Settlement, 3 BLC (AD) 42; Government of Bangladesh vs Ali , 49 DLR (AD) 161; Asma Begum vs Bangladesh, 21 BLD (AD) 134; arid Bangladesh vs Rowshan Ara, 57 DLR (AD) 167. He again argues that since the 'Ka' list was published on 23-9-1986, the suit in question, admittedly filed after publication of the said list, was barred by section 6 of the said Ordinance and, as such, the decree passed by the High Court Division arising out of the said suit was also barred, and as such, the petitioner has acquired to legal right by the said decree.

7. Heard the learned advocates of both the sides, perused the writ petition, affidavit-in-opposition, affidavit-in-reply and material papers on record. Since the suit and the decree in the instant matter are developments that to place after publication of the 'Ka' list in question, the restrictions provided in the proviso (a) & (b) to section 5 of the said  Ordinance have no manner of application in the present case. Consequently, the submissions of Mr Mahbubey Alam along with the decisions of our apex Court on that point deserve no consideration.

8. It appears that there is no dispute as to the initial title of the original lease-hold owner, the Austrian Lady. Several matters and papers relied upon by the parties in this case have been proved in the aforementioned Title Suit by the judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 545 of 2001. The admitted position is that after the independence of Bangladesh in 1971, the said property vested in the Government by operation of the provisions of PO 16 of 1972. After such vesting, the original owner filed an application before the Government to release her property on the plea the same was wrongly vested. Upon this, the Government by letter dated 13-5-1980 (Annexure-X-1 to the Affidavit-in-Reply) informed the said Lady Its decision to divest the said property in her favour. Relevant portion of the said letter is quoted below:

"Government of the People's Republic of

Bangladesh

Ministry of Public Works & Urban Development

No. XVII/IP-Gul-61/76/Pt/282

Dated: Dacca the 13th May, 1980.

From: HR Datta

Deputy Secretary

To : Mrs Inge Flatz

C/o His Excellency Georg Hennig,

Ambassador of Austria,

New Delhi, India.

Subject : Restoration of abandoned house No. NW (H)-6, Road No. 159, Gulshan Avenue, Dacca to its original owner Mrslnge Flatz an Austrian citizen.

The undersigned is directed to say that Government have been pleased to decide that the above house vested in the Government as an abandoned property would be transferred to her by a registered deed of sale. On fulfillment of the following terms and conditions :-

1.	Nominal consideration money of Taka 100 (Taka one hundred) only fixed for sale of the house shall be paid by her. The consideration money may be deposited to the Head of account XXXIX-Civil Works- Misc. of this Government through treasury in the Bangladesh Bank, Dhaka.

2.	All expenses involved in the registration of the sale deed shall be borne by her as the transferee.

She is therefore, requested to deposit the amount of Taka 100 (Taka one hundred) only to the Head of Account mentioned above and to see the undersigned or to send her representative duly authorized by her, for Registration of the proposed sale deed.

Sd/-HR Datta

Deputy Secretary"

9. One of the copies of the above letter was forwarded to the then DIT (presently RAJUK). After such decision, the Government executed a registered Sale Deed on 21-6-1980 (Annexure-X to the Affidavit-in-Reply) transferring the said property and restoring possession therein in her favour. The Sale deed stipulated that she would hold the said property subject to the convents and conditions contained in the Lease Deed dated 14-9-1965 executed by the then DIT in her favour meaning, amongst others, that she would hold it under RAJUK upon mutation. Under Clause-4 of the said Sale Deed, the Government recognized her peaceful possession in the said property.

10. Therefore, since Articles 4 and 5(2)(e) &(i) of PO 16 of 1972 have conferred ample power on the Government to dispose of the abandoned property in any manner including "transfer by way of sale", there should remain no semblance of doubt that the said property was divested lawfully and ceased to be an abandoned property and more, and as such, the said lady did have saleable interest on 10-8-1985 when she executed the said Agreement for Sale in favour of the petitioner. Even RAJUK in paragraph 21 of their affidavit-in-opposition admitted that the said property was sold by the government in 1980 and that they found support of the said fact in a letter dated 13-5-1980 of the concerned ministry. Therefore, after such divesting of the said property by the government itself, we are of the view that, no question can be raised from any side as to the character of the said property at any subsequent stage.

11. Now the question is whether after divesting of an abandoned property even if the property remains or included in the list published under section 5(1)(a) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, will that carry the legal consequences as provided by sub-section (2) of section 5, section 6 arid section 7 of the said Ordinance?

Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 has made provisions supplemental to the provisions of PO No. 16 of 1972. Consequently, when Sub-section (2) of section 5 provided that the list published under Sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of certain facts these facts are some incidents which occurred or took place on 28-2-1972, the date of commencement of PO No. 16 of 1972. Thus the legal consequence is that the property included in the list vested in the government on 28-2-1972, in view of Article 4 of the PO No. 16 of 1972, and the same is still abandoned property.

12. Here, there is no dispute that the property in question had in fact vested, rightly or wrongly, in the Government on 28-02-1972 by operation of PO No. 16 of 1972.There is also no dispute that the same has subsequently been divested through the aforesaid sale by Government in exercise of power under Articles-4 and 5(2) (e) & (i) of PO No. 16 of 1972.Now, under such circumstances, can there be any presumption, for any practical purpose, under sub-section (2) of section 5 of the Ordinance that the said property again vested in the Government on 28-2-1972 under PO No. 16 of 1972? In other words, can the same property vest twice? Or can there be double-presumptions, or can a matter already closed under the parent law be reopened subsequently under the supplemental law? The answer to all these .questions is 'No'. We find support of our this view in Sarwari Begum vs Bangladesh, 45 DLR 571 (at para 16). In this case, a' division bench of this Court also held (at para 17.& 18) that in such situation the petitioner can directly come to the High Court Division under Article 102(1) for enforcement of his/her fundamental' right to property guaranteed under Article 42 of the Constitution.

13. There is no such provision of double vesting or double-presumption either in PO No. 16 of 1972 or in Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. Thus, if a property is included in the list published under section 5(i)(a) of the said Ordinance even after the said property is admittedly divested, that inclusion is nothing but either a result of mistake on the face of it or is a product of non-application of mind by the officials vested with the responsibility or prepare the list, In both' situations, the inclusion is an act without jurisdiction and, as such, the said property should be deemed to have never included in the said list on the principle that an act without jurisdiction is an act never existed in the eye of law (void abinitio). Therefore, since the inclusion of the said property in the 'Ka' list is a non-existent act, we are of the view that, it does not carry with it any presumption or legal consequences as provided by sections 5(2), 6 and 7 of the said Ordinance as submitted by Mr Mahbubey Alam. Accordingly, the decisions of our apex court, as cited by Mr Alam on the point of presumption and legal consequences of inclusion of a building in the 'Ka' list, are not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case.

14. In the present case, since the said property has been included apparently as a result of either mistake or non-application of mind, the question of discharging any onus by the petitioner does not arise. Here the Government itself rebutted the presumption by its acts. Here the petitioner has stepped into the shoes of the said Austrian Lady and, as such, there is no onus on him to prove that the said property is not an abandoned property - because of the fact that the said property was divested by the Government itself in accordance with law and the inclusion of the same in the 'Ka' list in an act without jurisdiction. Thus, since the inclusion in the said list never existed in the eye of law, we are also dis-inclined to agree with the submissions of Mr Alam to the effect that the suit and the decree in question were barred by section 6 of the said Ordinance or that the petitioner should first go to the Court of Settlement under section 7 - even long after expiry of limitation period of 180 days. We are of the view that the unique facts in the present case deserve different approach, if not unique approach.

<u>15. Further, once a property is released by government from the clutch of abandoned properties, it cannot even subsequently cancel the said release order as there is no such provisions either in PO No. 16 of 1972 or in Ordinance 54 of 1985 allowing such cancellation. This view of our High Court Division in Messrs ATJ Industries case [28 DLR 27] was not interfered with by our apex Court in the same case on appeal [see 28 DLR (AD) 120]. The same principle is applicable in the present case, although the petitioner stands on the better footing - as the divesting of the said property has never been cancelled subsequently by the Government in the present case. [see also Ayesha Khatun s Case, 50 DLR 639]. This being so, we should not throwaway this petition and ask the petitioner to go to the Court of Settlement just because his property was included in the said 'Ka' list mistakenly. Since the inclusion of the said property in the 'Ka' list is ex-facie void for want of jurisdiction, we are of the view that he can come directly to the High Court Division to enforce his fundamental right guaranteed under Article 42 of the Constitution [see Bangladesh vs Syed Chand Sultana, 51 DLR (AD) 24, at para-4]. Thus, we have no hesitation to hold that RAJUK's refusal was without lawful authority and, as such, it has no option but to mutate the said property in the name of the petitioner upon accepting the transfer fee as per the terms of the decree passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 585 of 2001.</u>

16. In the facts and circumstances of the case and for the reasons stated above, we are of the view .that the petitioner has been able to establish his right to seek a direction under Article 120(1) & (2)(a)(i) of the Constitution and, as such, the Rule should be made absolute.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

Respondent RAJUK is directed to mutate the said property situated at Plot No. N(W)H Block-6, 159 Gulshan Avenue, Gulshan-2, Dhaka in the name of the petitioner upon receiving the transfer fee On the consideration money as directed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No, 585 of 2001 within 30 days from receipt of the copy of this judgment.

Communicate this order.

End.
