... They provide 'the flesh which clothes the dry bones of the law, they make the legal situation work, they keep in touch with the growth of ideas; a Constitution does not work itself, it is worked by men."

113. Above view was expressed by Mr Desai, J on behalf of the majority of seven Judges' bench. In the Supreme Court Advocates-an-Record Association vs Union of India: AIR 1994 SC 268 = (1993) 4 SCC 441 popularly known as Second Judges' Case, the constitutional bench of nine Judges considered the correctness of the ratio in SP Gupta on the status of Chief Justice of India in the matter of appointment of Judges for efficient functioning of the judicial system. On the conventions it was expressed, inter alia,:

"We agree that a convention while it is a convention ought to be distinguished from the law. But this does not mean that what was formerly a convention cannot later become law.

When customary rules are recognised and enforced by Courts as law, there is no reason why a convention cannot be crystallised into a law and become enforceable. 'Conventions' can become law also by judicial recognition' stated KC Wheare in 'Modern Constitution' 1966. Edition. ...

It is no doubt correct that the existence of a particular convention ought to be established by evidence on the basis of historical events and expert factual submissions. But once it is established in the Court of law that particular convention witness and constitutional functionaries are following the same as a binding precedent then there is no justification to deny to such a convention the status of law".

We are of the view there is no distinction between the 'constitutional law' and an 'established constitutional convention' and both are binding in field of their operation. Once it is established to the satisfaction of the Court that a particular convention exists and is operating then the convention becomes a part of the 'Constitutional law' of the land and can be enforced in the like manner."

114. In AI-Jehad Trust case, five Judges' bench of the Supreme Court of Pakistan accepted said nine Judges' view on the Constitutional convention as hereunder:

" ... the Courts while construing a Constitutional provision, can press into service an established constitutional convention in order to understand the import and working of the same, if it is not contrary to the express provision of the Constitution."

115. On the above authorities, we endorse the view of a Division Bench of this Division in the case of Manabjamin: 57 DLR 359 at page 455,

" ... a review of all the aforesaid authorities leads us to the irresistible conclusion that there is no distinction between the 'Constitutional law' and an 'established Constitutional convention' and both are binding in the field of their operation. Once it is established to the satisfaction of the Court that a particular convention exists and is operating then the convention becomes part of the 'Constitutional law' of the land and can be enforced in the like manner."

116. Under Article 152 of the Constitution 'law' is defined to mean any act, ordinance, order, rule, bye-law, notification or other legal instrument, and any custom or usage having the force of law in Bangladesh. There are various rules of customs or usage, namely, right to light or right to pathway, which do not form part of any codified law but are enforced by the Courts in Bangladesh as a law of the land.

117. Similarly, in the absence of written provision for consultation since 1975, consultation with the Chief Justice before appointment of Judges to the Supreme Court is followed and practiced by all administrations. Now, existence and operation of such convention in the matter of appointments of Judges to the Supreme Court is recognised by all the constitutional functionaries including the President and has therefore, become a part of the Constitutional law and accordingly, binding on the executive just like any other Constitutional provision.

118. What is meant by 'consultation with the Chief Justice' in the appointment of the Judges received close attention in the aforesaid decisions of both India and Pakistan. Mr Subba Rao, J (later Chief Justice of India) in R Pushpam vs State of Madras: AIR 1953 Madras 292 (at page 393) observed that,

"A person consults another to be elucidated on the subject matter of consultation. The consultation may be between an uninformed person and an expert or between two experts. A patient consults the doctor; a client consults his lawyer; two lawyers or two doctors may hold consultation between themselves. In either case, the final decision is with the consultor, but he will not generally ignore the advice except for good reasons."

119. In Shamsher Singh's case: AIR 1974 SC 2192 at page 2228 para 148, V R Krishna Iyer, J observed that,

" ... We are of the view that the President means, for all practical purposes, the Minister or Council of Ministers as the case may be and his opinion, satisfaction or decision is constitutionally secured when his Ministers arrived at such opinion, satisfaction or decision. The independence of the Judiciary, which is a cardinal principle of the Constitution and has been relied on to justify the deviation, is guarded by the relevant Article making consultation with the Chief Justice of India obligatory.

... in all conceivable cases consultation with that highest dignitary of Indian justice will and should be accepted by the government of India and the Court will have an opportunity to examine if any other extraneous circumstances have entered into the verdict of the Minister, if he departs from the Counsel given by Chief Justice of India. In practice, the last word in such sensitive subject must belong to the Chief Justice of India, the rejection of his advice being ordinarily regarded as prompted by oblique consideration vitiating the order."

120. Said observation of Krishna Iyer, J was reaffirmed by the Supreme Court of India in SCH Sheth's case: AIR 1977 SC 2328 where Chandra Chud, J observed,

"It is hoped that these words will not fall on deaf ears and since normalcy has now been restored, the differences, if any, between the executive and the Judiciary will be resolved by mutual deliberation, each party treating the views of the other with respect and consideration."

121. Then, in 2nd Judges' case, JS Verma wrote the opinion of the Constitutional bench of nine Judges on behalf of practically seven Judges as follows:

"This Court has, therefore, authoritatively laid down that in the process of consultation, under the Constitution the last word must belong to the Chief Justice of India"

"In order to ensure effective consultation between all the constitutional functionaries involved in the process, the reasons for disagreement, if any, must be disclosed to all others. All consultations with everyone involved, including all the Judges consulted, must be in writing and the Chief Justice of the High Court, in the case of appointment to a High Court, and the Chief Justice of India, in all cases, must transmit with his opinion the opinions of all of Judges consulted, as a part of the record.

Expression of opinion in writing is an inbuilt check on exercise of the power, and ensures due circumspection. Exclusion of justifiability, as indicated hereafter, in this sphere should prevent any inhibition against the expression of a free and fair opinion. The final opinion of the Chief Justice of India, given after such effective consultation between the constitutional functionaries, has primacy in the manner indicated."

122. Upon such view, in the 2nd Judges' case, the view of SP Gupta was overruled. Within four years, the President of India made a reference for opinion of the Supreme Court of India in respect of nine questions, which give rise to certain doubts about the principles laid down and procedural norms prescribed in said 2nd Judges' case being Special Reference Case No.1 of 1998: (1998) 7 SCC 739. Of the questions, the following are relevant for our purpose:

(i) whether the expression "Consultation with the Chief Justice of India" in Articles 217(1) and 222(1) requires consultation with a plurality of Judges in the formation of the opinion of the Chief Justice of India or does the sole individual opinion of the Chief Justice of India constitute consultation within the meaning of said Articles;

(iii) whether Article 224(2) as interpreted in the said judgment requires the Chief Jus- tice of India to consult only two senior-most Judges or whether there should be wider consultation according to past practice;

(iv) whether the Chief Justice of India is entitled to act solely in his individual capacity without consultation with other Judges of the Supreme Court in respect of all materials and information conveyed by the Government of India for non-appointment of a Judge recommended for appointment;

(vi) whether in the light of legitimate expectations of senior Judges of the High Court in regard to their appointment to the Supreme Court referred to in the said judgment, 'the strong cogent reasons' required to justify the departure from the order of the seniority has to be recorded in respect of each such senior Judge, who is overlooked, while making recommendation of a Judge junior to him or her;

(vii) whether the government is not entitled to require that the opinion of the other consulted Judges be in writing in accordance with the aforesaid Supreme Court judgment and that the same be transmitted to the Government of India by the Chief Justice of India along with his views;

(viii) whether the Chief Justice of India is not obliged to comply with the norms and requirement of the consultation process in making his recommendation to the Government of India; and

(ix) whether any recommendation made by the Chief Justice without complying with the norms and consultation process are binding upon the Government of India."

123. This time the Supreme Court of India unanimously answered the above questions as hereunder:

(i) "The expression 'Consultation with the Chief Justice of India" in Article 217(1) and 222(1) of the Constitution of India requires consultation with the plurality of Judges in the formation of the opinion of the Chief Justice of India. The sole individual opinion of the Chief Justice of India does not constitute consultation within the meaning of said Articles;

(iii) The Chief Justice of India must make a recommendation to appoint a Judge of the Supreme Court ... or Puisne Judges of a High Court in consultation with four senior-most Judges of the Supreme Court. Insofar as an appointment to the High Court is concerned, the recommendation must be made in consultation with two senior-most Puisne Judges of the Supreme Court;

(iv)The Chief Justice of India is not entitled to act solely in his individual capacity, without consultation with other Judges of the Supreme Court, in respect of materials and information conveyed by the Government of India for non-appointment of a Judge recommended for appointment.

(vi) 'Strong cogent reasons' do not have to be recorded as justification for a departure from the order of the seniority in respect of each senior Judge thereof who has been passed over. What is to be recorded is the positive reason for the recommendation;

(vii) the views of the other Judges consulted should be conveyed to the government of India by the Chief Justice of India along with his views to the extent set out in the body of this opinion;

(viii) the Chief Justice of India is obliged to comply with the norms and the requirement of the consultation process as aforestated, in making his recommendation to the government; and

(ix) Recommendation made by the Chief Justice of India without complying with the norms and requirements of consultation process as aforestated are not binding upon the government of India."

124. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in said AI- Jehad case adopted the following view on the consultation process:

"We are interpreting the word, 'consultation' to widen and enlarge its normal scope for the reasons, first, that the Constitution makers have not debated this word 'consultation' and fixed its parameters. Secondly, we would like to assign meaning to 'consultation', which is consistent and commensurate with the exalted position of Judiciary as in envisaged in lslam. Thirdly, we like to give positive interpretation to 'consultation' which promotes independence of Judiciary. Executive may have the last word and may issue notification of appointment, but cannot give loose interpretation to the word 'consultation' to ignore or brush aside expert opinion of the Chief Justice of the High Court and the Chief Justice of Pakistan. Fourthly, the President is administered oath by the Chief Justice of Pakistan as required under Article 42 of the Constitution and the Chief Justice of Pakistan administers oath to other Judges of the Supreme Court and Chief Justice of Province administers oath to Judges of his High Court as contemplated under Articles 178 and 194 respectively, it shows that both the Chief Justices are heads of their institutions and their opinion in their own field of expertise should not be treated particularly when they are Constitutional consultees and the appointments are also being made of the Judges within the Constitutional scheme."

125. The President of Bangladesh is required to make appointment of various Constitutional functionaries, namely, the Attorney-General, the Comptroller of Auditor-General, the Chairman and other members of the Public Service Commission, the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners, etc., which are also non-elective offices. The tenure of such offices is very limited. In no democracy, the Constitution provides for prior consultation with anybody in making such appointments by the President or head of the State. The President of Bangladesh under Article 48(3) appoints persons to such offices in accordance with the advice of the Prime Minister.

126. But in all democracies, the President is obliged to consult with the Chief Justice before making appointment of Judges of the superior Judiciary. Such consultation is necessary for the independence of the Judiciary. Measure of the independence could only be gauged by the respect of the executive to the opinion of the Judiciary. Security of the tenure, remuneration and other privileges, irremovability of Judges except on proved misbehavior or misconduct or incapacity and other assurances would be of no avail unless, the norms for selection of Judges vest in the Chief Justice and his opinion has got the final say in the appointments.

127. Purpose for consulting with the Judiciary is therefore to enable the appointment to be made of the person who is not merely qualified to be a Judge but also would be the most appropriate to be appointed. Such purpose would be defeated if the appointing authority is let free to take its own final decision by ignoring the advice of the Judiciary.

128. Part-VI of the Constitution deals with Judiciary. Under Article 94 the Supreme Court of Bangladesh known as the Supreme Court of Bangladesh comprising the Appellate Division and the High Court Division was established. The Supreme Court consists of Chief Justice to be known as the Chief Justice of Bangladesh and such number of other Judges as the President may deem it necessary to appoint in each Division. The Chief Justice and other Judges appointed to the Appellate Division shall sit only in that Division and the other Judges shall sit only in the High Court Division. The Chief Justice and other Judges shall be independent in the exercise of the judicial function.

129. Article 98 provides notwithstanding the provision of Article 94 if the President is satisfied that number of Judges of a Division of the Supreme Court should be for the time being increased, the President may appoint one or more duly qualified person to be Additional Judge of the Division for a period not exceeding two years as he may specify. Under the proviso to Article 98 nothing in this Article shall prevent a person appointed as an Additional Judge from being appointed as a Judge under Article 95 or as an Additional Judge for a further period under this Article.

130. Originally in 1972, if the President is satisfied 'after consultation with the Chief Justice' the number of Judges of a Division should be increased, he may appoint aforesaid duly qualified person as an Additional Judge of the Division. Satisfaction of the Chief Justice on the increase of Judges was naturally made expressly dependent on the consultation with the Chief Justice. It is the Chief Justice who is best placed to know as to when the number of Judges of a Division should be increased and the President could know such requirement only after consultation with the Chief Justice. In spite of the omission of such phrase, the position and requirement remains the same.

131. It may however, be mentioned that under Article 94 the strength of Judges either in the Appellate Division or the High Court Division was never fixed. Position in this regard is different both in India and Pakistan. There strength of Judges either in the Supreme Court or High Court is always fixed by the President after consultation with the superior Judiciary and Judges are appointed against the vacancy of such strength.

132. Here, the strength of the Judges either in the High Court Division and the Appellate Division was never fixed. At present it may be said that the strength of the Appellate Division comprise seven Judges including the Chief Justice on the basis of last strength. But nobody can certainly say what is the strength of Judges in the High Court Division. The practice since the adoption of the Constitution appears to have been followed for appointment of a Judge in order to fill the last sanctioned strength. On the basis of the last sanctioned strength of occupancy, the Chief Justice may determine the vacancy created. For instance, at the moment there are two vacancies in the Appellate Division to fill the last sanctioned strength of seven Judges. Similarly, about ten Judges are to be appointed to fill the last sanctioned strength of sixty-nine Judges in the High Court Division.

133. A practice has developed for recruitment of Judges in the Supreme Court by appointment as Additional Judges first in the High Court Division for two years under Article 98. Few of them expected to act as Additional Judge for a further period and still few of them were ultimately confirmed.

134. Another practice has now developed for recruitment of Judges that is permanent Judges, either in the High Court Division or the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court by appointment from amongst the Additional Judges of the High Court Division under Article 95 of the Constitution. It is on record, no one was ever appointed Judge to the High Court Division or the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court directly under Article 95. Under the Article, the Chief Justice and other Judges shall be appointed by the President.

135. The President is however still required to consult with the Chief Justice before he could appoint any person as such a Judge. The process is now an existing norm and convention, which the President recognised and followed since omission of the express requirement of consultation with the Chief Justice. Clause (2) of Article 95 prescribes the minimum qualification for appointment as a Judge but not as an Additional Judge. Minimum qualifications prescribed for a person for appointment are that (i) he must be a citizen of Bangladesh; (ii) has, for not less than ten years been an Advocate of the Supreme Court or (iii) has, for not less then ten years, held judicial office.

136. It is also a practice that the Judges who were appointed in the past from the subordinate Judiciary held the office of District Judge for quite number of years and were in active judicial service. With regard to the appointments from the members of the Bar, minimum qualifications of ten years being an advocate of the Supreme Court could not prevent one from being appointed as a Judge just by keeping his name on the roll of the Supreme Court Bar as an Advocate. It may be interesting to note that no qualification is prescribed for a person for appointment as an Additional Judge under Article 98. Here, comes the convention, which is the same minimum qualifications and was the measure in the past for appointment as an Additional Judge too.

137. In the Second Judges' case JS Verma, J who wrote his opinion for himself and also on behalf of four learned brethren, namely, Yogeshwar Dayal, JN Roy, S Anand and SP Bharucha, JJ recorded, inter alia, the conclusions of the majority for holding that in the matter of appointment of Judges to the High Court Division and the Supreme Court, the opinion of the Chief Justice of India shall have primacy. Primacy of the opinion of the Chief Justice of India shall be formed collectively after taking into account the views of his senior colleagues who were required to be consulted for the confirmation of his opinion. What is the opinion of the Judiciary is simplified by the view of Chief Justice of India. No appointment can be made by the President under Article 124(2) and 217(1) of the Indian Constitution unless it was not in conformity with the final opinion of the Chief Justice of India formed in the manner indicated.

138. Distinction between making an appointment in conformity with the opinion of the Chief Justice of India and in making an appointment recommended by the Chief Justice of India has to be borne in mind, even though no appointment can be made unless it is in conformity with the opinion of the Chief Justice of India. As number of exceptional cases where the facts justified the recommendation of the Chief Justice of India and considered unsuitable on the basis of positive materials available on record and placed before the Chief Justice of India might not be appointed.

139. The non-appointment of anyone recommended, on the ground of unsuitability must be for good reason, disclosed to the Chief Justice of India to enable him to reconsider and withdraw his recommendation on this consideration. If the Chief Justice of India does not find it necessary to withdraw his recommendation even thereafter, but other Judges of the Supreme Court having consulted in the matter are of the view that it ought to be withdrawn, non- appointment of that person, for reasons to be recorded, may be permissible in the public interest. If non-appointment in case on this ground turns out to be a mistake that mistake in the ultimate public interest is less harmful than a wrong appointment. However, after due consideration of the reasons disclosed to the Chief Justice of India if said recommendation is reiterated by Chief Justice of India with the unanimous agreement of the Judges of the Supreme Court consulted in the matter, with reasons for not withdrawing the recommendation, then that appointment as a matter of healthy convention ought to be made.

140. In order to enforce effective consultation between all constitutional functionaries involved in the process the reason for this agreement, if any, must be disclosed to all others, to enable reconsideration on this basis. All the opinions of the consul- tees including Judges consulted must be in writing and Chief Justice of the High Court, in case of appointment to a High Court and the Chief Justice of India in all cases must transmit with his opinion, the opinion of all Judges consulted by him as part of the record. Expression of the opinion in writing is an in-built check on the exercise of the power and ensured due circumspection. Exclusion of justifiability in this field should prevent any inhibition against the expression of free opinion. The final opinion of the Chief Justice of India given after such effective consultation between the constitutional functionaries has primacy in the manner indicated.

141. To achieve this purpose is to give legitimacy and greater accountability to the process of appointment. The process must be initiated by the Chief Justice of India in the case of Supreme Court and Chief Justice of the High Court in the case of High Court. This is the general practice preventing, by convention followed over the years and continuing to be general rule even now, after SP Gupta case. Supreme Court of Pakistan substantively followed the general rule, norms and principle developed and enunciated by the Supreme Court ofIndia in the Second Judges' Case and Al Jehad Trust case.

142. It is also here a long practice that an Additional Judge of the High Court Division appointed under Article 98 is confirmed as a Judge of the said Division under Article 95. Similarly, an Additional Judge of the High Court Division is appointed as a Judge of the Appellate Division under Article 95. This is the practice that developed for appointment in the High Court Division and the Appellate Division. Purport of Article 95 also does not prevent one for appointment as a Judge directly to the High Court Division or the Appellate Division. But since the establishment of Supreme Court, no one till today was appointed directly to the High Court Division or the Appellate Division. Prudence and experience might have not prompted and encouraged such appointment. Once one is appointed under Article 95 he becomes permanent Judge until he attains the age of sixty-seven years.

143. It is established that Article 98 is a gateway to the entry to the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. Now, the question is, who is 'duly qualified' for appointment as an Additional Judge. The phrase defines no doubt the merit and character of the person, which is not sufficient. In addition to the minimum qualification, the person to be appointed must be one, as was found in the 2nd Judges' case in India, who possesses the highest reputation for independence, uncommitted to any prior interest, loyalty and obligation and prepared under all circumstances or eventuality to pay any price, bear any burden and to meet any hardship and always wedded only to the principles of the Constitution and the rule of law. If the appointee bears a particular stamp for the purpose of changing the cause of decisions bowing to the diktat of his appointing authority, then the independence of Judiciary cannot be secured at his hands.

144. In the Al-Jehad case, the Supreme Court of Pakistan has held that political affiliation of a candidate for Judgeship may not be a disqualification provided he is a person of integrity and has active practice as an advocate of the High Court and has sound knowledge of law and has also been recommended by the Chief Justice. It is also true for our case, if the person is of an unimpeachable integrity and has a sound knowledge in law, particularly an understanding of the Constitution.

145. The Government has a constitutional obligation to treat all citizens alike and afford them equal opportunity in all spheres including superior Judiciary under Article 29 of the Constitution. It is therefore essential and vital for participatory democracy that all sections and classes of people irrespective of their colour, faith and language should be afforded equal opportunity so that the judicial administration is also participated in by the outstanding and meritorious candidates belonging to all such sections of society and not by any selective or insular group. Backward people representing the vast majority of the populace demands compassionate consideration of the Government. When the diversity of the population reflects in the superior Judiciary, the objective of the Constitution would be fulfilled. The Supreme Court should not be meant for persons coming from particular area of the country.

146. Besides, in the background of our constitutional history, time is up to consider about the uprightness and commitment of the person in the independence of the Judiciary of the executive organs of the State. When everywhere in all democracies, the presence of the government is shrinking in the life of its citizen, but increasing in every sphere of life in our society. When the government breathes on every shoulder, life of the citizen becomes suffocating. No citizen can think of living his life here without the intervention and/or permission of the government agencies, to breathe fresh air or take safe water up to the journey to the graveyard. A Judge therefore must be bold, independent and impartial to defend the rights of the people under the Constitution, oath of which he takes to defend without any fear or favour.

<u>147. A person of above calibre when accepts the offer of the executive for an Additional Judge leaving behind the successful career in the profession he generally never expects to return back to the Bar after two years. If he performs the functions of such an Additional Judge to the satisfaction of the Chief Justice and all, he can legitimately expect to go up and up to the high office of the Chief Justice. In the 2nd Judges' case, the Supreme Court of India held that due consideration of every legitimate expectation in the decisions making process is a requirement of the rule of non-arbitrariness and, therefore, this also is a norm to be observed by the Chief Justice of India in recommending appointments to the Supreme Court. Obviously, the factor applies only to those considered suitable and at least equally meritorious by the Chief Justice of India, for appointment to the Supreme Court. Just as a High Court Judge at the time of his initial appointment has the legitimate expectation to become Chief Justice of a High Court in his turn in the ordinary course, he has the legitimate expectation to be considered for appointment to the Supreme Court in his turn, according to his seniority.</u>

148. In SP Gupta case, the Supreme Court of India was of the following view on the confirmation of Additional Judge that

"the Additional Judges entered the High Court Judiciary with a legitimate expectation that they would not have to go back on the expiration of their term but they would be either reappointed as Additional Judges for a further term or in the meanwhile a vacancy in the post of a permanent Judge became available, they would be confirmed as permanent Judges. This expectation which was generated in the minds of Additional Judges by reason of the peculiar manner in which clause (1) of Article 224 was operated, cannot now be ignored by the Government and the Government cannot be permitted to say when the term of an Additional Judge expires the Government can drop him at its sweet will. By reason of the expectation raised in his mind through a practice followed for almost over a quarter of a century, an Additional Judge is entitled to be considered for appointment as an Additional Judge for further term on the expiration of his original term and if in the meantime, a vacancy in the post of a permanent Judge becomes available to him on the seniority amongst the Additional Judges, he has a right to be considered for appointment as a permanent Judge in his High Court."

But ultimately, it was held that,

"There can, therefore, be no doubt that an Additional Judge is not entitled as a matter of right to be appointed as Additional Judge for a further term after the expiration of his original term or as a permanent Judge. The only right he has is to be considered for such appointment and this right also belongs to him not because clause (1) of Article 224 confers such right upon him, but because of the peculiar manner in which clause (1) of Article 224 has been operated all these years."

149. The view of SP Gupta case did not find favour in the Second Judges' case. In this case, the question of confirmation of Additional Judges after the expiration of the term was not directly at issue. It was however, held on the legitimate expectation of such Judges as hereunder:

"Just as a High Court Judge at the time of his initial appointment has the legitimate expectation to become Chief Justice of the High Court Division in his turn in the ordinary course, he has the legitimate expectation to be considered for appointment to the Supreme Court in its turn, according to his seniority.

... this legitimate expectation has' relevance on the ground of longer experience on the bench and for factor material determining the suitability of appointee along with other factor, such as proper representation of all sections of the people from all parts of the country legitimate expectation of the suitable on the equal merit Judges to be considered in their turn is relevant factor for duly consideration while making them which of the most suitable and ... amongst them outing consideration being merit to select the post available for the Apex Court.

150. In the Al-Jehad case, in which non- appointment of six Additional Judges was directly at issue, the Supreme Court of Pakistan categorically stated,

"Additional Judges appointed in the High Court against permanent vacancies or if permanent vacancies occur while they are acting as Additional Judges, acquire legitimate expectancy and they are entitled to be considered for permanent appointment upon the expiry of their period of appointment as Additional Judges and they are entitled to be appointed as such if they are recommended by the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned and the Chief Justice of Pakistan in the absence of strong valid reason/ reasons to be recorded by the President/ Executive. "

<u>151. Position here is quite different from India and Pakistan as has already been stated hereinabove in the sense that the Additional Judges of the High Court Division are not appointed under Article 98 of our Constitution against any vacancies. After the expiration of the term of two years or any further term of extension, if they are recommended by the Chief Justice for appointment as Judge under Article 95, they become entitled to be confirmed as Judge of the High Court Division. If they are not appointed despite the recommendation of the Chief Justice, such non-appointment violates the above constitutional scheme. Most pressing reason for appointment of such Additional Judges is that the Constitution cannot be conceived to allow the executive to get rid of such suitable and capable Judges from the Supreme Court after the expenditure of huge money from the public exchequer to make them suitable and capable for performing most difficult job of the Republic, administering justice and appoint fresher ones in their place. Besides, they cannot go back to the Bar to resume their profession since they would be barred from practicing in the High Court Division.</u>

152. For reasons aforesaid, we arrive at following conclusions as to the norms and process for appointment and non-appointment of Judges to the Supreme Court:

(i) the proposal and process for appointment of Judges to the Supreme Court in both the High Court Division and the Appellate Division should emanate from the Chief Justice of Bangladesh;

(ii) the opinion of the Chief Justice of Bangladesh in the matter of appointment of Judges to the Supreme Court is entitled to have the primacy;

(iii) in case of appointment to the High Court Division, the Chief Justice shall consult with two senior most Judges of the Appellate Division and equal number of Judges of the High Court Division to form his opinion and he shall also consult senior members of the Supreme Court Bar and the Attorney-General; and in the case of appointment of Judges to the Appellate Division, he shall consult with three senior-most Judges of the Appellate Division to form his opinion;

(iv) the President or the Government shall have no right to directly initiate the process for appointment of Judges to the Supreme Court bypassing the Chief Justice of Bangladesh but the President! Government shall have the right of suggesting the names of suitable candidates for consideration of the Chief Justice for appointment to the Supreme Court;

(v) The non-appointment of anyone recommended, on the ground of unsuitability, must be for good reasons, disclosed and conveyed to the Chief Justice with the reasons, materials and information to enable him to reconsider and withdraw his recommendation. If the Chief Justice after consultation with the above Judges in respect of particular appointments in the Division concerned, does not find it necessary to withdraw and again recommend, then the President must adhere to such recommendation;

(vi) the President as a rule shall accept the recommendation of the Chief Justice for appointment of Judges. If the recommendation of the Chief Justice for appointment or non-appointment •of any person as a Judge either to the High Court or the Appellate Division could not be accepted by the Government, it cannot outright, reject such recommendation and go ahead with appointment of persons of its own choice. The Government in such case shall send the recommendation back to the Chief Justice for reconsideration on the reasons supported by materials and information conveyed by the Government;

(vii) after consideration of the reasons of the Government along with the materials and the information conveyed, the Chief Justice may withdraw his recommendation. But if he again recommends the same recommendation after consultation with the aforesaid senior-most Judges of the Appellate Division for appointment, the Government shall be obliged to complete the process of appointment;

(viii) 	appointment or non-appointment of an Additional Judge as Judge under Article 95 of the Constitution by the executive disregarding the recommendation of the Chief Justice violates the Constitution;

(ix) when the executive may not accept such recommendation of the Chief Justice for reasons to be recorded, it may request the Chief Justice for reconsideration on the materials and information conveyed;

(x) the Chief Justice shall then reconsider the case on the materials and information furnished, and then, if after such reconsideration, he again recommends for appointment or non-appointment, the executive would be left with no choice but to complete the process of appointment of such an Additional Judge on the basis of such recommendation;

(xi) after successful conclusion of the period under Article 98, an Additional Judge acquires legitimate expectation and he becomes entitled to be considered for appointment under Article 95 of the Constitution in the absence of positive valid reason(s) to be recorded by the Executive; and

(xii) non-appointment of the petitioners, in the circumstances, as Judge of the High Court Division under Article 95 of the Constitution therefore, violates the constitutional scheme and conventions and is accordingly, declared to be arbitrary, mala fide, without any lawful authority and, as such, of no legal effect.

In view of above conclusions, we direct:

(a) The Government shall within one month of receipt of this order complete the process of appointment of the petitioners, Md Abdus Salam and Md Mumtazuddin Ahmed with effect from 24 October,2002; Md Shamsul Huda, Faruque Ahmed, Hasan Foez Siddique, Md Abdul Hye, Md Abdur Razzaque and Md Marzi-ul-Hoque from 22 February, 2003 and AHM Shams uddin Chowdhury and Md Nizamul Huq from 3 July, 2003, that is the due date of their confirmation; and

(b) The intervening period since their non- appointment shall be treated to be special leave without pay and other benefits.

153. It may however be mentioned that if the consultation process as aforesaid is made purposive and effective involving all the constitutional functionaries and wider including the senior members of the Bar and the Attorney-General, it may not take much time for them to converge to the common and acceptable candidate for appointment of an Additional Judge or a Judge to the Supreme Court and then, the primacy of the opinion of any particular functionary would lose all its importance.

154. It is on record that during the Awami League Government from 1996-200 I all the Additional Judges appointed either by the previous BNP Government or the Caretaker Administration were appointed Judges of the High Court Division under Article 95 of the Constitution, not a single Additional Judge was dropped. But during the BNP- Jamaat alliance Government of 2001-2006, fifteen Additional Judges including the petitioners who were appointed from 24-9-99 to 23-8-2001 were not appointed and confirmed under Article 95. The alliance government appointed 45 Additional Judges in their place. Of them, one Additional Judge could not be confirmed and appointed by said Government as the Chief Justice did not recommend him for appointment. One was removed on the report of the Supreme Judicial Council by the President and the other one most ignominiously resigned after confirmation.

155. It is now no secret that none of the petitioners and other Additional Judges were appointed and confirmed under Article 95 only because of the fact that they were appointed by the previous Awami League Government. Even the petitioners who were appointed from the judicial service were not spared from the wrath and vengeance of the alliance government. Such a course adopted by an elected government in the appointment of Judges to the Supreme Court is no doubt, a slur in the history of the Supreme Court.

156. Humiliation, agony and sufferings, mental, physical and social the petitioners were put into after non-appointment could only be Judged by them who had to pass through such a situation in life. After we found the non-appointment of the petitioners as Additional Judges under Article 95 unconstitutional, we thought a lot as to how the wrong done to them could be undone. Following the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan reinstating six Additional Judges in similar circumstances, we had no difficulty to restore them in the Supreme Court as Judges under Article 95 of the Constitution. But then, the question arose as to the date to be made effective for such appointments.

157. We could not find any reason for not to apply the fundamental principles of reinstatement after removal from service in the case of the petitioners. The petitioners who administered Justice for others definitely deserve the same yardstick for them to be treated equally under the Constitution. Under clause (1) of Article 148 of the Constitution, the petitioners took oath before they entered upon the office of Additional Judges and under clause (3) of said Article they deemed to have entered upon such office from the date of such oath for all purposes even after appointments as Judges under Article 95. Fresh oath meant for a Judge appointed under Article 95 would not invalidate the date of the petitioners entering upon their office after oath under Article 148(1). Service of every Judge of the Supreme Court is so treated and recorded with effect from the date of oath taken by them after appointment under Article 98, not under Article 95. We were therefore left with no choice but to make the appointments of the petitioners under Article 95 of the Constitution effective from respective date of non-appointment, that is the date they were scheduled to be appointed such Judges however, without pay.

158. In the result, Rules in Writ Petition No. 1543 of 2003 and Writ Petition No. 2875 of 2003 are made absolute in the terms and to the extent as mentioned hereinabove while that in Writ Petition No. 3217 of 2003 is discharged as not pressed.

SK Sinha J: I have read the judgment delivered by my brother Md Abdur Rashid J making an exhaustive in-depth analysis exploring the process of appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (SCB) under Article 95(1) of the Constitution of Bangladesh (the Constitution) and the independence of Judiciary; I find myself in agreement with the opinion of my learned brother, yet I would like to give my reason since the points involved in these petitions are on the Constitutional question of special importance in relation to the powers of the Executive to appoint Judges of the highest Judiciary of the country.

160. Dr Kamal Hossain, Mr M Amirul Islam and Mr Ajmalul Hossain, QC, learned Counsel, appearing for the petitioners, point out different view-points focusing on the role of the Chief Justice of Bangladesh (CJB) in the matter of appointment of Judges to the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (SCB), and the cm has primacy and the Executive having the role of merely making appointments with the opinion of the cm. They have also highlighted as to the appointment of Judges in the higher Judiciary are being made as per recommendation of the CJB in order to uphold the independence of Judiciary and the rule of law. In this connection they have argued on the point of the constitutional convention, legitimate expectation, malafide exercise of power by the Executive in the matter of appointment and on other fascinating points. In order to avoid repetition, I would like to discuss those points chronologically. All the learned Counsels refer different Articles of the Constitution and argue that according to the Constitutional scheme, in order to preserve the independence of Judiciary, the appointment of Judges is handled directly by the President and not by the Prime Minister who is the head of the Executive of the Republic. This is done mainly with a view to keep distance between Judiciary and the Executive. Article 48(3) it is argued has no direct role in the appointment of Judges other than the CJB; otherwise under the scheme of the Constitution independence of Judiciary will be hampered on a large scale amounting to the breach of the basic feature of the Constitution. In support of their contention they have cited many decisions. Of them, they have stressed upon SC Advocate-on-Record Association vs Union of India, AIR 1994 SC 268, (Second Judges case), SP Gupta vs Union of India, AIR 1982 SC 149, AI-Jahed Trust vs Federation of Pakistan, PLD 1996 SC 323, State vs Chief Editor, Manabjamin, 57 DLR 359, Secretary, Ministry of Finance vs Masdar Hossain 52 DLR (AD) 82, and Anwar Hossain Chowdhury vs Bangladesh 41 DLR (AD) 165.

Process of appointment

161. Dr Hossain has highlighted the convention over sixty years in the process of appointment of Judges. Dr. Hossain contended, there was no provision in the High Courts Act, 1861 for appointment of Additional Judges of the High Courts with restricted tenure until the Government of India Act 1915 was promulgated. Under the Act of 1915, a. provision was enacted in section 101 (2) for appointment of Additional Judges in any High Courts for a period not exceeding two years. The Government of India Act 1915 was replaced by the Government of India Act 1935. Under this Act of 1935, the appointments of Judges in the High Courts were made at the pleasure of the Crown but the Judges were given security of tenure. It is pointed out that under the Act of 1935 there was no provision for appointment of Additional Judges on the consultation with the Chief Justice of a High Court but, as a matter of convention, the Judges were appointed with prior consultation.

162. In the Second Judges' case it was observed by Kuldip Singh, J, that prior to coming into force of the Constitution of India the appointments of Federal Court Judges and Judges of the High Courts were made under sections 200 and 220, respectively of the Government of IndiaAct, 1935. The appointments were in the absolute discretion of the Crown. In other words, the Executive, by itself, with no pro- vision at all for consultation with the Chief Justice of India or with the Judiciary in any manner, was the authority to make appointments to the superior Judiciary. We have, it is stated, however, contemporaneous evidence to show that under the Government of India, Act 1935 the said appointments were invariably made with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of India.

163 Sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 222 of the Government of India Act 1935 provide for appointment of a Judge and an Additional Judge in the High Courts in the following terms:

"Section 222(2).-If the office of any other Judge of a High Court becomes vacant or if any such Judge is appointed to act temporarily as a chief justice, or is by reason of absence, or for any other reason, unable to perform the duties of his office, the Governor-General may in his discretion appoint a person duly qualified for appointment as a Judge to act as a Judge of that Court, and the person so appointed shall, unless the Governor-General in his discretion thinks fit to revoke his appointment, be deemed to be a Judge of that Court until some person appointed by His Majesty to the vacant office has entered on the duties thereof, or until the permanent Judge has resumed his duties.

"Section 222(3).-If by reason of any temporary increase in the business of any High Court or by reason of arrears of work in any such Court it appears to the Governor-General that the number of the Judges of the Court should be for the time being increased, the Governor-General in his discretion may, subject to the foregoing provisions of this chapter with respect to the maximum number of Judges, appoint persons duly qualified for appointment as Judges to be Additional Judges of the Court for such period not exceeding two years as he may specify."

164. These provisions show that the appointments of the High Courts were in the absolute discretion of the Crown there was no provision at all for consultation with the Chief Justice of India.

165. In Manabjamins case, Syed Amirul Islam J had extracted the exposition as made in the case of Al-Jahed Trust case while discussing the appointment of the Judges of the superior Courts during pre-partition period. It was observed that under the Government of India Act, 1935, the appointment of Judges of the Superior Courts remained a matter of pleasure of the Crown but the Judges were given security of tenure up to the age of superannuation. The procedure for appointment was that the Governor of a Province used to consult the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned and then used to advise the King through the Secretary of the State of India with the recommendation of the Chief Justice. On the basis of the above advice, the appointments were made by the Crown. This procedure was followed till 4th November, 1947, on which date the then Home Minister attempted to control the Judiciary and issued a memorandum providing the procedure for appointment of High Court Judges. Under this provision, the Chief Minister of a State, acting in consultation with the Home Minister of the State concerned, was to send his recommendations to the Home Minister in the centre. After circulation of the said memorandum there was resistance and consequently Sir Frederick Gentle, Chief Justice of Madras High Court, communicated the Government expressing his desire to resign as a symbol of protest of the said memorandum. Sir Archibala Nye, Governor of Madras also protested the said memorandum. They were of the view that the above procedure would lead to political jobbery and would impair the independence of Judiciary. A conference of the Chief Justices of the High Courts of India was held on 26th March, 1948 to consider the said memorandum in which a number of recommendations were made in the said conference suggesting amongst others, that "every Judge of the High Court should be appointed by the President by a warrant under his hand and seal on the recommendation of the Chief Justice of High Court after consultation with the Governor of the State and with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of India." It has been observed in SP Gupta's case that the system of appointment of Additional Judges was therefore in vogue when the Constituent Assembly met to frame the Constitution. Article 199 of the draft Constitution was almost in the same terms as sub- section (3) of section 222 of the Government of India Act, 1935.

166. Before the Constitution of India came into force the appointments of the higher Judiciary were made at the absolute discretion of the Executive- there was no provision for consultation with the Chief Justice of India in any manner-the Executive was the authority to make appointments, although a convention as observed above, the appointments were invariably made with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of India. The question arose regarding the procedure for appointment. of Judges in the higher Judiciary at the time of drafting the Constitution of India. In the Second Judges' case, Kuldip Singh, J, reproduced the memorandum prepared by the Judges of the Federal Court and the Chief Justice of the High Courts on 26th, 27th March 1948 about their views on the draft Constitution regarding the Judiciary which is as follows:

"We do not think it necessary to make any provision in the Constitution for the possibility of the Chief Justice of India refusing to concur in an appointment proposed by the President. Both are officers of the highest responsibility and so far no case of such refusal has arisen although a convention now exists that such appointments should be made after referring the matter to the Chief Justice of India and obtaining his concurrence. If per chance such a situation were ever to arise it could of course be met by the President making a different proposal, and no express provision need, it seems to us, be made in that behalf."

167. In this connection in Al-Jehad Trust case, it was observed as follows:

"Now we take up the interpretation of the Judiciary-related Articles as mentioned in the Constitution. The first which shall come up for consideration will be the meaning of the word "consultation" which is very pivotal in nature because the whole controversy with regard to the independence of the Judiciary and the appointments of the Judges have close nexus with it or, in other words, deep-rooted in it. In order to find out the true import or meaning of this word "consultation" the whole history of the judicial set-ups in India and Pakistan has been traced going back to the Government of India Act, 1935 and even the period earlier than that as mentioned in the preceding paragraphs of this judgment. It is manifest that in earlier legal instruments before the partition, the word "consultation" is not used because there was no need to mention it as the appointments were directly made by the British Rulers who enjoyed the supreme control and the appointees were at the receiving end. The need was felt to use the word "consultation" in the scheme of appointments in the superior Judiciary in the Constitution when India and Pakistan became independent countries to enjoy the benefit and fruits of democratic rule for which agitation was made by the people who rendered sacrifices of lives and property and millions of them were uprooted and migrated for achievement of freedom. It was made known to the people that they were fighting for freedom and in consequence of freedom what would they gain would be democracy and their own Government and perception of such democracy was Government of the people, for the people and by the people. To set up such democratic Governments, Constitutions were made in India and Pakistan in order to produce system of governance with trichotomy of powers among the three pillars, namely, the Legislature, Executive and Judiciary. The word "consultation" has been used for the first time in the Constitution of India and the Constitution of Pakistan in connection with appointments of Judges in the Superior Judiciary. The history of India and Pakistan, as mentioned in detail in the preceding part of this judgment, very clearly shows that always effort was made to seek that the Judiciary functioned independently and should not be controlled by the Executive. There is no cavil with the proposition that the Legislature has to legislate, the Executive has to execute laws and the Judiciary has to interpret the Constitution and laws. The success of the system of governance can be guaranteed and achieved only when these pillars of the State exercise their powers and authority within their limits without transgressing into the field of the others by acting in the spirit of harmony, cooperation and coordination. So far the powers of the Judiciary are concerned, we are exactly going to do that and we are going to interpret the relevant provisions of the Constitution within the limits prescribed so that the provisions are harmonised and the Constitution becomes workable".

168. After the partition, India went for absolute independence of Judiciary. A committee was set up for preparation of constitutional proposals on the subject of Judiciary headed by Sir Taj Bahadur Sapru. The committee kept in mind that if the High Courts are put above party politics or influences, it will not be possible that the provincial governments may "under political presence affect prejudicially the strength of the High Court within its jurisdiction or the salary of its Judges." It was thus recommended that "the High Court and the Government concerned will be more or less interested parties in the matter, the intervention of the Supreme Court and the Head of the State would rule out all possibility of the exercise of political or party influences." In Al-Jahed Trust case it was pointed out that in the draft Constitution of India, "views were obtained from Federal Court and Chief Justices of the High Courts in March 1948 in connection with which a conference was held and detailed discussions took place on the subject of the independence of the Judiciary and the mode of the appointments of Judges keeping in view the tendency growing up to detract from the status and dignity of the Judiciary and to whittle down their powers, rights and authority, which were to be checked." This was due to the procedure that was adopted after the partition in the matter of appointment of Judges did not ensure purely on merit without political influence. Finally after a long debate in the Articles relating to the Judiciary provided for appointment to be made by the President after "consultation" with such of the Judges of the Supreme Court and of the High Courts in the states as the President may deem necessary and in the case of the appointment of a Judge, other than Chief Justice, the Chief Justice of India shall always be consulted.

169. In the Second Judges' case, Kuldip Singh, J reiterated Mr Gobind Ballabh Pant's Speech, then Home Minister of India in the debate of the Rajya Sabha on 24th November, 1959 over 14th Law Commission Report which is as follows:

"Sir, so far as appointments to the Supreme Court go, since 1950 when the Constitution was brought into force, nineteen Judges have been appointed and everyone of them was so appointed on the recommendation of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. I do not know if any other alternative can be devised for this purpose. The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court is, I think, rightly deemed and believed to be familiar with the merits of his own col- leagues and also of the Judges and advocates who hold leading positions in different States. So we have followed the advice of the most competent, dependable and eminent person who could guide us in this matter.

Similarly, Sir, so far as High Courts are concerned, since 1950, 211 appointments have been made and out of these except one, i.e. 210 out of 211 were made on the advice, with the consent and concurrence of the Chief Justice of 	India ...........................

"I have listened to some of the speeches that were made and also gone through the record of the speeches, which unfortunately, I could not myself personally listen to. It was suggested that the Chief Justice of India might make these appointments. Well, I do not know if that would improve matters because virtually they have been made by the Chief Justice of India. Only the orders were issued by us, and in any case the orders would have to be issued by the executive authority."

170. In his speech, the Home Minister high- lighted the appointment of Judges to the Superior Courts after coming of the Constitution followed conventions and was made with the consent and concurrence of the Chief Justice of India. He emphasised that the appointments of Judges were virtually being made by the Chief Justice of India and the Executive was only the order issuing authority. The Home Minister acknowledged the existence of a convention to the effect that the opinion and recommendation of the Chief Justice of India were taken as final by the Executive government.

171. Under the Constitution of India, the appointment of Judges and conditions of office of a Judge of a High Court is made under Article 217 and an Additional and acting Judges are appointed under Article 224, which are as follows:

"Article 217. Appointment and conditions of the office of a Judge of a High Court-(1) Every Judge of High Court shall be appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State, and, in the case of appointment of a Judge other than the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice of the High Court, and shall hold office, in the case of an Additional or acting Judge, as provided in Article 224, and in any other case, until he attains the age of sixty- two years.

Provided that-

(2) A person shall not be qualified for appointment as a Judge of a High Court unless he is a citizen of India and -

(a) has for at least ten years held a judicial office in the territory of India; or

.......................................................................................

"Article 224. Appointment of Additional and acting Judges-(1) If by reason of any temporary increase in the business of a High Court or by reason of arrears of work therein, it appears to the President that the number of the Judges of that Court should be for the time being increased, the President may appoint duly qualified persons to be Additional Judges of the Court for such period not exceeding two years as he may specify.

(2) When any Judge of a High Court other than the Chief Justice is by reason of absence or for any other reason unable to perform the duties of his office or is appointed to act temporarily as Chief Justice, the President may appoint a duly qualified person to act as a Judge of that Court until the permanent Judge has resumed his duties.

172. Chapter III of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan 1973 relates to the judicature. Articles 193 and 197 relate to the appointment of a Judge and Additional Judge of High Courts, which read as follows:

"Article 193. Appointment of High Court Judges-(l) A Judge o(a High Court shall be appointed by the President after consultation-

(a) with the Chief Justice of Pakistan: (b) with Governor concerned; and

(c) except where the appointment is that of Chief Justice, with the Chief Justice of the High Court.

(2) A person shall not be appointed a Judge of a High Court unless he is a citizen of Pakis- tan, is not less than forty years of age, and-

(a) he has for a period of, or for periods aggregating, not less than ten years been an Advocate of a High Court (including a High Court which existed in Pakistan at any time before the commencing day); or

(b) he is and has for a period of not less than ten years been, a member of a civil service prescribed by law for the purposes of this paragraph, and has, for a period of not less than three years, served as or exercised the functions of a District Judge in Pakistan; or

(c) he has for a period of not less than ten years held a judicial office in Pakistan.

"Article 197 Additional Judges. At any time when-

(a) the office of a Judge of a High Court is vacant; or

(b) a Judge of a High Court is absent or is unable to perform the functions of his office due to any other cause; or

(c) for any reason it is necessary to increase the number of Judges of a High Court; the President may, in the manner provided in clause (1) of Article 193, appoint a person qualified for appointment as a Judge of the High Court to be Additional Judge of the Court for such period as the President may determine, being a period not exceeding such period, if any, as may be prescribed by law."

173. Our Constitution provides for the appointments as Judges and Additional Judges in Articles 95 and 98 which read as follows:

"Article 95(l)-The Chief Justice and other Judges shall be appointed by the President.

(2) A person shall not be qualified for appointment as a Judge unless he is a citizen of Bangladesh and-

(a) has, for not less than ten years been an Advocate of the Supreme Court; or

(b) has, for not less than ten years, held judicial office in the territory of Bangladesh; or

(c) has such other qualifications as may be prescribed by law for appointment as a Judge of the Supreme Court.

"Article 98-Notwithstanding the provision of Article 94, if the President is satisfied that the number of the Judges of a division of the Supreme Court should be for the time being increased , the President may appoint one or more duly qualified persons to be Additional Judges of the division for such period not exceeding two years as he may specify, or, if he thinks fit, may require a Judge of the High Court Division to sit in the Appellate Division for any temporary period as an ad hoc Judge and such Judge while so sitting, shall exercise the same jurisdiction, powers and functions as a Judge of the Appellate Division :"

174. Under the Indian provision, the President appoints a Judge in the High Courts under Article 217(1) after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State and the Chief Jus- tice of that High Court. This provision is applicable in all cases of appointment of an acting Judge or an Additional Judge, inasmuch as, in Article 217(1) the expression "Every Judge" has been used. Though there is no bar for appointment of a Judge directly but it is noticed in SP Gupta's case, in rare cases such an appointment has been made. There is similar procedure in India and Pakistan in the matter of appointment of a Judge but there is dissimilarity in the matter of appointment of an Additional Judge. In the Pakistan Constitution, there is no provision for appointing of an acting Judge in the High Courts. In India the strength of Judges of a High Court are fixed by law. Article 216 authorises the President to promulgate law fixing the number of Judges. Similar provision is contained in Article 192 of the Constitution of Pakistan. The purpose and the procedure for an appointment of Judges under Article 217 of the Constitution of India and Article 193 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan are deferent from that of our provision. In our Constitution, the provisions of appointment after 'consultation' is absent; it is said that if the President is satisfied that the number of Judges should be "increased", the President may appoint a qualified person to be Additional Judge, but there is no law fixing the limit of number of Judges of the High Court Division. Therefore, the President may appoint any number of Judges irrespective of the number of Judges working in the Division and the arrears of work. In this connection, Mr Ajmalul Hossain has drawn our attention to the statements in Paragraph 3(IX) of the second supplementary affidavit in Writ Petition No. 2975 of 2003. It is stated that this power should be restricted and the number of Judges should be fixed by law and if there is increase in the business of the High Court Division (HCD) and if it appears to the President that either by reason of temporary increase in the business of the Court or by reason of arrears of work, or retirement, removal or for any other cause the number of Judges should be increased, the appointment should be made according to the requirement otherwise, every political government would indulge in appointing any number of Judges for satisfying its oblique purpose.

175. There is provision for appointment of an acting Judge in a High Court in India for filling the vacancy of a permanent Judge for a temporary period and an Additional Judge for a period not exceeding for two years for clearing arrears of work but there is no corresponding provision for appointment of an acting Judge in the High Courts in Pakistan and Bangladesh. There is however, a provision for appointment of an ad-hoc Judge in the Appellate Division in our Constitution from amongst the Judges of the High Court Division on temporary basis if there is shortage in the quorum. An acting Judge in India and an ad-hoc Judge in Bangladesh cannot claim as of right for appointment on permanent basis after being appointed as such. In Article 127 of the Constitution of India there is provision for appointment of ad-hoc Judge in the Supreme Court for filing up the quorum of the Judges or for continuing any session of the Court. The Ad-hoc Judges are appointed by the Chief Justice of India with the consent of the President and after consultation of the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court. These appointments are purely made on temporary basis and no specific period for such appointment has been provided in the Constitution. The Additional Judges in Pakistan and Bangladesh are appointed against permanent vacancies while an Additional Judge or acting Judge of a High Court in India is appointed for clearing off arrears of work. They cannot claim as of right for appointment as a permanent Judge. As regards acting Judge, there is specific provision in Article 224(2) that if any permanent Judge other than Chief Justice is absent or for any other reason a qualified person may be appointed for a temporary period. The tenure and object for appointment of an Additional or Acting Judge is limited because he is appointed to clear off the arrears of work or back log cases. It has been observed in SP Gupta's case "whenever a vacancy occurred in the post of a permanent Judge, he would be confirmed as a permanent Judge in that vacancy in accordance with the seniority amongst the Additional Judges. The practice therefore grew up of a person being first appointed as an Additional Judge and then being confirmed as a permanent Judge in the same High Court."

176. Our provision for appointment of an Additional Judge is completely different from the Indian provision. A practice is prevailing and/or being followed in our country that if for any reason the CJB recommends an Additional Judge for appointment for a further period, he is appointed for a period of one year only meaning thereby that the constitutional provision for further appointment is specified for one year. The Bengali version clearly provides that “আরো এক মেয়াদের জন্য” which means, an Additional Judge is appointed initially for a period of two years and therefore such Additional Judge may be appointed for a further period of two years. The process of consultation in the appointment of Judges is needed in order to uphold the independence of Judiciary for, it was realised that the independence of Judiciary is not possible by only safeguarding merely by providing security tenure and other conditions of service but also by resorting to devices by preventing influence of political pressure in making appointments. To avoid this eventuality it is necessary that the process of appointment should be initiated by the CJB and not by the Executive.

177. Article 95(1) states that the Judges including the Chief Justice of Bangladesh shall be appointed by the President. The qualification of a person for appointment as a Judge has been provided in sub-Article (2) of Article 95 and one of the qualifications is mentioned in clause (c). It is stated that the qualifications may be "prescribed by law" but no law has yet been promulgated in this regard. In the absence of law, Dr. Hossain argues that the Constitutional conventions that are being followed since 1861 have to be observed. In the process of appointment selection should be made by adopting a course which will enable the CJB to discharge his duty objectively to select the best available Advocates and from the lower Judiciary the senior-most efficient Judges as Judges.

178. It is expected that the CJB may take into account the views of his colleagues, senior Judges of the HCD including the senior Advocates of the SCB, if necessary, regarding the affairs of the practicing Advocates, whose opinions are likely to be significant in the formation of his opinion, and the opinion of the senior Judges involved must be given due weight in the formation of opinion of the CJB. It was the convention being followed that appointment of Judges were usually made from amongst persons of mature age with known background and reputation in the legal profession. This convention has not been followed in recent past and there has been deviation from the above recognised principles. If there is non-appointment of anyone from the Additional Judges recommended by the CJB on the ground that he is not otherwise suitable it must be assigned to the CJB to enable him to reconsider and withdraw his recommendation. The materials supplied to the CJB by the Executive do not find it necessary to the CJB; such Additional Judge may be appointed. If, however, other senior Judges who have been consulted in the matter are of the view that materials supplied by the Executive are sufficient to withdraw recommendation, the non- appointment of such Additional Judge, for reasons to be recorded, may be permissible.

179. The criteria for appointment of duly qualified persons as Additional Judges from amongst the Advocates of the Supreme Court or from the Judicial Service should be character, merit, integrity and conduct. The purpose of judicial function is for the purpose of seeing that every organ of the state must act within limits of its power and carry out the duty imposed upon it by the Constitution and the law. If the state acts beyond the scope of its power and causes legal injury to a person, such injury is actionable. Therefore, it is desirable that the qualified persons are chosen for the job as per mandate of the Constitution so that the prime aim of the judicial process to protect individual rights is secured. If the persons have no basic qualification, one cannot expect proper administration of justice in their hands. An erroneous appointment of an unsuitable person is bound to produce irreparable damage to the faith of community of administration of justice. It is because of his or her character that one commands respect in the society. Credibility of the institution is held high if the persons who have composed are respected in their own right and not because of the institution.

180. The edifice of the SCB will not shine or this institution will not be able to protect the persons who are wronged by the injury caused by the act of the state unless the persons compose of the Court conduct their performance, in a way expected for them to conduct. A lawyer's merit is to be Judged not by volume of his practice but by his knowledge in law, literature, history, logic and philosophy; the number of cases argued by him which contributed to the growth of law and his fairness in Court. To add with this, his/her commitment to the cause of justice has to be seen by his/her work as a legal aid Advocate or Amicus curiae The merit of a Judge from the services is to be assessed by the quality of his judgments. Emphasis therefore, cannot be based on seniority alone at the cost of other qualities. A person having excellent merit without integrity is dangerous for the Judiciary. Therefore, integrity is the main criteria to be looked into and over which there cannot be any compromise. The persons who have questionable integrity should not be appointed as Judges of the highest Court. The procedures for screening Judges for appointments must ensure that no wrong person passes through the filter.

181. In C Ravichandran Lyer vs Justice AM Bhattacharjee (1995) 5 see 457, K Ramaswami, J observed:

"To keep the stream of justice clean and pure, the Judge must be endowed with sterling character, inpeccable integrity and upright behaviour. Erosion thereof would undermine the efficacy of the rule of law and the working of the Constitution itself. The Judges of higher echelons, therefore, should not be mere men of clay with all the frailties and foibles, human failings and weak character which may be found in those in other walks of life. They should be men of fighting faith with tough fibre not susceptible to any threats. The actual as well as the apparent independence of Judiciary would be transparent only when the office holders endow those qualities which would operate as impregnable fortress against surreptitious attempts to undermine the independence of the Judiciary. In short, the behaviour of the Judge is the bastion for the people to reap the fruits of the democracy, liberty and justice and the antithesis rocks the bottom of the rule of law".

182. It is thus clear that unless the Judges function without fear and favour, the question of their being impartial or independent does not arise.

183. It is always said and a recognised concept that the duty of a Judge is divine duty. The people of the country look up to the Judiciary to administer Justice; Justice that is fair; Justice that is equal, Justice that is unpolluted. In order to do justice the first and foremost expectation from a Judge is to be just and this expectation itself is the fountain source of all that can be put in the realm of canons of Judiciary ethics. The office of a Judge is not a service or employment; it is office of public service; it is an honour. It is said, a Judge remain a Judge all the time, all hours of a day, all days a week and all days a year. In order to ensure that the Judiciary is able to discharge its onerous responsibility the concept of independence of the Judiciary was planted into the Constitution as one of its basic organs.

184. In a democracy the need for competent, independent and impartial Judiciary is indispensable and has been recognised. It is sometimes said, the availability of independent and impartial Judiciary is synonymous with the existence of civilisation in society. There are so many rights of the citizen enshrined in the Constitution and the protection of those rights and implementation depends on the proper administration of justice. The administration of justice is not possible in the absence of an independent Judiciary. Courts assume their role as guardians of the rule of law. The source of judicial power is the effective exercise of judicial power originating firstly, from public acceptance of the authority of the Judiciary and secondly, the source is the integrity of Judiciary. This depends upon the Judges who constitute the system.

185. Alexander Hamilton said, "the Judiciary has no influence over either the sword or the purse; no direction either of the strength or of the wealth of the society, and can take no active resolution whatever. It may truly be said to have neither force nor will but merely judgment"

186. Socrates counseled, "Judges to hear courteously, answer wisely, consider soberly and decide impartially."
