187. An excellent Judge is impartial and fairness. He is independent of the Executive and the Legislature, but equally important he is independent to his own predilection and prejudices. He should be patient, cautious but realises that he is a Manager of Court's time. He should have possessed the qualities of giving full attention to the arguments advanced before him, but by the same time he is duty bound to curb irrelevant or frivolous arguments. He practices restraint in what he speaks in Court or out side and maintains dignity in the Court room and outside. His social relationship and personal life-style are correct and appropriate, conscious as he is that respect has to be earned by deserving and desiring and not by forcing or dictating.

188. In K Veeraswani vs Union of India, (1991) 3 see 655, it has been observed by Sharma J.

"The society's demand for honesty in a Judge is exacting and absolute. The standards of judicial behaviour, both on and off the Bench are normally extremely high. For a Judge to deviate from such standard of honesty and impartiality is to betray the trust reposed in him. No excuse or no legal relativity can condone such betrayal. From standpoint of justice, the size of the bribe or scope of corruption cannot be the scale for measuring a Judge's dishonour. A single dishonest Judge not only dishonours himself and disgraces his office but jeopardises the integrity of the entire judicial system. As a judicial scandal involving either the executive or a member of the legislature. The slightest hint of irregularity or impropriety in the Court is a cause for great anxiety and alarm. A legislature or an administrator may be found guilty of corruption without apparently endangering the foundation of the State. But a Judge must keep himself absolutely above suspicion; to preserve the impartiality and independence of the Judiciary and to have the public confidence thereof."

189. Rule of law and judicial review are the basic features of our Constitution and independence of Judiciary is an essential attribute of rule of law. Administration of justice requires Judiciary committed to the Constitution and law of the land. Judiciary must be free from pressures or influence from any quarter. The ultimate saviour of an independence of Judiciary is a brave and fearless Judge who truth fully discharges the duties of his office without in any manner being influenced from any quarter.

190. Emphasis shall be given while appointing a Judge of the highest calibre, competence and utmost integrity. A Judge in the performance of his or her duties will be complemented by a competent and ethical bar who will view their profession as a service-oriented one. The process of administration of justice will be speedy and inexpensive without sacrificing quality, keeping in mind that dispensing justice is not only to the disposal of cases. The criteria for appointment to the Bench, whether from the Bar or from the services, should be character, merit and integrity. It is because of his character that one commands respect in the society. Credibility of the institution is held high if those who compose it are respected in their own right and not because of the institution.

191. Mr M. Amirul Islam while arguing on the point of rule of law has emphasised on Al-Jahed Trust case and argues that in that case a distinction has been drawn between the concept of justice in Islam and the natural justice of the Romans, the formal justice of the Anglo-Saxons and the English common law system. Mr Islam argues that Islam seeks to attain a higher standard of 'absolute justice' the foundation of which is on justice. He contends that the Judges should not possess personal likes or dislikes, love or hate they should maintain strict impartiality. The power to appoint is a secret trust the same should be exercised in utmost good faith. Mr Islam contends that the Islamic literature on the subject of administration of justice spoke that any extraneous consideration other than merit is a great sin entailing severe punishment.

192. All religions spoke that while selecting Judges, the person should possess excellent character and to treat all as equal in the eye of law. According to Shri Bhagvad Gita, a Judge is a person bestowed with excellence. A Judge ought to be bestowed with the sense of complete detachment and humility. He is only an actor who has to play his role conforming to the script which represents the will of the author and thus surrendering to the will of Almighty. According to Islam, a Judge surrendering himself to the will of Almighty and such surrender is the supreme act of religion. Islam enjoins that while selecting Judges the authority should select a person of excellent character, of superior calibre and meritorious record and profound knowledge. The Christians in their daily prayer say "thy will be done, O Lord? A Judge, according to religious concepts whether of Hinduism, Islam or Christianity, would never be heard claiming with egotism that a particular judgment was written by him or particular sentence or decree was pronounced by him. He would always feel and proclaim what he had done or he does is to carry out the will of Almighty. His every action he would surrender to the Almighty and thereby be a totally detached and humble person.

193. Clause (a) of sub-Article (2) of Article 95 states that a person shall be qualified for appointment as a Judge if he has ten years practice as an Advocate of the SCB, and in case of persons from judicial office, clause (b) of the sub-Article (2) states, if such person has ten years in judicial service. Dr. Hossain contends that the immediate past political Government taking advantage of these clauses has appointed unqualified persons as Judges over which there has been widespread criticism. Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) also adopted a resolution condemning such appointment. It is contended that an Advocate after taking enrolment has taken a job of legal adviser to any organisation or has engaged himself in other business or for any other reason due to personal cause has not practiced in Court for a long time, such person cannot be said to be eligible for appointment as Additional Judge only because he/she has crossed 10 years as an Advocate of the Supreme Court. Similarly, a judicial officer has been on deputation for a long time and detached completely from judicial works such person cannot be appointed only because the Constitution permits appointment of judicial officer having held judicial office for 10 years. The persons to be selected for appointment are only those who are functioning within the judicial sphere and are known to the CJB and other senior Judges. The consultation should be effective, meaningful, and purposive; consensus oriented leaving no room for complaint of arbitrariness or unfair play. The experience of a particular period in profession or judicial service means practical experience, not theoretical or hypothetical and has to be determined by the CJB and Senior Judges who have to initiate the panel of candidates for appointment of Judges.

194. Mere enrolment of an Advocate for a period of 10 years is not sufficient to make him eligible for his appointment. It should also be borne in mind that the persons should possess integrity, capacity, character, merit, efficiency and fitness which are prerequisite components for judging the suitability of a person for the appointment of a Judge. Apart from the qualifications mentioned, certain other criteria should have to be looked into before selecting a person as Judge of the Supreme Court that he must have excellent academic qualification; he has continuous practice in Court; he has attended a senior's chamber of reputation; he has conducted cases independently; he has been an Advocate of the Appellate Division and appeared in some cases and so on. It is contended that immediate past Government has totally ignored this criteria and picked up some persons who have no basic qualification.

Independence of Judiciary

195. The Preamble of our Constitution reads as follows:

"We, the people of Bangladesh, having proclaimed our Independence on the 26th day of March, 1971 and through historic war for national independence, established the independent, sovereign People's Republic of Bangladesh.

Further pledging that it shall be a fundamental aim of the State to realise through the democratic process a socialist society, free from exploitation - a society in which the rule of law, fundamental human rights and freedom, equality and justice. political, economic and social, will be secured for all citizens;

Affirming that it is our secret duty to safe- guard, protect and defend this Constitution to maintain its supremacy as the embodiment of the will of the people of Bangladesh so that we may prosper in freedom and may make our full contribution towards international peace and cooperation in keeping with the progressive aspirations of mankind "

196. We achieved our Constitution after sacrificing millions of lives for common cause to ensure equality, human dignity and social justice. It is the people who in exercise of their self- proclaimed power achieved the independence for ensuring social justice, democratic process, a society free from exploitation - a society in which the rule of law will prevail. Our independence is completely different from others. We pledged to secure for all citizens a society in which the rule of law, fundamental human rights and freedom, equality and justice, political, economic and social and the affirmation of the sacred duty to safeguard, protect and defend the Constitution and maintain its supremacy as the embodiment of the will of the people.

197. The independence of our country generated in the minds of our people after witnessing whole scale violations, negation of basic human rights the prime ones being the right to life, rights to liberty, the rights of equality, the right of individual dignity and the freedom of thought and expression. The naked greed, lust for power and myth of racial superiority, coupled with the sense of impunity had led to the liberation struggle that saw three million precious human lives of extirpation for no reason. The concept of the rule of law and human rights are included in the preamble on the principle that they are sacrosanct bundle of rights vested in human beings so that they can live a dignified life "not by chance or choice but by being human." The preamble reflects the hopes and aspirations of the people. It also contains the ideologies of the State. The proclamation of independence and the preamble indicate the principles and ideals for which our heroes of the liberation struggle sacrificed their lives. These are people's sovereignty, Constitutional supremacy, independence of Judiciary.

198. The concept of 'independence of Judiciary' as part of the basic structure of the Constitution, to secure 'rule of law' is apparent from the preamble of the Constitution which is essential for the preservation of the democratic system in the state. Article 7 gives the powers of the Republic to the people and the exercise of the people's power on behalf of the people shall be affected under and by the authority of the Constitution. In the Fundamental Principles of State Policy it is said in Article 22 "The State shall ensure separation of the Judiciary from the executive organs of the State" which provide the true meaning in the different provisions in the Constitution relating to the composition of the Judiciary. It is in accord with the fundamental concepts in the constitutional scheme to preserve the Constitution as the resonant organism.

199. Similarly, by Article VI of the Constitution of the United States of America it is declared that "the Constitution, and the laws of the United States which shall be made in pursuance thereof, and all treaties made, or which shall be made, under the authority of the United States, shall be supreme law of the land; and the Judges, in every state, shall be bound thereby, anything in the Constitution and laws of any state to the contrary notwithstanding." Similar to our Constitution, the American Constitution does not determine the number of Judges of the Supreme Court - the number may be changed at pleasure, except that it cannot be diminished so as to deprive a Judge of his office. The other Courts exist at the will of Congress, and may be changed and modified at discretion, subject to a like limitation that a Judge cannot be legislated out of his office while the office itself remains.

200. The rule of law envisages the preeminence of law as opposed to anarchy or capricious dictates. It involves equal accountability of all before the law irrespective of high or low status. The rule of law will prevail if there is independence of Judiciary. One of the most important principles of just democratic governance is the presence of constitutional limits on the extent of government power. This includes guarantees of civil rights, and an independent Judiciary, which allows citizens to seek protection of their rights and redress against government actions. An independent Judiciary is important for preserving the rule of law.

201. Dr Kamal Hossain contends that a basic structure of the Constitution is the independence of Judiciary which is entrusted as a coordinate organ of the legislature, Executive with constitutional responsibility to act as a guardian of the Constitution to ensure that the limits upon the powers laid down by the Constitution are observed. Dr. Hossain argues that doctrine of "basic structure" in the context of constitutional reality in Bangladesh was explained in Anwar Hossain's case. In this connection Dr. Hossain has read a passage from Anwar Hossain's case which is as follows:

"Learned Attorney-General does not dispute that people's sovereignty, democracy, independence of the Judiciary and the principles as to separation of power are basic structure of the Constitution and says that no question arises as to their destruction or abolition-again the doctrine of basic structure cannot be rejected if consequence of its rejection is taken into consideration."

202. Dr Hossain adds that without independence of Judiciary, constitutional limit on powers would become illusory and the existence of fundamental rights precarious. In this connection Dr. Hossain has taken us to Article 22 of the Constitution and argues that with the objective of establishing an independent Judiciary, Article 22 as a fundamental principle of state policy provides for the separation of Judiciary from the executive organ of the State. Dr. Hossain has also referred Masdar Hossain's case in this connection.

203. Mr Ajmalul Hossain contends that independence of Judiciary is necessary for guardianship of the Constitution and for the establishment of the Rule of Law. According to Mr Hossain, the Judiciary is one of the three organs of the Republic. The Constitution vests the executive power of the Republic upon the Executive under Article 55(2), the legislative power has been vested upon the Parliament under Article 65(1) and judicial power has been vested upon the Judiciary in Part VI of the Constitution. Mr Hossain contends that an independent and impartial Judiciary is a pre-condition to the Rule of Law. He has referred the case of Anwar Hossain. In that reported case it was observed:

"if there is one principle which runs through the entire fabric of the Constitution, it is the principle of the Rule of Law and under the Constitution, it is the Judiciary which is entrusted with the task of keeping every organ of the State within the limits of the law and thereby making the Rule of Law meaningful and affective".

It was further added:

"independence of Judiciary, a basic structure of the Constitution is also likely to be jeopardised or affected by some of the provisions of the Constitution. Mode of their appointment and removal, security of tenure particularly fixed age for retirement and prohibition against employment in the Service of the Republic after retirement or removal are matters of great importance in connection with the independence of Judiciary. Selection of a person for appointment as a Judge in disregard to the question of his competency and his earlier performance as an Advocate or a judicial officer may bring in a "spineless Judge" in words of President Roosevelt; such a person can hardly be an independent Judge."

204. The Constitutional scheme of independence of Judiciary and the constitutional convention of consultation with the CJB in matters of appointment of Judges of the SCB cannot and is not a mere formality insofar as the recommendation of the CJB in such matters of appointment can be arbitrarily disregarded. The disregard of the opinion and recommendation of the CJB in matters of appointment of Judges and usurpation of that authority by the Executive is totally incompatible with the fundamental notions of supremacy of the Constitution and the independence of Judiciary.

205. In the entire Constitutional scheme the independence of Judiciary is a basic feature and so long the Judiciary performs independently, the people's right can never be endangered from any quarters and the Judiciary to be protector of the constitutionally guaranteed rights of the citizens.

206. The Constitutional provision for appointment of Additional Judges for a period not exceeding two years or for a further period cannot be treated, understood or interpreted as a contractual agreement or appointment for performing duties for a specified period which stands terminated or annulled at the end of the stated period without giving and/or communicating any reason is violative of the independence of the Judiciary and ultra vires of the constitutional provisions for securing the independence of the Judges of the highest Court, and thus the mode of appointment is reduced to the archaic 19th century rule of "master and servant" which could not have been the intention of the framers of the Constitution.

207. Judicial independence and accountability have come to be viewed as critical elements in the society's development of a stable government that may preserve the rights of all. This responsibility extends not only to individual rights and security of persons and property but to the capacity for determining rights in disputes in a fair and transparent manner. The Judiciary must become a co-equal branch of the government. Judicial independence is a fundamental principle for the governance of the democratic states. Its linkage to the rule of law - the applicability of legal standards of both those who govern and those who are governed-make the principle of judicial independence.

208. It is contended by all the counsel that independence of Judiciary is the backbone of a good judicial government. Administration of justice requires Judiciary committed to Constitution and the law of the land. Judiciary must therefore, be free from pressures or influence from any quarter. A Judiciary manned by Judges with vision, wisdom and compassion can do more justice and the welfare of the people who are deprived of the privilege than all the laws. The concept of judicial independence, takes within its sweep, independent from any pressure or prejudice. The Judiciary stands between the people of the country and the State as a bulwark against Executive pressure, excesses and misuse of power by the Executive.

209. Independence of Judiciary is an indispensable condition for democracy - if the Judiciary fails, the Constitution fails and the people might opt for some other alternative.

210. It is no doubt true that the constitutional assurances relating to the basic service conditions are absolutely necessary to protect the independence of the Judiciary but in my view they are not be all and end all. One other basic and inseparable vital condition is absolutely necessary for timely securing the independence of Judiciary that concerns the methodology, followed in the matter of sponsoring, selecting and appointing a proper and fit person in the higher Judiciary. The holistic condition is a major component that goes along with other constitutionally guaranteed service condition in securing a complete independence of Judiciary. To say differently, a healthy independent Judiciary can be said to have been firstly secured by accomplishment of the increasingly important condition in regard to the method of appointment of Judges and, secondly, protected by the fulfilment of the rights, privileges and other service conditions. The resultant inescapable conclusion is that only the perfection of all the requisite conditions beginning with the method and strategy of selection and appointment of Judges will secure and protect the independence of the Judiciary. Otherwise, not only will the credibility of the Judiciary totter and decline but also the entire judicial system will explode which in turn may cripple the proper functioning of democracy and the philosophy of this cherished concept will be only a myth rather than a reality.

211. It has been observed by Kuldip Singh, J, in Second Judges' case:

"Independence of Judiciary is the sine qua non of democracy. So long as the Judiciary remains truly distinct from both the Legislature and the Executive, the general power of the people can never be endangered from any quarters. Montesquieu in his book "Spirit of Laws" observed "there is no liberty if the power of judging be not separated from the Legislative and the Executive powers." The framers of the Constitution made it known in an emphatic voice that separation of Judiciary from Executive, which is the lifeline of independent Judiciary, is a basic feature of the Constitution."

Dr. BR Ambedkar in his speech in the Constituent Assembly on June 7, 1949 stated as under:

"I do not think there is any dispute that there should be separation between the executive and the Judiciary and, in fact, all the Articles relating to the High Court as well as the Supreme Court have prominently kept that object in mind."

It is further added:

"Then the question which comes up for consideration is, can there be an independent Judiciary when the power of appointment of Judges vests in the Executive? To say yes, would be illogical. The independence of Judiciary is inextricably linked and connected with the constitutional process of appointment of Judges of the higher Judiciary. Independence of Judiciary is the basic feature of our Constitution and if it means what we have discussed above, then the framers of the Constitution could have never intended to give this power to the Executive. Even otherwise the Governments-Central or the State-are particles before the Courts in large number of cases. The Union Executive have vital interests in various important matters which come for adjudication before the apex Court. The Executive-in one form or the other  is the largest single litigant before the Courts. In this view of the matter, the Judiciary being the mediator-between the people and the Executive-the framers of the Constitution could not have left the final authority to appoint the Judges of the Supreme Court and of the High Courts in the hands of the Executive. This Court in SP Gupta's case (AIR 1982 SC 149) proceeded on the assumption that the independence of Judiciary is the basic feature of the Constitution but failed to appreciate that the interpretation, it gave, was not in conformity with the broader facets of the two concepts-independence of Judiciary, and 'judicial review'-which are interlinked".

212. Under our constitutional scheme, the Judiciary has been assigned the onerous task of safe- guarding the fundamental rights of our citizens and upholding the rule of law. Since the Courts are entrusted the duty to uphold the Constitution and the laws, it often comes in conflict with the State when it tries to enforce its orders by exacting obedience from recalcitrant or indifferent state agencies. It is therefore, needed an independent and impartial Judiciary manned by persons of quality and character, determination and resolute impartially and independence who would dispense justice without fear or favour.

"Independence and impartiality are almost crucial concepts, the concepts of which are distinct. Impartiality refers to a state of mind and attitude of the Court in relation to the issues and the parties in a given case, while independence refers not only to the state of mind or attitude, but also to a status or relationship to others-particularly to the Executive branch of government-that rests on objective conditions and guarantees." (University of New Brunswick Law Journal Vol. 45, 1999).

213. The CJB is the head of the Judiciary and may be familiar of the brotherhood of Judges and it is not possible to say that so far as the consultative process is concerned, he is in any way less important.

214. Bangladesh, like other modern democratic countries has three vital organs-the legislature, executive and judicial. These three limbs of the state have nexus to each other in the maintenance rule of law. The Constitution devised powers among these three organs and makes them independent of each other, although there are systems of check and balance. One system cannot be given precedence over the other system. Judiciary is one of the most important systems in our Constitution which has been clearly highlighted in Articles 94(4), 96, 99, 101, 112, 113 and 116A of the Constitution. This organ has been vested with the responsibilities to up-hold the Constitution and guarantee that the rule of law emphasised in our Constitution will always prevail to ensure that the Judiciary will be able to discharge its responsibility. The concept of independence of Judiciary has been provided in the Constitution as one of the basic structures of it.

215. The concept of rule of law is dependent on an independent, fair and competent Judiciary. The rule of law has different meanings; its primary meaning is that everything must be done according to law. Applied to the powers of the government, this requires that every government authority which does some act which would otherwise be a wrong or which infringes a person's liberty, must be able to justify its action as authorised by law. Every act of governmental power every act which affects the legal rights, duties or liberties of any person, must be shown to have been a strictly legal pedigree. The rule of law demands something more, since otherwise it would be satisfied by giving the government unrestricted discretionary powers, so that everything that they did was within the law. The secondary meaning of the rule of law, therefore, is that government should conduct within a frame-work of recognised rules and principles which restrict discretionary power. A third meaning of the rule of law is that disputes as to the legality of acts of government are to be decided by Judges who are wholly independent of the Executive.

Constitutional convention

216. Dr Kamal Hossain points out that the long standing Constitutional convention mandates the consultation with the CJB in matters of appointment of Additional Judges and Judges of the HCD is a well recognised rule and constitutional convention which has been respected and acted upon, as in the past the Chief Justice did and do now send their recommendations, and this constitutional convention and the requirement of consultation will be rendered meaningless and a mere formality when such recommendation is disregarded without any reason and without any communication to the CJB in the appointment of Judges by the President and this clearly undermined the very foundation and scheme of judicial independence, which is violative of the Constitution, illegal and without lawful authority. In this connection, the learned Counsel has referred the case of Manob Jamin.

217. Mr Ajmalul Hossain contends that in our original Constitution the President is under obligation to consult with CJB in relation to the appointment of Judges of the SCB though this Constitutional Provision of consultation was changed in the 4th Amendment but it has been the constant practice that always the CJB has been consulted in the appointment process.

218. It is contended by Mr M Amirul Islam that two sets of rules make up the Constitutional Law: one set consistent of the rules contained in the written Constitution and the other set is referred to as the constitutional conventions which stem from the fact that written Constitutions cannot and do not provide for all eventualities and constitutional experts and Courts, over a period of time, evolve principles of aid in implementing the Constitution and to reflect the spirit of Constitution in concrete fact situations and thereby evolve constitutional conventions. The constitutional provisions are interpreted with the help of conventions which grow by passage of time.

219. Kuldip Singh, J observed in Second Judges' case, "Conventions are vital insofar they fill up the gaps in the Constitution itself, help solve problems of interpretation, and allow for the future development of the constitutional frame work." Constitutional conventions which are vital insofar as necessary for efficiency of constitutional deeds, aids in its interpretation, and contribute to strengthen and development of constitutional frame work. The conventions are built in the first instance on the foundation of law but once they are established, they tend to form the basis for the law. The practice of consultation with the CJB in matters of appointment of Judges of the SCB is a well recognised rule and a constitutional convention which has been recognised and acted upon as to fundamental importance for maintaining the independence of Judiciary.

220. The CJB, who is in the best position to assess the performance and determine the suitability of Additional Judges for appointment as Judges of the SCB, since the Additional Judges perform their responsibilities of dispensing justice without fear or favour under his constant supervision, in the majestic realm of SCB, far removed from the turmoil of political and other issues and in these circumstances, it is the CJB and not the political Executive functionaries of the State who from the political standpoint should decide who is appointed as Judge to the Apex Court. The opinion and recommendation of the CJB in regard to the appointment of Judges and usurpation of that authority by the political Executive is totally incompatible with the fundamental notions of supremacy of the Constitution and the independence of the Judiciary. In this connection Mr Islam points out that the successive disregard of the recommendation of the CJB is tantamount to not discharging duties as contemplated by the Constitution, disregarding his oath of office and the Judges of the Apex Court are oath bound to uphold the dignity and integrity of the opinion and recommendation . of the CJB and the Supreme Court is duty bound under the constitutional mandate to preserve and protect the rule of law and the cutting edge of law is the grant of remedial measures fashioned by the highest Court and the art of justice has to respond effectively to ensure that transparency wins over opaqueness and justice over injustice.

221. In the original Constitution of 1972 there was provision for "consultation" with the CJB by the President in the matter of appointment of a Judge under Article 95(1), which reads as follows:

"(a)The Chief Justice shall be appointed by the President, and other Judges shall be appointed by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice."

222. The Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1975 came into force on 24th January, 1975 which deleted this requirement of "consultation" with the cm in the matter of appointment of Judges of the HCD. Despite the deletion of the expression "consultation" in matters pertaining to the appointment of the Judges of the SCB, all appointments have, in fact, been made in consultation with the CJB; when one attempted departure from this constitutional convention of consultation made in February, 1994, and 9 Additional Judges were purported to be appointed to the HCD without any consultation with CJB. This appointment was resisted by the members of the Bar and ultimately the notification of appointment of these 9 Additional Judges was rescinded and fresh appointments were made in consultation with the CJB.

223. Though the appointment rests with the Executive but it must be in accord with the constitutional practice prevailing in all democratic countries. In the United Kingdom, a country from which we have inherited our system of administration of justice, appointment of Judges is made by or on the advice of the Lord Chancellor, who is a member of the Cabinet while appointments to the Court of appeal and the House of Lords and to the officers of Lord Chief Justice Master of the Rolls and President of the Family Division. Thus, though the appointment of a Judge belonging to the higher echelons of judicial service is wholly in the hands of the Executive, it is being made with the consultation with the Chief Justice. In the Commonwealth countries like Canada, Australia and New Zealand, the appointment of High Court and Supreme Court Judges is made by the Executive in consultation with the Chief Justices. The appointment of Judge in the Apex Court does not depend solely on professional suitability of the person concerned in terms of experience or knowledge of law but also on several other considerations, such as honesty, integrity and general pattern of behaviour which would ensure dispassionate and objective adjudication with an open mind, free and fearless approach to matters in issue, social acceptability of the person concerned to the high judicial office in terms of current norms and ethos of the society, commitment to democracy and rule of law. These various considerations, apart from professional and functional suitability, have to be taken into account while appointing a Judge.

224. There are authorities and it is now almost accepted by the Apex Courts both at home and other Commonwealth countries that there is no distinction between the "Constitutional Law" and "Constitutional Convention", both are binding in their field. Once a convention is established and operated then the convention becomes a "Constitutional Law" of the land and can be enforced in the like manner as "constitutional law". The existence of constitutional convention may be established on the basis of historical events and once this convention is in the field of operation, the constitutional functionaries are bound to follow the same.

225. Learned Assistant Attorney-General frankly concedes that he has no objection in allowing the petitions and in the appointment of the petitioners. He admits that the petitioners have illegally not been appointed by the past government as Judges. He, however, faintly argues that in view of the deletion by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1975, the requirement of consultation with the CJB in matters of appointment of Judges has become a mere routine work, inasmuch as under the present constitutional provisions the President has prerogative under Article 95(1) of the Constitution in the matter of appointments and he is not bound to follow the convention. According to the learned Assistant Attorney-General, a constitutional convention will not prevail over the constitutional provisions. Learned Assistant Attorney-General has referred a decision in the case of SN Goswami, Advocate vs Government of Bangladesh, 55 DLR 332 in support of his contention. I find no force in the contention. The conventions are built in the first instance on the foundation of law but once they are established, they tend to form the basis for the law. Even after the amendment of the Constitution, the constitutional convention prevailed in case of appointment of the aforesaid 9 Judges in 1994. After deletion of the expression "consultation" no written context has been provided that the Judges would mandatorily be appointed without the concurrence of the CJB. A constitutional convention of consultation when spread over a long period, here in this country it is being followed about 30 years, invariably becomes entrenched as a constitutional law.

"Now, therefore, in making appointment of a Judge of the Supreme Court the President is under no obligation, legal or constitutional, to consult Chief Justice, and as a matter of fact, after the 4th Amendment of the Constitution the President never consulted the Chief Justice. The Executive on their own appointed Judges."

Syed Amirul Islam J, observed in the above case:

"This consultation is a conventional consultation, which has no binding force, for it is not a rule of law. This sort of consultation cannot have primacy ............... 	"

226. In this connection I would like to repro- duce a passage of the author Judge in Manabjamin case, wherein the same Judge made contrary view which is as follows:

"A Review of all the aforesaid authorities leads us to the irresistible conclusion that there is no distinction between "constitutional law" and an established "constitutional convention" and both are binding in the field of their operation. Once it is established to the satisfaction of the Court that a particular convention becomes a part of the "constitutional law" of the land and can be enforced in the like manner."

227. In Manabjamin's case, in an issue published on 16th September, 2000 of daily Manobjamin a news item under the caption “একটি রাজকিয় কেলেংকারীর খসড়া”was published. The Attorney-General of Bangladesh filed an application to the Registrar of this Court enclosing the issue of the newspaper for bringing the said news to the notice of the CJB. The CJB sent the said application with the newspaper to a Division Court for consideration whether the said news undermined the authority of the Court. Pursuant thereto, a Rule was issued against the Chief Editor, Editor, Printer, Publisher, owner, the diplomatic reporter. Two other newspapers daily Janakantha in its issue on 31st October, 2000 and the daily Ittefaq in its issue on 1st November, 2000 had also published news on the point. In the said reported case, the question of independence of Judiciary and appointment of Judges of the SCB came under consideration. As regards the appointment of Judges the constitutional convention of consultation with the CJB has been highlighted in the said reported case. Dr. Hossain contends that in that case the point regarding the appointment of Judges of this Court is not in issue but since the said historical fact regarding the appointment of Judges has been considered and discussed while discussing on the point of independence of Judiciary, the decision has persuasive value. On the point of constitutional convention, it was observed:

"In our original Constitution the constitutional provision was that in the matter of appointment of a Judge in either of the Divisions of the Supreme Court it has to be made in consultation with the Chief Justice of Bangladesh. But after the Fourth Amendment the provision so far it relates to the consultation with the Chief Justice in the matter of appointment of a Judge of this Court was done away and the notifications which have been issued after the Fourth Amendment do not reflect that Judges of this Court were appointed in consultation with the Chief Justice of Bangladesh but it is revealed that even after the Fourth Amendment the Judges were appointed in consultation with the Chief Justice of Bangladesh even during the Martial Law regime though the matter of consultation was not reflected in the notification. This state continued until February 1994. On second of February 1994 nine Judges were appointed in this Division but giving a go-by to the convention. This time the appointment was made without any consultation with the then Chief Justice. After the publication of the notification it came to the notice of the learned Chief Justice that the said notification was issued appointing nine Judges of this Division without any prior consultation with him. This caused great anger and commotion in the mind of the learned Chief Justice."

It is added:

"After working out the compromise the earlier notification was withdrawn and a fresh notification was issued on 9th of February 1994 and in that notification for the first time after the Fourth Amendment it was mentioned that the aforesaid appointment of the Judges in this Division was made by the President in consultation with the Chief Justice."

It has been further added:

"Therefore, it appears that even after the Fourth Amendment although the provision of consultancy was deleted from the Constitution, nevertheless, the Chief Justice played the pivotal role in the appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court."

228. We find in the Manabjamin case that after the omission of the expression "consultation" from Article 95 (1) by a constitutional amendment the Executive wanted to break the convention taking advantage of the amendment by appointing Judges of their choice but ultimately the Executive was compelled to rescind the notification of the appointment of 9 Judges and appointed 9 Judges with prior consultation with the CJB. In this connection I would like to reiterate a passage from the book of Mr Justice Mustafa Kamal "Bangladesh Constitution; Trends and Issues" at page 29 which reads as follows:

"Article 95(1) provided that "the Chief Justice shall be appointed by the President, and the other Judges shall be appointed by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice." The Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1975 took away the provision of consultation. As it stands now, "the Chief Justice and other Judges shall be appointed by the President." The element of consultation in the selection of other Judges was a major safeguard against political and expedient appointments. The metamorphosis of Article 95( I) renders the highest judicial appointment in the country subject to valid objection. A Judge's appointment is now an exclusive privilege of the Chief Executive. The office of the President was the office of the Chief Executive. The office of the President was the office of the Chief Executive from 1975 to 1991. Since 1991 the President is a titular head. As Article 48(3) stands now, the President has the power to appoint the Prime Minister and the Chief Justice without the advice of anyone, but in all other matters he "shall act in accordance with the advice of the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister is now the Chief Executive, on whose advice the President is obliged to act. Therefore, it is, in fact, the Chief Executive who advises the President to appoint the other Judges of the Supreme Court.

The original Article 95(1) contained a constitutional acknowledgment of the role of the Chief Justice in the matter of appointment of the Judges of the Supreme Court. It implied a tacit recognition of the premises that appointments to the highest Judiciary need to be above political considerations and that the Chief Justice being head of the Judiciary is the most competent person to opine who is most suitable for such appointment. Consultation with him was, therefore, made a constitutional imperative. The withdrawal of consultation is tantamount to a negation of that premise. However, in spite of this constitutional change in 1974, all appointments as Judges of the Supreme Court have, in fact, been made in consultation with the Chief Justice. One departure was made in February, 1994 when 9 Additional Judges were appointed to the High Court Division without consultation with the Chief Justice. Following a protest, the Notification was rescinded and fresh appointments were made recognising in the fresh Notification itself that the appointments were made in consultation with the Chief Justice."

229. In SP Gupta's case the Supreme Court of India exhaustively discussed different decisions and authors on the point of constitutional conventions. Tulzapurkar, J after reproducing a passage from the book "The Law and the Constitution" of Sir Ivor Jennings stated thus:

"Constitutional convention is broadly defined as rules of political practice which are regarded as binding by those to whom they apply but which are not laws as they are not enforced by the Courts. It may be an aid to construction but not positive rule of law, breach of which is remediable by Court action. It must, however, be remembered that the conventions grow around and upon the principles of a writ- ten Constitution. The conventions generally grow where the powers of the Government are vested in different persons or bodies or where, in the words of Sir William Holdsworth, the Conventions of the Eighteenth Century Constitution, 17 Iowa Law Review, page. 162, there is a mixed Constitution. But conventions do pre- suppose the law and any convention contrary to the written context is of no validity. The conventions are built in the first instance, on the foundation of law but once they are established, they tend to form the basis for the law. It may, however, be noticed that these rules of law which are conventions are a mere matter of practice and their effect must change with the changing circumstances of national life."

230. It is further stated, implications arising from the provisions of the Constitution, constitutional conventions and constitutional practice all stand on a different footing. A constitutional convention when spread over a long period, of immemorial antiquity, followed invariably becomes entrenched as a rule of law but any convention contrary to the written provision is of no validity. Implications may arise from the context in which a language in the provision or from the nature of the power claimed vis-a-vis the whole constitutional scheme. That was how implied limitations on the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution were spelt out in Keshavananda Bharatis case (AIR 1973 SC 1461). Constitutional practice may be spelt out as a course of conduct over a reasonably long period which may indicate how the authorities charged with a duty to implement the Constitution have worked out or implemented a certain provision of the Constitution.

231. Sir Ivor Jennings in his book stated, "we have to ask ourselves three questions: First- what are the Precedents, Secondly, did the actors in precedents believe that they were bound by a rule, and thirdly, is there a reason for the rule?

232. Kuldip Singh, J after considering three tests laid down by Sir Ivor Jennings adopted in the facts of the Second Judges' case and observed that those tests are applicable in the matter of appointment of Judges in the highest Courts and that the convention to the effect that the opinion and the recommendation of the Chief Justice of India in the matter of appointment of Judges is binding on the Executive." The relevant portions of the observations as under:

"The first test is what are the precedents? Under the Government of India Act 1935, which remained operative till 1950, all appointments of Judges to the Federal Court and the High Courts were made with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of India. The apex Judiciary in its memorandum dated March 1948 recorded in writing that the appointments of Judges were made under the British Raj with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of India on the basis of an established convention. We have the precedents for the period from 1950 to 1959 and from January 1, 1983 to April 10, 1993. Almost all the appointments during the said period were made with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of India. The precedents thus clearly indicate the existence of the convention and, as such, the first question, according to us, is complied with.

"We now come to the second test. Did the actors in the precedents believe that they were bound by a rule? The actors in the precedents are more than vocal on the issue. As back as 1959, the Home Minister of the stature of Gobind Ballabh Pant declared on the floor of the Rajya Sabha that "the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court is, I think, rightly deemed and believed to be familiar with the merits of his own colleagues and also of the Judges and Advocates who hold leading positions in different States. We have quoted the speech of Mr Jagannath Kaushal made on the floor of Rajya Sabha in November 1959. He held the office of the Union Law Minister during the period 1980 to 1983 and, as such, was also one of the actors in the precedents who firmly believed that the Executive was bound by the recommendations made by the Judiciary. During the course of arguments before us the stand of the Executive was consistent to the extent that they have almost invariably accepted the recommendations of the Judiciary in the matter of appointment of Judges. We have, therefore, no hesitation in holding that the second test laid down by Sir Ivor Jennings is also satisfied.

"Is there a reason for the Rule" is the third test. There are two primary reasons in support of the convention that the primacy rests with the Judiciary. There is no dispute that independence of Judiciary is the basic feature of the Constitution. We have already dealt with in detail the concept of independence of Judiciary and we have come to the conclusion that the exclusion of the final say of the executive in the matter of appointment of Judges is the only way to maintain the independence of Judiciary. If that be so then there cannot be a better reason for reading such a convention while interpreting Articles 124(2) and 217(1) of the Constitution. The second and the more important reason for giving weight to the opinion of the Judiciary is that the appointments are made to the "superior Judiciary" and to find out the suitable persons for such appointments the expertise for that purpose is only available with the Judiciary. It is difficult rather impossible to accept the submission that all the consulting functionaries must be regarded as of coordinating authority because on various aspects like integrity, capacity, character, merit, efficiency and fitness which are relevant for the purpose of judging the suitability of a person, the executive authorities would be the least informed and will have nothing to say. On the other hand the Chief Justice of the High Court and the Chief Justice of India, being best informed, are well equipped to express their views and tender advice on the suitability of the persons. All the constitutional functionaries being very high authorities in their respective spheres there may not ordinarily be any conflict in their assessment of a person regarding his suitability for appointment of a Judge but in the event of any difference the advice tendered by the Judiciary being in the nature of an "expert advice" has to be preferred. With a view to remove any controversy in future at the time of drafting the Constitution of India, the need was felt for collective "consultation" in the scheme of appointments of Judges in superior Courts to enjoy the benefit and fruits of democratic rule by its citizens.

The persons to be selected for appointment as Judges are those who have been functioning within the judicial spheres and are known to the CJB. The Executive as a layman can have no knowledge about their suitability for appointment. It is only in the consultative process the right one can be picked up. If the Executive is left to ignore the advice of cm in the process of consultation, the very purpose of providing consultation will be defeated.

260. Our original Constitution 1972 has been borrowed from the British form of Government making the cabinet collectively responsible to the people-the machinery of government is in resemblance of the British pattern-the British constitutional conventions have either been incorporated or are being followed as unwritten constitutional conventions. The conventions necessary to ignore the cabinet system are being followed in our country. Therefore, the constitutional conventions which are being followed for over sixty years are binding in the field of their operation. There is no scope for deviation from these established conventions. It is absolutely necessary for the independence of Judiciary that there must be consultation with the CJB before appointment of a Judge, which is one of the basic features of the Constitution.

261. Even after laying down the principles and prescribed procedural norm in regard to the appointment of Judges in the Second Judges' case, doubts arose about the interpretation of the law laid down in the above case, and the President of India in the public interest felt that the said doubts relating to appointment be resolved and accordingly, in exercise of powers under Article 143 made Special Reference No.1 of 1998 to the Supreme Court of India for clarification of the principles laid down in the case of Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association and its opinion on questions amongst others;

"(1) Consultation between the Chief Justice of India and his brother Judges in the matter of appointments of Supreme Court and High Court Judges and transfers of the latter;

(2) judicial review of transfer of Judges;

(3) the relevance of seniority in making appointments to the Supreme Court;

262. Of the three questions the point No. (1) above has relevancy in our case and thus I have omitted the other points while narrating the reply of the Full Court. In the above reference, the Full Court answered the point as under:

"The expression 'consultation with the Chief Justice of India' in Articles 217( 1) and 222( 1) of the Constitution of India requires consultation with a plurality of Judges in the formation of the opinion of the Chief Justice of India. The sole individual opinion of the Chief Justice of India does not constitute 'consultation' within the meaning of the said Articles.

The Chief Justice of India must make a recommendation to appoint a Judge of the Supreme Court and to transfer a Chief Justice or puisne Judge of a High Court in consultation with the four senior most puisne Judges of the Supreme Court. Insofar as an appointment to the High Court is concerned, the recommendation must be made in consultation with the two senior-most puisne Judges of the Supreme Court.

The Chief Justice of India is not entitled to act solely in his individual capacity, without consultation with other Judges of the Supreme Court, in respect of materials and information conveyed by the Government of India for non- appointment of a Judge recommended for appointment.

The Chief Justice of India is obliged to comply with the norms and the requirement of the consultation process, as aforestated, in making his recommendations to the Government of India."

263. Recommendations made by the Chief Justice of India without complying with the norms and requirements of the consultation process, as afore- stated, are not binding upon the Government of India.

264. Petitioners in paragraph 7 in Writ Petition No. 2975 of 2003 stated that the Law Minister in an interview with a private television channel admitted that there was constitutional convention of taking recommendation from the CJB. The Law Minister, in fact, admitted that the CJB recommended the petitioners but as per present constitutional scheme the President was not bound to appoint the Judges on the basis of recommendation. No rejoinder was so far made from the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs disputing the statements of the Law Minister.

265. Therefore, there is no doubt that the government did not appoint the petitioners despite recommendation of the learned Chief Justice. Some of the petitioners had practiced in the SCB before being appointed as Additional Judges. In their affidavits they asserted that they had very good practice with reputation and accepted the government's proposal for honour and respect and that they accepted their appointments on the premises that at the end of the initial period of two years, if the Chief Justice recommended for their confirmation as permanent Judges reflecting their assumption of satisfactory performance as Additional Judges, they would be confirmed as permanent Judges in the ordinary course. Four petitioners were elevated from the lower Judiciary. They were in judicial service for more than 25 years and performed judicial works with reputation. It is not expected that they are not competent or that they have political background or nexus with any political party. These facts sufficiently suggest that they have not been appointed Judges of SCB without just cause despite the fact that they have performed judicial works as Additional Judges to the satisfaction of the CJB and that the CJB has recommended their appointments as Judges. The constitutional jurisprudence on the subject of judicial appointments indicates that if there is any reason why the CJB's recommendation is not accepted then those reasons should be communicated to the CJB, and the matter resolved through further consultation giving due respect to the view of the CJB. The past government remained silent despite criticism, and arbitrarily did not appoint them.

267. Dr Hossain contends that the Constitutional Jurisprudence from other jurisdiction in South Asia, particularly India and Pakistan have elucidated the critical importance of effective consultation with the CJB as the Constitutional requirement for appointment of Judges. In this connection Mr Ajmalul Hossain argues that the recommendation of the CJB requires primacy under our Constitutional dispensation.

Article 94(4) of the Constitution reads as follows:

(4) Subject to the provisions of this Constitution the Chief Justice and the other Judges shall be independent in the exercise of their judicial functions."

268. This sub-article (4) states that the Judges shall be independent in the exercise of their judicial works. Now the question is if the Executive has the primacy in the appointment of Judges how the Judges will perform their judicial works independently? The independence of Judiciary is dependent on the appointment of Judges, and if the remote control in the process of the appointment of Judges lies in the hands of the Executive, how the Judges will perform their judicial works independently in accordance with the mandate of Article 94(4) is the main question to be looked into if in true sense the Executive wants as per mandate of the Constitution, the Judges to exercise judicial functions independently?

269. It was observed by JS Verma, J in Second Judges' case that "the primary aim must be to reach an agreed decision taking into account the views of all the consultees, giving the greatest weight to the opinion of the Chief Justice of India who, as earlier stated, is best suited to know the worth of the appointee. No question of primacy would arise when the decision is reached in this manner by consensus, without any difference of opinion. However, if conflicting opinions emerge at the end of the process, then only the question of giving primacy to the opinion of any of the consultees arises. "For reasons indicated earlier, primacy to the Executive is negative by the historical change and the nature of functions required to be performed by each. The primacy must, therefore, lie in the final opinion of the Chief Justice of India, unless for very good reasons known to the Executive and disclosed to the Chief Justice of India, that appointment is not considered to be suitable. However, it need hardly be stressed that the primacy of the opinion of the Chief Justice of India in this context is, in effect, primacy of the opinion of the Chief Justice of India formed collectively, that is to say, after taking into account the views of his senior colleagues who are required to be consulted by him for the formation of his opinion."

270. In the Second Judges' case the majority view was that the constitutional scheme excludes the scope of absolute power in anyone individual. Such a construction of the provisions also matches the constitutional scheme and the constitutional purpose for which these provisions were enacted. Attention has to be focused on the purpose, to enable better appreciation of the significance of the role of each participant, with the consciousness that each of them has some inherent limitation, and it is only collectively that they constitute the selector. The provision for consultation was introduced because of the realisation that the Chief Justice is best equipped to know and assess the worth of the candidate, and his suitability for appointment as a superior Judge; and it was also necessary to eliminate political influence even at the stage of the initial appointment of a Judge, since the provisions for securing his independence after appointment were alone not sufficient for an independent Judiciary. At the same time, the phraseology used indicated that giving absolute discretion or the power of veto to the Chief Justice as an individual in the matter of appointments was not considered desirable, so that there should remain some power with the Executive to be exercised as a check, whenever necessary. The selection should be made as a result of a participatory consultative process in which the Executive should have power to act as a mere check on the exercise of power by the Chief Justice to achieve the constitutional purpose. No question of primacy would arise when the decision is reached in this manner by consensus, without any difference of opinion. The primacy must, therefore, lie in the final opinion of the Chief Justice.

271. Primarily, it is this indication which is given by the constitutional provisions, and the constitutional purpose would be best served if the decision is made by consensus without the need of giving primacy to anyone of the consultees on account of any difference remaining between them. The question of primacy of the opinion has to be reached by consensus. The object of selecting the best men to constitute the superior Judiciary is achieved by requiring consultation with not only the Judiciary but also the Executive to ensure that every relevant particular about the candidate is known and duly weighed as a result of effective consultation between all the consultees, before the appointment is made. It is the opinion of the Judiciary symbolised by the view of the Chief Justice which is given greater significance or primacy in the matter of appointments. In other words, the view of the Chief Justice is to be expressed in the consultative process as truly reflective of the opinion of the Judiciary, which means that it must necessarily have the element of plurality in its formation. In actual practice, this is how the Chief Justice does, and is expected to function, so that the final opinion expressed by him is not merely his individual opinion but the collective opinion formed after taking into account the views of some other Judges who are traditionally associated with this function. The opinion of the Judiciary 'symbolised by the view of the Chief Justice is to be obtained by consultation with the Chief Justice and it is this opinion which has primacy.

272. This opinion has to be formed in a pragmatic manner and past practice based on convention is a safe guide. There may be a certain area, relating to suitability of the candidate, such as his antecedents and personal character, which at times, consultees, other than the CJB, may be in a better position to know. In Second Judges' case two questions came under consideration in the Constitutional Bench which are:

(1) Primacy of the opinion of the Chief Justice of India in regard to the appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts and in regard to the transfers of High Court Judges/Chief Justice and

(2) Justifiability of these matters including the matter of fixation of the Judges strength in the High Court.

S Ratnavel Pandian , J observed:

"It cannot be gainsaid that the CJI being the head of the Indian Judiciary and pater familias of the judicial fraternity has to keep a vigilant watch in protecting the integrity and guarding the independence of the Judiciary and he in that capacity evaluates the merit of the candidate with regard to his/her professional attainments, legal ability, etc. and offer his opinion. Therefore, there cannot be any justification in scanning that opinion of the  CJI by applying a superimposition test under the guise of over- guarding the Judiciary."

"When an argument was advanced in Gupta's case (AIR 1982 SC 149) to the effect that where there is difference of opinion amongst the Constitutional functionaries required to be consulted, the opinion of the CJI should have primacy, since he is the head of the Indian Judiciary and pater familias of the judicial fraternity. Bhagwati, J rejected that contention posing a query, as to the principle on which primacy can be given to the opinion of one constitutional functionary, when clause (I) of Article 217 places all the three constitutional functionaries on the same pedestal so far as the process of consultation is concerned. The learned Judge by way of an answer to the above query has placed the opinion of the CJI on par with the opinion of the other constitutional functionaries. The above answer, in our view, ignores or overlooks the very fact that the judicial service is not the service in the sense of employment, and is distinct from other services 	and that "the members of the other services 	. .......... cannot be placed on par with the members of the Judiciary, either constitutionally or functionally." (See All India Judges' Association and others case (1993(4) JT (SC) 618 (Supra). There are innumerable impelling factors which motivate, mobilise and impart momentum to the concept that the opinion of the cn given in the process of 'consultation' is entitled to have primacy.

They are:

(1) The 'Consultation' with the CJI by the President is relatable to the Judiciary and not to any other service.

(2) In the process of various Constitutional appointments, 'consultation' is required only to the judicial office in contrast to the other high ranking constitutional offices. The prior 'consultation' envisaged in the first proviso to Article 124(2) and Article 217(1) in respect of judicial offices is a reservation of limitation on the power of the President to appoint the Judges to the superior Courts.

(3) The 'consultation' by the President is a sine-qua-non or a condition precedent to the exercise of the constitutional power by the President to appoint Judges and this power is inextricably mixed up in the entire process of appointment of Judges as an integrated process. The 'consultation' during the process in which an advice is sought by the President cannot be easily brushed aside as an empty formality or a futile exercise or a mere casual one attached with no sanctity.

(4) The context in which the expression 'shall always be consulted' used in the first proviso of Article 124(2) and the expression "shall be appointed 	..............after consultation" deployed in Article 217(1) denote the mandatory character of 'consultation', which has to be and is of a binding character.

(5) Articles 124 and 217 do not speak in specific terms requiring the President to consult the executive as such" but the executive comes into play in the process of appointment of Judges to the higher echelon of judicial service by the operation of Articles 74 and 163 of the Constitution. In other words, in the case of appointment of Judges, the President is not obliged to consult the executive as there is no specific provision for such consultation.

(6) The President is constitutionally obliged to consult the Cll alone in the case of appointment of a Judge to the Supreme Court as per the mandatory proviso to Article 124(2) and in the case of appointment of a Judge to the High Court, the President is obliged to consult the CJI and the Governor of the State and in addition the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned, in case the appointment relates to a Judge other than the Chief Justice of that High Court. Therefore, to place the opinion of the en on par with the other constitutional functionaries is not in consonance with the spirit of the Constitution but against the very nature of the subject matter concerning the Judiciary and in opposition to the context in which 'consultation' is required. After having observed that the 'consultation' must be full and effective by Bhagwati, J in Gupta's case there is no conceivable reason to hold that such 'consultation' need not be given primary consideration.

(7) The very emphasis of the word 'always be consulted" signifies and indicates that the mandatory consultation should be unfailingly made without exception on every occasion and at every time by the President with the constitutional consultees."

273. Kuldip Singh, J while concurring with the majority view expressed by Verma J, observed:

"The constitutional scheme does not give primacy to any individual. Article 124(2) provides consultation with the Chief Justice of India, Judges of the Supreme Court and Judges of the High Courts. Likewise Article 217( 1 ) talks of Chief Justice of India and the Chief Justice of the High Court. Plurality of consultations has been clearly indicated by the Framers of the Constitution. On first reading one gets the impression as if the Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts have not been included in the process of consultation under Article 217(1) but on a closer scrutiny of the constitutional scheme one finds that this was not the intention of the framers of the Constitution. There is no Puisne Judges of the Supreme Court and of the High Court from the "consultee zone' under Article 217(1) of the Constitution."

274. Law is not static - it is creating more and more a new category of rights in favour of a person who is wronged by the action of the state or a public authority or any other person or who has suffered a legal injury by reason of violation of his legal right. It is also imposing a new category of duties on the government and the public officials with a view to reaching social justice to the common man. In the language of PN Bhagwati, J quoting Krishna Iyer's observations:

"Justice Cardozo approvingly quoted President Theodore Roosevelt's stress on the social philosophy of the Judges, which shakes and shapes the course of a nation and, therefore, the choice of Judges for the higher Courts which makes and declares the law of the land, must be in tune with the social philosophy of the Constitution. Not mastery of the law alone, but social vision and creative craftsmanship are important imputs in successful justicing."

275. The Constitutional Law is dynamic and cannot be static if it is to meet the needs of the people. Whenever new situation arises a new look at the existing legal concept requires interpretation of the constitutional text for advancing the policy and purpose underlying its provisions. The Courts must face the facts and meet the needs and aspirations of the times. Interpretation of the Constitution is a continual process. It is said that "the Constitution has not only to be read in the light of contemporary circumstances and values, it has to be read in such a way that circumstances and values of the present generation are given expression in its provisions." Jurists say 'constitutional interpretation is as much a process of creation as one of discovery."

276. Lord Denning in this connection made the following observation:

"Law does not stand still. It moves continually. Once this is recognised, then the task of the Judge is to put it on higher plane. He must consciously seek to mould the law so as to serve the needs of the time, must not be a mere mechanic, a mere working mason, laying brick on brick, without thought to the overall design. He must be an architect-thinking of the structure as a whole building for society, a system of law which is strong, durable and just."

Legitimate expectation

277. Mr Hossain contends that the writ petitioners have legitimate expectation of being appointed under Article 95 after successfully performing the functions as Additional Judges. According to Mr Hossain the legitimate expectation cannot be limited only "being considered for appointment". He contends that after successfully performing as Additional Judges the next stage will have to be followed automatically i.e. unless there are good reasons for non appointment, an Additional Judge must be appointed as Judge. In this connection Messrs Islam and Hossain have referred the case of Chairman, Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation vs Nasir Ahmed Chowdhury, 7 MLR (AD) 265 = 7 BLC (AD) 144. In that case the claim of legitimate expectation was not found in favour of the writ petitioner. His Lordship however referred a passage from (1984) All ER 935 which is as follows;

"In (1985) AC 374, (1984) 3 that for a legitimate expectation to arise, the decisions of the administrative authority must affect the person by depriving him of some benefit or advantage which either (i) he had in the past been permitted by the decision maker to enjoy and which he can legitimately expect to be permitted to continue to do until there has been communicated to him some rational grounds for withdrawing it on which he has been given an opportunity to comment; or (ii) he has received assurance from the decision maker that they will not be withdrawn without giving him first an opportunity of advancing reasons for contending that they should not be withdrawn, the substantive part the principle, is that if a representation is made that a benefit of a substantive nature will be granted or if the person is already in receipt of the benefit that it will be continued and not be substantially varied, then the same could be enforced. The interest in regard to which a legitimate expectation could be had must be one which was protectable. An expectation could be based on an express promise or representation or by established past action of settled conduct. The representation must be clear and un-ambiguous."

278. In this connection Mr Hossain also has placed Halsbury's Laws of England, Vol. 1(1), 4th Edn, para 81 at pages 151-52, it is stated thus:

"Legitimate expectations-A person may have a legitimate expectation of being treated in a certain way by an administrative authority even though he has no legal right in private law to receive such treatment."

279. The petitioners had performed their judicial works as Additional Judges satisfactorily and since the CJB had recommended for appointments under Article 95, they had legitimate expectation to be appointed as Judges of the SCB as a convention being followed for over sixty years. All the learned Counsels submitted that the writ petitioners not only had legitimate expectations, they had acquired a constitutional right for being appointed as Judges of the SCB. It can be said that as the appointments were made against permanent vacancies, and since the CJB had recommended them for appointment they had acquired legitimate expectation to be appointed as Judges in the absence of strong reasons to the contrary, which must be recorded by the Executive. The functions of a Judge in the highest Court are not a service of the Republic rather it is an honour and dignity and public service and in lieu of their service, he or she gets emolument prescribed by law. As public servant they do not draw any salary and other benefits and therefore, after successfully performing the functions as Additional Judges, there is strong legitimate expectation that they will be appointed as Judges of SCB.

280. Expectation means the act or state of expecting: that which is or may fairly be expected: that which should happen, according to general norms or custom or behavior: that the degree of probability or the value of something expected.

281. In SP Gupta's case PN Bhagwati, J observed as follows:

"By and large, every person entered the High Court Judiciary as an Additional Judge in the clear expectation that as soon as a vacancy in the post of a permanent Judge became available to him in the High Court he would be confirmed as a permanent Judge and if no-such vacancy became available to him until the expiration of his term of office, he would be reappointed as an Additional Judge for a further term in the same High Court. Therefore, far from being aware that on the expiration of their term, they would have to go back because they were appointed only as temporary Judges for a short period in order to clear off the arrears which would have been the position if cl. (1) of Art, 224 had been implemented according to its true intendment and purpose - the Additional Judges entered the High Court Judiciary with a legitimate expectation that they would not have to go back on the expiration of their term but they would be either reappointed as Additional Judges for a further term or if in the meanwhile a vacancy in the post of a permanent Judge became available, they would be confirmed as permanent Judges. This expectation which was generated in the minds of Additional Judges by reason of the peculiar manner in which Cl (1) of Art, 224 was operated, cannot now be ignored by the Government and the Government cannot be permitted to say that when the term of an Additional Judge expires, the Government can drop him at its sweet will. By reason of the expectation raised in his mind through a practice followed for almost over a quarter of a century, an Additional Judge is entitled to be considered for appointment as an Additional Judge for a further term on the expiration of his original term and if in the meanwhile, a vacancy in the post of a permanent Judge becomes available to him on the basis of seniority amongst Additional Judges, he has a right to be considered for appointment as a permanent Judge in his High Court".

On the said point Tulzapurkar, J, expressed his views as under:

"Frankly, there is some force in the submission that a practice has grown up for over last quarter of a century (1956-81) that whenever an Additional Judgeship is offered to a person, he accepts it in the reasonable belief that in course of time he would get a berth as a permanent Judge. It may generate hope in him and his expectations could be said to be well founded and reasonable, moreso it is, save in rarest of rare cases, invariably done so far. At the minimal most he is entitled to be first, considered for a fresh tenure of two years or when the permanent vacancy arises for appointment to that perm anent vacancy before any rank outsider is considered given the situation that the pre-requisites which necessitated his initial appointment continue to exist."

"No cases were pointed out to us that where there were Additional Judges in the High Court and a perm anent vacancy occurred someone was appointed who had not functioned as an Additional Judge. An Additional Judge was usually offered permanent Judgeship.
