May be there might be some rare cases in which some fortunate few were directly appointed as permanent Judges but no case was brought to our notice where there were Additional Judges in a High Court and a permanent vacancy occurred and overlooking the claims of all Additional Judges either a member of the Bar or a District Judge was directly appointed to that perm anent vacancy. Therefore, there is no gainsaying the fact that a practice was followed for over 25 years that an Additional Judge was always first considered and he was entitled to be considered for a fresh tenure if there was no perm anent vacancy and if there was vacancy in the permanent strength, for being appointed as a permanent Judge."

282. Bhagwati, J was of the view that an Additional Judge had legitimate expectation for appointment as permanent Judge in accordance with the seniority whenever a vacancy occurred but did not apply this principle in case of SN Kumar in view of the fact that the Chief Justice of Delhi High Court pointed out by letter dated 6th March, 1981 that he was not in a position to recommend the "extension for Justice Kumar for an Additional term", that there were "serious complaints against SN Kumar both oral and in writing" through the Law Minister, that SN Kumar had not been very hopeful in disposing of cases; and that some respectable members of the Bar and some of the colleagues of the Chief Justice had also expressed doubt about "SN Kumar's integrity." The case of the petitioners is quite distinguishable, inasmuch as no such sort of complaint against the petitioners has been made, rather the Bar, the CJB and the civil society stand in support of their permanent appointment.

283. Monzoor Hussain Sial J, in Al Jahed Trust case observed as follows:

"A practice/convention has developed in Pakistan for the last about 25 years that Additional Judges are appointed against permanent vacancies and after the expiry of the period for which they were initially appointed they are considered for permanent appointment as Judges of the High Court. Invariably, if Additional Judge of High Court performs his functions during the period for which he is appointed to the satisfaction of the Chief Justice of the High Court as also the Chief Justice of Pakistan, he is appointed as permanent Judge of the High Court. The Additional Judge, who is appointed against a permanent vacancy, or the vacancy having occurred during the period he was working as Additional Judge clearly acquires a reasonable expectancy to be considered for appointment as permanent Judge. In order to secure the independence of Judiciary if the Additional Judge is recommended by the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned and the Chief Justice of Pakistan, he is normally to be appointed as a permanent Judge in the absence of strong reasons to the contrary, which must be recorded by the appointing authority. It is in accord with the spirit of the Constitution that the period of his initial appointment as Additional Judge can only be extended on the recommendation of the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned or Chief Justice of Pakistan and not otherwise by the appointing authority. It is pointed out that legitimate expectancy of an Additional Judge, who had performed his functions to the satisfaction of the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned and Chief Justice of Pakistan for the period he was initially appointed, is only with regard to his being considered for permanent appointment".

284. Sajjad Ali Shah, CJ observed as follows:

"Under Article 197 of the Constitution there is a provision for appointment of Additional Judges and it appears that there is no requirement that they can be appointed only after the sanctioned strength of the Judges of the High Court is filled in with the permanent appointees. From this it appears that even against the vacancies within the sanctioned strength a person can be appointed as Additional Judge of the High Court for a period to be specified and then can be made permanent as communicated under Article 193. We are of the view that such Judges have legitimate expectancy to be entitled and considered for appointment upon expiry of their period of appointment as Additional Judges if and when they are so recommended for the purpose by the Chief Justice of the High Court and the Chief Justice of Pakistan. If such appointments are refused to be made then there should be strong reasons recorded in writing. Extension to be made or not is not the sole discretion of the Federal Government unless such request is made by the Chief Justice of the High Court and the CJP".

285. In AI-Jahed Trust case, the Supreme Court of Pakistan approved the views taken by Bhagwati, J, in SP Gupta's case on the point of legitimate expectancy. Ajmal Mian, J in consideration of the observations of Bhagwati, J observed as follows:

"However, in Pakistan, the above Article 197 is on different footing as it inter alia postulates the appointment of an Additional Judge against a permanent vacancy. It is also well established practice/convention that if an Additional Judge performs his functions during the period for which he was appointed to the satisfaction of the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned and the Chief Justice of Pakistan, he has always been appointed as a permanent Judge except in a rare case. In this view of the matter, a person who is appointed against a permanent vacancy as Additional Judge in a High Court or if a permanent vacancy occurs during his period as an Additional Judge, he acquires a reasonable expectancy to be considered as a permanent Judge and in case he is recommended by the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned and the Chief Justice of Pakistan, he is to be appointed as such in the absence of very strong reasons to be recorded by the President Executive which may be justifiable. Additionally, the Executive, instead of accepting the recommendations of the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned and the Chief Justice of Pakistan for permanent appointments without further consulting them, cannot extend the period instead of appointing them on permanent basis as recommended by the two Chief Justices."

286. Monzoor Hussain Sial, J observed as follows:

"Invariably, if Additional Judge of High Court performs his functions during the period for which he is appointed to the satisfaction of the High Court as also the Chief Justice of Pakistan, he is appointed as permanent Judge of the High Court. The Additional Judge, who is appointed against a permanent vacancy, or the vacancy having occurred during the period he was working as Additional Judge clearly acquires a reasonable expectancy to be considered for appointment as permanent Judge. In order to secure the independence of the Judiciary if the Additional Judge is recommended by the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned and the Chief Justice of Pakistan, he is normally to be appointed as a permanent Judge in the absence of strong reasons to the contrary, which must be recorded by the appointing authority. It is in accord with the spirit of the Constitution that the period of his initial appointment as Additional Judge can only be extended on the recommendation of the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned or the Chief Justice of Pakistan, and not otherwise by the appointing authority. It is pointed out that legitimate expectancy of an Additional Judge, who had performed his functions to the satisfaction of the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned and Chief Justice of Pakistan for the period he was initially appointed, is only with regard to his being considered for permanent appointment. "

287. On the point of legitimate expectation the unanimous view of the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the AI-Jahed Trust case is as follows:

"That Additional Judges appointed in the High Court against permanent vacancies or if permanent vacancies occur while they are acting as Additional Judges, acquire legitimate expectancy and they are entitled to be considered for permanent appointment upon the expiry of their period of appointment as Additional Judges and they are entitled to be appointed as such if they are recommended by the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned and the Chief Justice of Pakistan in the absence of strong valid reason/reasons to be recorded by the President-Executive."

288. Accordingly the Supreme Court of Pakistan directed that the cases of 5 Additional Judges (appellants No. 3-7) who were dropped to be processed and considered for their permanent appointment by the permanent Chief Justice within one month from the date of assumption of office by him as such. The Supreme Court of Pakistan found that the said 5 Additional Judges acquired legitimate expectancy and therefore, they were entitled to be considered for permanent appointment.

289. The views taken in SP Gupta's case have been approved in the Second Judges' case. The consistent views of the superior Courts of India are that whenever a person was appointed as a Judge in the High Court, he would be first appointed as an Additional Judge and only when a vacancy occurred in the post of a permanent Judge he would be confirmed as a permanent Judge in that vacancy in accordance with the seniority from amongst the Additional Judges. The practice, therefore, drew up of a person being first appointed as an Additional Judge and then being confirmed as permanent Judge in the same High Court. By and large every person enters into office as an Additional Judge in the clear expectation that as soon as a vacancy in the post of a permanent Judge becomes available to him in the High Court, he would be confirmed as a permanent Judge and if no such vacancy is available to him until expiration of his term of office he would be recommended as Additional Judge for a further term in the same High Court. The legitimate expectation has relevance on the ground of longer experience on the Bench and is a factor material for determining the suitability of the appointee.

290. These views are taken in the context of Indian Constitution where Additional Judges are being appointed for a particular period on the basis of work loads and to clear off backlog cases but the provisions of our Constitution and those of Pakistan are completely different because, the Additional Judges are not appointed for clearing off arrears of work they are appointed against permanent vacancies and after expiry of the period of two years or in case of further extension for the period which they were reappointed, they are considered for permanent appointment as Judges of the High Court. If the Additional Judges perform judicial works to the satisfaction of CJB, they are appointed as permanent Judges except in rare cases. In view of the above, a person who is appointed against a permanent vacancy as Additional Judge, he acquires a reasonable expectancy to be appointed as permanent Judge. The Additional Judges thus enter in the High Court Division with a legitimate expectation of their being appointed under Article 95(1) if the CJB recommends him for such appointment.

291. In the supplementary affidavit in Writ Petition No. 2975 of 2003, the petitioners stated that out of 8 Additional Judges appointed on 24th October 1999, two Additional Judges were not appointed, as Judges under Article 95, out of five Additional Judges appointed on 25th May, 2000 four of them were dropped, out of nine appointed on 22nd February 2001, six of them were dropped, out of nine Additional Judges appointed, five of them were dropped, totaling 15 were not appointed. It is further stated that the last government while drop- ping 15 Additional Judges, appointed 45 Additional Judges from 29th July 2002 to 23rd August 2003. This fact proved that when the petitioners were dropped there were permanent vacancies in the HCD and thus there was no reason for dropping them other than oblique consideration. The government in power did not consider their appointment in violation of the constitutional provisions.

292. In Union of India vs Hindustan Developent Corporation AIR 1994 SC 988 it was observed:

"For legal purposes, the expectation cannot be the same as anticipation. It is different from a wish, a desire or a hope nor can it amount to a claim or demand on the ground of a right. However earnest and sincere a wish, a desire or a hope may be and however confidently one may look to them to be fulfilled, they by themselves cannot amount to an assertable expectation and a mere disappointment does not attract a legal consequence. A pious hope even leading to a moral obligation cannot amount to a legitimate expectation. The legitimacy of an expectation can be inferred only if it is founded that on the sanction of law or custom or an established procedure followed in regular and natural sequence. Again, it is distinguishable from a genuine expectation. Such expectation should be justifiably legitimate and protectable. Every such legitimate expectation does not by. itself fructify into a right and therefore, it does not amount to a right in the conventional sense."

293. On consideration of some decisions of House of Lords, American and Australian, it was further observed in that case that legitimate expectation given the applicant sufficient locus standi for judicial review, and the legitimate expectation is to be confined mostly to right of a fair hearing before a decision which results in a negative promise. What I have inferred from the decisions considered therein, the legitimate expectation does not give scope to claim relief straightaway from the administrative authority as no crystallised right, as such, is involved. Where a person's legitimate expectation is not fulfilled by taking a particular decision then decision maker should justify the denial of such expectation by showing some overriding public interest. It simply ensures the circumstances in which that expectation may be denied or restricted. The doctrine would arise when a body by representation or by past practice aroused expectation which it would be within its powers to fulfil. However, if a person bases his claim on the doctrine, in the first instance, he must satisfy that there is a foundation and has locus standi to make such a claim.

294. A legitimate expectation of a person may not by itself be an enforceable right, but failure to consider and give due weight to it may render the decision of the public authority arbitrary. This legitimate expectation is a relevant factor requiring due consideration in a fair decision making process. Whenever the question of legitimate expectation arises it is to be determined in large public interest wherein other more important considerations made outweigh what would otherwise have been the legitimate expectation of the claimant. A bonafide decision of public functionary reached in this manner would satisfy the requirement of non arbitrariness and withstand judicial scrutiny. The public authorities possess the duty to act fairly and to adopt a procedure which is fair. The unfairness in the exercise of power may amount to an abuse of power and the decision would be exposed to challenge on the ground of arbitrariness.

295. I quote a passage of the Administrative Law, Eighth Edition by Davit Foulkes which reads as follows:

"(III) Legitimate expectations are enforced in order to achieve fairness. Thus where it was argued that a previous practice of giving an oral hearing gave rise to a legitimate expectation of a hearing, the House of Lords said that the question was whether the official in question (the district auditor) had acted unfairly, he had not. In the circumstances a decision on the papers was fair."

296. In Bangladesh Soya Protein Project Ltd. vs Secretary Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief 6 BLC 681, the writ petitioner took leasehold right to manufacture Soya Products developed by the Bangladesh Council of Scientific and Industrial Research for its commercial production. The writ petitioner thereupon started manufacturing products and supplying them to different schools required by the Ministry of Relief in connection with their school feeding programme for under-nourished children of the disaster areas. The writ petitioner also set up an industry on taking loan from the banks. Suddenly the government discontinued the programme consequent upon which, the writ petitioner's Industrial Units were closed. In the facts of the given case the High Court Division considered some decisions on the point of legitimate expectations and observed as follows:

"From the discussion of the above noted cases, I would conclude that the expression 'legitimate expectation' first used by Lord Denning MR in the case of Schmidt in 1969 opened a new vista and has by now been established as a principle of law. This principle, as I understand, in essence imposes a duty to act fairly and requires of the concerned authorities to act reasonably in dealing with the rights and interest of the people in the given circumstances. This is certainly expected of them. If there is any breach, the Courts should not be slow in holding so. If the situation so demands, the Court shall certainly strike down such orders in exercise of its powers of judicial review of executive actions. In the case of their unreasonableness or inertness or even laches on their part for which some benefit is lost causing prejudice to the people at large or even to an individual, the Court may also direct the concerned authorities to exercise their functions fairly, reasonably and in accordance with law."

297. In the Second Judges' case, with a view to get rid of that caused by the excessive dominance of the Executive in the matter appointment of Judges to the superior Judiciary as well as in the formation of its structural composition; to give primacy to the opinion of the Chief Justice of India in all matters thereof and to enjoy judicial independence and integrity of the Judiciary consistent with the letter and spirit of the Constitution, Verma J, observed as follows:

"Due consideration of every legitimate expectation in the decision making process is a requirement of the rule of non-arbitrariness and, therefore, this also is a norm to be observed by the Chief Justice of India in recommending appointments to the Supreme Court. Obviously, this factor applies only to those considered suitable and at least equally meritorious by the Chief Justice of India, for appointment to the Supreme Court. Just as a High Court Judge at the time of his initial appointment has the legitimate expectation to become Chief Justice of a High Court in his turn in the ordinary course, he has the legitimate expectation to be considered for appointment to the Supreme Court in his turn, according to his seniority."

"This legitimate expectation has relevance on the ground of longer experience on the Bench, and is a factor material for determining suitability of the appointee."

298. In Pakistan though each High Courts has sanctioned strength of Judges, the vacancies are filled in against permanent posts but in our country though it is stated in Article 98 that if the President is satisfied that the number of Judges of a Division should for the time being be increased the President may appoint Additional Judges of the said Division for two years-there is no law providing the sanctioned posts in the HCD. Therefore, the use of the expression "increased" is misnomer and/or superfluous. I am, therefore, of the view that whenever a person is appointed as Additional Judge of the SCB, the Additional Judge was appointed against permanent vacancy and that if he had performed functions as Additional Judge to the satisfaction of the cm and if the cm recommended him for appointment as Judge, he had acquired a legitimate expectation for appointment under Article 95(1) of the Constitution.

299. The writ petitioners claimed that when they were appointed they had the impression that at the end of the initial period if the cm had recommended for their confirmation as permanent Judges reflecting their assessment of satisfactory performance as Additional Judges, they would be appointed in the ordinary course. The Constitutional Jurisprudence on the subject of judicial appointments clearly indicate that if there is any reason why CJB's recommendations are not accepted then those reasons should be communicated to the CJB, and the matter should be resolved through further consultations giving due respect to the views of the CJB and the principle of independence of Judiciary. This expectation of the writ petitioners is fundamental and natural and there cannot be any departure from the established practice being followed over thirty years.

Privileged documents

300. The next point is immunity claimed by the Government in respect of the papers and correspondences exchanged between the CJB and the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs regarding the appointment of some of the petitioners and other Additional Judges.

301. In Writ Petition No. 2975 of 2003 the petitioners moved an application for a direction upon the respondent, Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs and the Registrar, Supreme Court of Bangladesh to produce the papers regarding the recommendation of the CJB relating to the appointment of Mr Abdul Hye, Mr Md Faruque Ahmed, Mr Md Marzi-ul-Hoque, Mr Md Shamsul Huda, Mr Md Abdur Razzaque, Mr Justice Syed Mahmud Hossain, Mr Justice Md Imman Ali and Mr Hasan Foez Siddique. Respondent did not file affidavit-in-opposition against the said application or claimed immunity in writing against the production of the relevant file. The learned Attorney-General opposed the prayer orally. The Special Division Court allowed the prayer and called for the relevant communications and files by order dated 27th May, 2003. The respondent moved the Appellate Division against that order and prayed for stay. It appeared from the certified copy of the order, the Chamber Judge of the Appellate Division made the following order:

"Prayer for staying further proceedings of Writ Petition Nos. J 543 of 2003, 2975 of 2003 and 3217 of 2003 till disposal of the leave petition. Stay as prayed for is granted till 16th July, 2003 on which date Leave Petition will come up for hearing before the Full Court."

302. The Appellate Division granted leave to the petition and accordingly, Civil Appeal No. 50 of 2004 was registered. The Appellate Division upon hearing allowed the appeal, set aside the order of the Special Division Court directing the respondent to produce the relevant papers containing the opinion of the cm about the appointment of 8 Judges. The Appellate Division while allowing the appeal gave some guidelines and directed the Special Division Court to dispose of the petitions in the light of the directions as under:

"The High Court Division shall hold a preliminary enquiry and determine the validity of the objections raised by the Attorney-General to the production of the papers containing opinion or recommendation of Chief Justice and to hold enquiry into questions as to whether the papers relate to an affair of the State under section 123 or not. The High Court Division may require appellants, who are respondents in the writ petition, to file affidavit-in-opposition pinpointing whether any such opinion or recommendation of the Chief Justice in writing is available and, if so, under what grounds the appellants are seeking for the privilege."

"The High Court Division is further directed to ascertain whether the papers in question are relevant on the basis of which the Prime Minister advised the President and to ascertain whether such advice was relevant for the appointment. The High Court Division is further directed to ascertain whether the papers are necessary for the proper adjudication of the issues involved in the writ petition."

The High Court Division is to ascertain whether it can hold an enquiry into the possible injury to public interest which may result from disclosure of the document in question of which privilege has been claimed and if it decides in the affirmative then to decide the question of possible injury to public interest which may result from the disclosure and lastly, the High Court Division is to decide what papers and relating to whom are to be called for and then to limit the enquiry as to the opinion of the Chief Justice only so far as it relates to the persons who are really seeking relief before the Court."

303. In pursuance of the above direction we directed the respondent to file affidavit-in- opposition but the respondent did not file any affidavit and also did not claim immunity of the papers called for earlier. In view of the direction of the Appellate Division, despite non filing of the affidavit, I would like to address the points. The hearing of the above petitions have been delayed for about 5 years on this point, for the Government moved the Appellate Division and initially secured an interim order of staying further proceedings of the writ petitions and thereafter, the order of this Court directing the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs to produce relevant papers was stayed. It is contended that despite endeavours made for expeditious disposal of the appeal, the appeal could not be heard expeditiously. Mr M Amirul Islam expresses concern in the manner the writ petitioners' right to have the matters heard have been delayed for five years for this reason. Mr Islam submits that the Appellate Division should not have stayed the further proceedings of writ petitions pending before the High Court Division.

304. The Appellate Division on consideration of the cases of SP Gupta (supra), State of Punjab vs SS Singh, AIR 1961 SC 493, RK Join vs Union of India, AIR 1993 SC 1793 and SR.Bammai vs Union of India, AIR 1994 SC 1918 was of the view that Bhagwati J, while speaking for the majority view in SP Gupta's case "did not follow the conclusion of the judgment delivered in the case of State of Punjab vs SS Singh but on a close reading of the case of RK Join vs Union of India and SR Bammai vs Union of India as mentioned earlier it is apparent that the judgment of AIR 1961 SC 493 will hold the field".

305. Sections 123 and 162 of the Evidence Act read as follows:

"Section 123 Evidence as to affairs of State-No one shall be permitted to give any evidence derived from unpublished official records relating to any affairs of State, except with the permission of the officer at the head of the department concerned, who shall give or withhold such permission as he thinks fit."

"Section 162-Production of documents- A witness summoned to produce a document shall, if it is in his possession or power, bring it to Court, notwithstanding any objection which there may be to its production or to its admissibility. The validity of any such objection shall be decided on by the Court. The Court, if it sees fit, may inspect the document, unless it refers to matters of State, or take other evidence to enable it to determine on its admissibility."

306. The respondent did not claim immunity of the papers in accordance with section 123 of the Evidence Act and also did not claim privilege against the production of the papers in Court in accordance with section 162 of the Evidence Act. The learned Attorney General simply opposes the application orally claiming that they are privileged documents and that they are protected under the proviso to Article 48(3) of the Constitution.

307. Whether immunity from disclosure is claimed under section 123 on the ground that disclosure of the contents of document would be injurious to the interest of the State or the Public service, the claim ought to have been made by an affidavit either by the Minister or Adviser in charge of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs or in their absence, by the Secretary of same Ministry as the head of the Ministry. If the Minister, Adviser or the Secretary asserts that the disclosure of the contents would or might do harm to the nation or the public service a grave injury, the Court will be slow to question his opinion or to allow its disclosure in the interest of the administration of justice. The protection under section 123 can be claimed if the document relates to "affairs of state" within the meaning of the section. Unless it can be shown that there exists some factor suggesting either lack of good faith or an error of judgment or an error of law on the part of the Minister/Adviser or the head of the department, even in such cases, as settled by Apex Court of India, that the Court is not bound by the statement made by the Minister/ Adviser or the head of the department in the affidavit (no such affidavit has been filed in these cases) and even if a claim is made on the ground of public interest for immunity from production of a document is not conclusive and the Court has the power to inspect the document before deciding whether they should be disclosed after balancing the competing interests of preventing harm to the State or public service by disclosure. Reference in this connection is the case of Burmah Oil Co Ltd. vs Bank of England (1979) 3 All ER. 700.

308. Let me now discuss the cases referred by the learned Deputy Attorney General in support of the immunity in the Appellate Division. In the case of SS Singh (supra), SS Singh, a District Judge, was removed by the President of India. His representation for re-instatement was considered by the Members of the Council and ordered for re- employment in some suitable post. SS Singh then filed a suit claiming his removal as illegal and for recovery of salary. The trial Court directed the government for production of the documents mentioned in the list under Order XI, rule 14, CPC. The matter ultimately went to the Supreme Court at the instance of the State of Punjab challenging the order for production of the documents. It has been observed that when an objection is made claiming immunity for production of document which relates to any affair of the State, the head of the department must file an affidavit showing that each document has been read carefully, that the person making the affidavit is satisfied that its disclosure would lead to public injury, and lastly, the reasons must be stated why the State is apprehensive to disclose the document.

309. In that case Gajendragadkar, J, speaking for the majority pointed out that the principle behind the exclusionary rule enacted in section 123 is that a document should not be allowed to be produced in Court if such production would cause injury to public interest in the disclosure and private interest in non-disclosure, the latter must yield to the former. His Lordship emphasised that though section 123 does not expressly refer to injury to public interest, but that principle is obviously implicit in it and indeed it is the sole foundation and proceeded to add that even though administration of justice is a matter of very high public importance, if there is a real conflict between 'public interest' and 'private interest' it may reluctantly have to be conceded that the interest of the individual will not prevail over the public interest. His Lordship has given precedence to public interest over private interest and then proceeded to consider when a document can be said to be relating to 'affairs of state' within the meaning of section 123.

310. According to his Lordship, the documents relating to the affairs of the State are broadly divisible into two classes, one, the disclosure of which will cause no injury to the public interest - they may be described as "innocuous documents" and the other, the disclosure of which may cause injury to public interest - they may be described as "noxious documents," it is the head of the department to decide which class of document in respect of which the claim for protection against disclosure is made belongs; if he comes to the conclusion that the document is innocuous, he will give permission for the production; if, however, he comes to the conclusion that the document is noxious, he will withhold such permission; in any case, the Court does not materially come into the picture. It is further observed that even if the documents are relating to the affairs of the State. which are noxious documents, it !s for the Court to determine the character of the documents and if, necessary, to enquire whether its disclosure would lead to injury to public interest. His Lordship then concluded as under:

"Thus there can be little doubt that where a privilege is claimed at the stage of inspection and the Court is required to adjudicate upon its validity, the relevant provisions of the Act under which the privilege is claimed as well as provisions of section 162 which deal with the manner in which the said privilege has to be considered are equally applicable; and if the Court is precluded from inspecting the privileged document under the second clause of section 162 the prohibition would apply as much to a privilege claimed by the State through its witness at the trial as a privilege similarly claimed by it at the stage of inspection. It is hardly necessary to point out that a contrary view would lead to this manifestly unreasonable result that at the stage of inspection the document can be inspected by the Court, but not at the subsequent stage of trial. In our opinion, the provisions of Order XI, rule 19, sub-rule (2) must, therefore, be read subject to section 162 of the Act."

311. This decision was reconsidered in SP Gupta's case. PN Bhagwati J, speaking for the majority view overruled the views taken in the case of SS Singh. The relevant portion is as follows:

"Thus our conclusion is that reading sections 123 and 162 together the Court cannot hold an enquiry into the possible injury to public interest which may result from the disclosure of the document in question. That is a matter for the authority concerned to decide; but the Court is competent, and indeed, is bound, to hold a preliminary enquiry and determine the validity of the objections to its production, and that necessarily involves an enquiry into the question as to whether the evidence relates to an affair of State under section 123 or not.

In this enquiry the Court has to determine the character or class of the document. If it comes to the conclusion that the document does not relate to affairs of State then it should reject the claim for privilege and direct its production. If it comes to the conclusion that the document relates to the affairs of State, it should leave it to the head of the department to decide whether he should permit its production or not."

It is further added:

"The learned Judge thus took the view in no uncertain terms that documents relating to affairs of State are documents belonging to the noxious class, that is, documents which by reason of their contents or the class to which they belong, are such that disclosure may cause injury to public interest. The learned Judge agreed that it is for the Court to determine whether a particular document in respect of which the claim for non-disclosure is made is a document relating to affairs of the State or, in other words, it is a document falling within the noxious class, but introduced a serious impediment in the way of the Court making such determination by holding that the Court cannot for this purpose inspect the document or hold "an enquiry into the possible injury to public interest which may result from the disclosure of the document." Now, if the Court has no power to inspect the document, it is difficult to understand how the Court can find without conducting an enquiry as regards the possible effect of the disclosure of the document upon public interest, that the document is one relating to affairs of State, as ex hypothesis a document can be said to relate to affairs of State only if its disclosure will cause injury to public interest. It might be that there are certain classes of documents which are of such a character that even without inspecting them or conducting an enquiry, it might be possible to say that by virtue of their character, their disclosure would be injurious to public interest and in case of such documents it would not be possible for the Court without inspecting them or at any rate without holding an enquiry, to determine whether their disclosure would be injurious to public interest and they should therefore be classified as documents relating to affairs of State. Even so, according to Gajendragadkar,J: and the other learned Judges, the Court can and must determine whether such documents relate to affairs of State without inspecting them and without even holding an enquiry into the possible injury to public interest which might result from their disclosure. The view taken by Gajendragadkar, J and the other learned Judges in Sodhi Sukhdev Singh's case (AIR 1961 SC 493) (supra) thus runs into an inconsistency and creates an illogical situation."

It is then, further added:

"There is also another infirmity from which the view taken in Sodhi Sukhdev Singh's case (supra) suffers, Gajendragadkar J, speaking on behalf of himself and the other learned Judges, observed that when an objection against the disclosure of a document is raised under section 123, the Court must first determine the character of the document and it comes to the conclusion that the document relates to affairs of State, it should leave it to the head of the department to decide whether he should permit its production or not. Now even according to GajendragadkarJ, and the other learned Judges, a document can be said to relate to affairs of State only if it is a document of such a character that its disclosure will injure public interest and therefore, the Court would have to reach the conclusion that the disclosure of the document will be injurious to public interest before it can find that the document relates to affairs of State. If that be so, it is difficult to understand, after the Court has enquired into the objection and came to the conclusion that disclosure of the document would be injurious to public interest, what purpose would be served by reserving to the head of the department the power to permit its disclosure, because the question to be decided by him would practically be the same, namely, whether disclosure of the document would be injurious to public interest-a question already decided by the Court. In other words, if injury to public interest is the foundation of the immunity from disclosure, when once the Court has inquired into the question and found that the disclosure of the document will injure public interest and therefore, it is a document relating to affairs of State, it would in most cases be a futile exercise for the head of the department to consider and decide whether its disclosure should be permitted as he would be making an enquiry into the identical question."

312. It has further been observed that there may be a few rare cases where in regard to a document which by reason of the class to which it belongs may be regarded as relating to affairs of State, the head of the department may be able to take the view that though it belongs to the noxious class, its disclosure would not be injurious to public interest and therefore, allow it to be disclosed. But, by and large, once the Court has found that the document is of such a character that its disclosure will cause injury to public interest, it would be futile to leave it to the head of the department to decide whether he should permit its production or not.

313. The Court would allow the objection if it finds that the document relates to affairs of State and its disclosure would be injurious to public interest, but, on the other hand, if it reaches the conclusion that the document does not relate to affairs of State or that the public interest does not compel its non- disclosure or that the public interest in the administration of justice in the particular case before it overrides all other aspects of public interest, it will overrule the objection and order disclosure of the document. The basic question, it is observed, to which the Court would therefore, have to address itself for the purpose of deciding the validity of the objection would be, whether the document relates to affairs of State, or in other words, it is of such a character that its disclosure would be against the interest of the State or the public service and if so, whether the public interest in its non-disclosure is so strong that it must prevail over the private interest in the administration of justice and on that account, it should not be allowed to be disclosed. The final decision in regard to the validity of an objection against disclosure raised under section 123 would always be with the Court by reason of section 162.

314. The papers or documents that are directed to produce in Court are not such documents even though they are affairs of the State-they are not related to affairs of the State involving security of the country or foreign affairs where public interest requires that if they are disclosed, the security of the country or the relationship with a foreign country will be affected or the minutes of the cabinet over policy matter. It should also be borne in mind that it is a well recognised principle that a fair administration of justice is itself a matter of public interest. The Court, therefore, should give precedence to the public interest which would not impair the administration of justice by non-disclosure. Therefore, I have no hesitation in accepting the views taken by PN Bhagwati, J.

315. In SR Bommais case the facts are as follows: on 5th March 1985 the Karnataka Legislative Assembly election was held in which Janata Dal won 139 seats, the Congress was the next largest party securing 66 seats. RK Hedge was elected as leader of Janata Dal and became Chief Minister. Due to his resignation SR Bommai became the Chief Minister. There was dissatisfaction to some aspirants in the ministerial berth. One Kalyan Malakery with some followers defected from Janata Dal and he wrote to the Governor enclosing letters of 19 other members expressing want of confidence in Bommai. On 19 April 1989 the Governor sent a report to the President. On the following day, 7 members out of those 19 that supported Malakery wrote to the Governor that their signatures were obtained by misrepresentation and they supported Bommai. On the same day the cabinet decided to convene the Assembly session on 27th April 1989 for obtaining vote of confidence and Bommai met the Governor on the same day and requested him to allow floor test to prove the majority. Under such pretext, the Governor sent a second report to the President and pursuant thereto, the President issued proclamation dismissing the Bommai government. The point involved in the case was about interpretation of Article 74(2) of the Constitution of India which is equivalent to proviso to Article 54(3) of our Constitution, and Article 356(1) of the Constitution of India. Since the proclamation under Article 356(1) was issued by the President on the advice of the cabinet given under Article 74(2) and since sub-clause (2) bars enquiry into the question whether any, and if so, what advice was tendered by the cabinet to the President, judicial review of the reasons which led to the issuance of the proclamation also stands barred.

316. The majority views in the said case have been expressed by Sawant J and are as follows:

"What is further, although Article 74(2) bars judicial review so far as the advice given by the Ministers is concerned, it does not bar scrutiny of the material on the basis of which the advice is given. The Courts are not interested in either the advice given by the Ministers to the President or the reasons for such advice. The Courts are, however, justified in probing as to whether there was any material on the basis of which the advice was given, and whether it was relevant for such advice and the President could have acted on it. Hence when the Courts undertake an enquiry into the existence of such material, the prohibition contained in Article 74(2) does not negate their right to know about the factual existence of any such material. This is not to say that the union government cannot raise the plea of privilege under section 123 of the Evidence Act. As and when such privilege against disclosure is claimed, the Courts will examine such claim within the parameters of the said section on its merits. In this connection, we may quote Justice Matthew, who in the case of State of UP vs Raj Narain, (1975) 3 SCR 333 at 360: (AIR 1975 SC 865 at p.884) observed as follows:

"To justify a privilege, secrecy must be indispensable to induce freedom of official communication or efficiency in the transaction of official business and it must be further a secrecy which has remained or would have remained inviolable but for the compulsory disclosure. In how many transactions of official business is there ordinarily such secrecy? If there arises at any time a genuine instance of such otherwise inviolate secrecy, let the necessity of maintaining it be determined on its merits."

317. In the reported case, Ahmadi, J while agreeing with the minority view expressed by K.Ramaswamy, J, added few paragraphs in support of the minority view. In that case, SP Gupta's case was not at all considered although section 123 of the Evidence Act came up for consideration under different pretext and the said decision is still viewed as the authority on the question of privileged documents under section 123 read with section 162 of the Evidence Act.

318. At this juncture, let us examine whether the claim of immunity has any substance in view of the proviso to sub-clause (3) of Article 48 and Article 55.

319. Articles 48 and 55 of the Constitution are relevant to address the point, relevant provisions are as follows:

"Article 48(1) There shall be a President of Bangladesh who shall be elected by Members of Parliament in accordance with law.

(2) The President shall, as Head of State, take precedence over all other persons in the State, and shall exercise the powers and perform the duties conferred and imposed on him by this Constitution and by any other law.

(3) In the exercise of all his functions, save only that of appointing the Prime Minister pursuant to clause (3) of Article 56 and the Chief Justice pursuant to clause (1) of Article 95, the President shall act in accordance with the advice of the Prime Minister;

Provided that the question whether any, and if so what, advice has been tendered by the Prime Minister to the President shall not be enquired into in any Court.

(5) The Prime Minister shall keep the President informed on matters of domestic and foreign policy, and submit for the consideration of the Cabinet any matter which the President may request him to refer to it."

Article 55(1) reads as follows:

"55(1) There shall be a Cabinet for Bangladesh having the Prime Minister at its head and comprising also such other Ministers as the Prime Minister may from time to time designate.

(2) The executive power of the Republic shall, in accordance with this Constitution, be exercised by or on the authority of the Prime Minister.

(3) The Cabinet shall be collectively responsible to Parliament.

(4) All executive actions of the Government shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President.

320. Under the Parliamentary System of Government, there is no doubt that the decision of the President under Article 95 to appoint a Judge as Judge of the SCB is really a decision of the Prime Minister as per Article 55 of the Constitution and the reasons which have weighed the decision would necessarily be part of the advice tendered by the Prime Minister to the President. In view of the proviso to clause (3) of Article 48, the advice given by the Prime Minister to the President is protected from judicial inquiry but as a convention, the CJB has expressed views regarding the appointment of a person as Judge in consultative form, which formed part of the advice by the Prime Minister. The views expressed by the CJB precede the formation of advice and this advice is protected. It is held in State of Punjab vs Union of India AIR 1977 SC 1361 that the reasons which have weighed with the cabinet in giving the advice would certainly form part of the advice. But the material on which the reasoning of the Prime Minister is based and the advice is given cannot be said to form part of the advice. In this connection, in SP Gupta's case an illustration was given in the following manner. A judgment given by a Court is based upon the evidence led by the parties in the trial Court and in the judgment the evidence are referred and discussed. But the evidence do not form part of the judgment, for the judgment consists of the reasons in support of it and the decision thereon and the evidence on which the reasoning and the decision are based would not be part of the judgment.

321. The material on which the advice given by the Prime Minister is based cannot be said to be part of the advice. Before the advice was given, there were correspondences between the CJB and the Law Minister which may not be constituted the material in forming the basis of the advice of the Prime Minister they are not protected against judicial scrutiny as they are not protected under the proviso to clause (3) of Article 48.

322. The government may in a given case choose to disclose advice of the Prime Minister or it may be possible to gather them from the other circumstances in which event the Courts would be entitled to examine whether they bear any reasonable nexus with the question of appointment of a Judge or they are constitutionally or illegally prohibited. Article 95 requires that there must be full and effective consultation between the President on one hand and the CJB on other hand. The reasons which have persuaded the Prime Minister to take decision on the basis of correspondences exchanged between the Law Minister and the CJB would throw light on the question as to what are the reasons which have prompted the President to take decision regarding the appointment or non-appointment of a Judge after performing successfully as an Additional Judge. These correspondences will also reveal whether full and detailed facts and meaningful consultation on which the decision of the President is based are placed before the CJB before they gave their opinion in the course of consultative purpose. The President exercises power of appointing Judges is so integrally connected with the constitutional requirement of effective consultation with the CJB, which cannot be delinked from views expressed by CJB on consultation and it would not be possible for the President to exercise power in accordance with the Constitution without the opinion of the CJB placed before him.

323. Bhagwati J, in SP Gupta's case observed as follows:

"There can be no doubt that the advice tendered by the Council of Ministers to the President is protected against judicial scrutiny by reason of Article 74(2). But can it be said that the views expressed by the Chief Justice of the High Court and the Chief Justice of India on consultation form part of the advice. The advice is given by the Council of Ministers after consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court and the Chief Justice of India. The two Chief Justices are consulted on "full and identical facts" and their views are obtained and it is after considering those views that the Council of Ministers arrives at its decision and tenders its advice to the President. The views expressed by the two Chief Justices precede the formation of the advice and merely because they are referred to in the advice which is ultimately tendered by the Council of Ministers, they do not necessarily become part of the advice. What is protected against disclosure under Article 74(2) is only the advice tendered by the Council of Ministers. The reasons which have weighed with the Council of Ministers in giving the advice would certainly form part of the advice."

His Lordship added:

"That takes us to the next question whether the correspondence exchanged between the Law Minister, the Chief Justice of the Delhi and the Chief Justice of India is protected from disclosure under any other provision of law. We do not have in India any common law protection under the label of "Crown Privilege" as it was known a decade ago and now called "Public interest immunity" as there is in England and the only provision of law under which such immunity can be claimed is section 123 of the Indian Evidence Act and therefore, it is this provision which we must now turn to consider. But, before we do so, we would like to indicate the socio-political background in the context of which this section has to be interpreted. It is true that this section was enacted in the second half of the last century but its meaning and content cannot remain static. The interpretation of every statutory provision must keep pace with changing concepts and values and it must, to the extent to which its language permits or rather does not prohibit, suffer adjustments through judicial interpretation so as to accord with the requirements of the fast changing society which is undergoing rapid social and economic transformation,

His Lordship further added:

"Now, if secrecy were to be observed in the functioning of government and the processes of government were to be kept hidden from public scrutiny, it would tend to promote and encourage oppression, corruption and misuse or abuse of authority, for it would all be shrouded in the veil of secrecy without any public, there would be greater exposure of the functioning of government and it would help to assure the people of a better and more efficient administration. There can be little doubt that exposure to public gaze and scrutiny is one of the surest means of achieving a clean and healthy administration. It has been truly said that an open government is clean government and a powerful safeguard against political and administrative aberration and inefficiency."

324. In Conway vs Rimmer, 1968 A C 910 Lord Reid observed as follows:

"To my mind the most important reason is that such disclosure would create or fan ill- informed or capricious public or political criticism. The business of government is difficult enough as it is, and no government could contemplate with equanimity the inner working of the government machine being exposed to the gaze of those ready to criticise without adequate knowledge of the background and perhaps, with some axe to grind." .

325. The objection against disclosure of a document on the ground that it relates to affairs of State may be made before the Court either because it would be against the interest of the State or the public service to disclose its content or because it belongs to a class of document which in the public interest ought not to be disclosed, whether or not it will be harmful to disclose the contents of the particular document. Where immunity from disclosure is claimed on the ground that the disclosure of the contents of the documents would be injurious to the interest of the State or the public service, it would not be difficult to decide the claim because it would almost invariably be supported by affidavits made by the Minister/Adviser or by head of the department i.e. the Secretary. If they asserted that to dis- close the contents of the document what or might do to the nation or the public service a grave injury, the Court will be slow to question his opinion unless it can be shown some factor suggesting lack of good faith.

326. The object of granting immunity to documents is to ensure the proper working of the government and not to protect the cabinet or its Minister's or government servant from criticism, however intemperate and unfairly based. If the processes of the government are kept hidden from public scrutiny it would tend to promote corruption and misuse of power, and if there is greater exposure of the functioning of the government it would help to assure the people a better and efficient administration. The reason can have little validity in a democratic society, particularly in the present context of democratic system of government which believes in transparency in every sphere of activities. It is only through exposure of its functioning that a democratic government can hope to win the trust of the people, if full information is made available to the people and every action of the government is bonafide and actuated only by public interest. When ever an objection to the disclosure is raised two questions followed to the determination of the Court namely, whether the document relates to affairs of the State and whether its disclosures would in a particular case before the Court be injurious to the public interest.

327. In this connection I would like to profitably refer the observations of Lord Reid in the case of Conway:

"It is universally recognised that there are two kinds of public which may clash. There is the public interest that harm shall not be done to the nation or the public service by disclosure of certain documents, and there is the public interest that the administration of justice shall not be frustrated by the withholding of documents which must be produced if justice is to be done. There are many cases where the nature of the injury which would or might be done to the nation or the public service is of so grave a character that no other interest public or private can be allowed to prevail over it. With regard to such cases it would be proper to say, as Lord Simon did, that to order production of the document in question, would put the interest of the State in jeopardy. But there are many other cases where the possible injury to the public service is much less and there one would think that it would be proper to balance the public interests involved."

328. The next question is the manner upon which such privilege can be claimed. In case of claiming immunity from disclosure under section 123 if an affidavit is not filed or affidavit filed is defective, Justice PN Bhagwati observed the Court may give opportunity to the State to file a proper affidavit, for the immunity against disclosure claimed is not a privilege which can be waived by the State; it is an immunity which is granted in order of public interest and therefore, even if the State has not filed an affidavit or the affidavit filed is not satisfactory, the Court cannot abdicate its duty of deciding whether the disclosure of the document in question would be injurious to public interest and the document should not therefore, be allowed to be disclosed.

329. In SP Gupta's case, it was again observed:

"The public interest in non-disclosure of a document belonging to this class may in an appropriate case yield to the public interest that in the administration of justice, the Court should have the fullest possible access to every relevant document would be liable to be disclosed even though it belongs to the protected class. The Executive cannot by merely invoking the scriptural formula of class immunity defeat the cause of justice by withholding a document which is essential to do justice between the parties, for otherwise the doctrine of class immunity would become a frightful weapon in the hands of the executive for burying its mistakes, covering up its inefficiencies and sometimes even hiding its corruption. Every claim for immunity in respect of a document, whatever be the ground on which the immunity is claimed and whatever be the nature of the document, must stand scrutiny of the Court with reference to one and only one test, namely, what does public interest require: disclosure or non-disclosure."

330. Before we take up the matter for hearing, we have drawn the attention of the learned Additional Attorney-General and the learned Assistant Attorney-General whether or not the respondent-government will be able to file affidavit- in-opposition or that it will claim immunity by making a formal application. Learned Additional Attorney-General and the learned Assistant Attorney-General refrained from making any comments despite their attention was drawn about non-filing of application claiming immunity by the government. The matter was adjourned on two occasions for the said purpose but no such application has been filed. In the context of the matter, I failed to see how the government could claim immunity from production of the papers sought by the petitioners?

331. There is no dispute that the correspondences exchanged between the CJB and the Government cannot at all be said to be injurious to public interest. In SP Gupta's case Bhagwati, J observed that the harm that would be caused to the public interest, injustice by non disclosure of the documents would in the circumstances far outweigh the injury which may possibly be caused by their disclosure, because the non-disclosure would almost inevitably result in the dismissal of the writ petitions and consequent denial of justice even though the claim of the writ petitioners may be true and just. The charge against the government was that there was recommendation by the CJB before the decision was reached by the President in regard to the non- appointment of the petitioners and in any event, the decision of the government was actuated by the oblique or improper consideration. This was a serious charge against the government and there can be no doubt that it would be very much in public interest that the necessary documents throwing light on the truth or otherwise of this charge should be disclosed, so that the full facts may be known to the public and the doubts raised and entertained about the influence of extraneous factors in case of the petitioners should be resolved and removed. It is significant to note that had there been non- disclosure of these documents, a certain doubt or misgiving would have continued to prevail in the mind that the decision of non-appointment of the petitioners as Judges was taken by the Government ignoring the recommendations of the CJB and that this decision was motivated by oblique or irrelevant consideration.

332. The petitioners' positive statement is that the CJB recommended for their appointment as Judges under Article 95 (1). The then Law Minister also impliedly admitted the claim of the petitioners. This Court is not bound by the oral submission of the law officer of the government because the respondent would be concerned primarily with the assertion of the public interest which would be injured by the disclosure of the documents and he would have very little concern with the public interest in the fair administration of justice. The respondent would not be in a position to appreciate and assess the relative importance of the two competing public importance, so as to be able to Judge as to which in the particular case before the Court should be allowed to present. The government withheld the papers which raised doubt that those were withheld by oblique consideration. These papers are extremely material for deciding whether there was full and effective consultation with the CJB before the decision for non appointment of the writ petitioners were made. Law requires that even if a document is confidential, it must be produced, notwithstanding its confidentiality, it is necessary for fair disposal of the issues involved in the petitions.

333. The government is duty bound to furnish all information to the Court as per Article 112 of the Constitution which provides that all Authorities, Executive and Judicial in the Republic, shall act in aid of the Supreme Court. If the Court desires a document for the, administration of justice the Executive is bound to produce it, except those that fall within the exclusionary rule enacted in the proviso to clause (3) of Article 48. As observed above, State's secret documents and minutes of the proceedings of the cabinet or diplomatic correspondences between the state and another friendly country, national security, public peace, security and good neighbourly, documents relating to commercial activities undertaken by the state in pursuit of public policies of social welfare, etc; the disclosure of which would materially affect the freedom but the documents which the petitioners called for did not fall in any of such category.

334. This Court with an anxiety to secure administration of justice required the papers relating to the recommendation or otherwise of the CJB regarding the appointment of the writ petitioners. As per constitutional mandate the Executive is bound to act in the aid of this Court so that the administration of justice is not hampered. According to the views taken above, in the public interest the nondisclosure of the documents would seriously handicap the writ petitioners in showing that there was full and effective consultation with the cm and that the cm recommended for their appointment. In view of the above, I am of the view that injury which is alleged to have been caused to the public interest in the disclosure and nondisclosure of the papers and documents and the correspondences between the CJB and the Law Minister relating to the appointment of the writ petitioners far outweigh the injury which may, if at all, be caused to the public interest of their disclosure and hence those documents are liable to be disclosed in the interest of administration of justice. Since the government did not file affidavit-in-opposition, we presumed that there was proper recommendation of the CJB relating to the petitioners' appointment and therefore, we refrained from calling for the papers for avoiding the delay in the disposal of the matters.

Lack of bonafide

335. It is stated that on 21st February, 2003, then President of the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) late Mr Md Ozair Farook, Mr Abdul Matin Khasru, ex-Law Minister, Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud, Mr Mahbubey Alam, Senior Advocates met the CJB and discussed about the issue of non-appointment of the petitioners. In course of discussion the CJB disclosed that he had recommended for appointment of all the Additional Judges as Judges of the SCB. Mr Md Shamsul Huda and Mr Md Faruque Ahmed met the CJB on 21st February, 2003, and on that occasion also the CJB told them that he had recommended all the Additional Judges for appointment as Judges' of the SCB. The CJB also disclosed that before such recommendation, he had discussed about the matter with other learned Judges' of the Appellate Division. In the issue of the daily Jugantor (Annexure-A) dated 23rd February, 2003 a news under caption “ ছয়জন বিচারপতি নিয়োগ স্থায়ী করার প্রতিবাদ-সুপ্রীম কোর্টের আইনজীবিদের আদালত বর্জন। was published"

In the said issue of the newspaper, a statement of the then Law Minister Mr Moudud Ahmed was published which reads as follows:

“ সংবিধান অনুযায়ী বিচারপতি নিয়োগের প্রধানবিচারপতির সুপারিশের যে বিধান ছিল আওয়ামীলীগ তা ১৯৭৪ সালে সংবিধান সংশোধন করে বাতিল করে দিয়েছে। এক্ষেত্রে প্রধান বিচারপতির যে কোন পরামর্শ বা সুপারিশ অত্যন্ত গুরুত্বের সংগে বিবেচনা করা হয়। তবে নিয়োগের সাংবিধানিক দায়িত্ব রাষ্ট্রপতি।”

The Law Minister had tacitly admitted that despite recommendation by the cm, the President did not appoint the petitioners as he was not bound to follow the recommendation. The daily Janakanta in its issue on 23rd February, 2003 published news as under:

“ আইনজীবিদের অল্টিমেটাম ছয় অতিরিক্ত বিচারপতিকে স্থায়ী করার দাবী তাদের বিক্ষোভ মিছিলে প্রকম্পিত হয় সুপ্রীমকোর্ট প্রাংগন এছাড়া তারা বিচার বিভাগের নগ্ন হস্তক্ষেপের প্রতিবাদে বিক্ষোভ মিছিল বাহির করে।”

The issues of daily Bhorer Kagaj and Prothom Alo also published news expressing concern about non-appointment of Judges breaking constitutional convention for political reasons. They stated that their non-appointment is manifest disregard of the recommendation of the CJB, a palpable arbitrariness as to the process of appointment of Judges.

336. Petitioners by supplementary affidavit in Writ Petition No. 2975 of 2003 gave the particulars of the Judges appointed between 1972 and 1998 and stated that from 1978 to April 1998, 101 persons were appointed as Additional Judges, of them, 7 were dropped. The percentage of dropping was only 7%. Whereas the past government dropped above 50% of the Additional Judges appointed by the earlier government and appointed 45 Additional Judges during their tenure of five years. They also claimed that the Executive had appointed some of their batchmates although the CJB recommended all of them for appointment. These facts sufficiently indicate the malafide motive of the last government in the matter of appointment and non appointment of the Judges. This non-appointment of the petitioners is also discriminatory and is violative of Article 29 of the Constitution, inasmuch as the petitioners and those appointed under Article 95(1) of the Constitution stand on the same footing. The Government giving no reason and without referring the matters back to the CJB did not appoint them, this act amounts to an arbitrary exercise of power, the breach of a constitutional duty, and an assault upon the independence of the judiciary. This non- appointment and appointments were made by breaking the constitutional obligations, norms and conventions. It is stated that the petitioners were appointed as Additional Judges against permanent vacancies but the government without appointing them appointed the persons of their choice. This conduct of the past government proved that the non- appointments were not made with malafide motive.

337. They have stated that the Executive by exercising malafide constitutional power arbitrarily and discriminately refrained from appointing the petitioners as Judges of the SCB and it was done with a view to implement their ill political motive of controlling the higher Judiciary and politicisation of the institution. This political motivation, it is stated, is evidenced from the statement of Mr Justice Md Ruhul Amin, then CJB, made in the Noakhali Bar Association on 30th April, 2007, which statement was published in the issue of daily Jugantor on 30th April, 2007 under caption “ বিচারক নিয়োগ ভুলের কারনে প্রলয় ঘটেছে, নোয়াখালী আইনজীবি সমিতির অনুষ্ঠানে প্রধান বিচারপতি মোঃ রুহুল আমিন।”

338. No affidavit-in-opposition has been filed by the Government traversing those statements despite giving time to file in the matters. In course of hearing, we adjourned the matters twice for enabling the government to file affidavits but the respondent opted not to file affidavit-in-opposition. In view of the above, Dr. Kamal Hossain contends that if an averment is not traversed by the respondent by affidavit it must be taken to have been admitted and thus, disregarding the recommendation of CJB constitutes a violation of the constitutional requirement and the appointment of the writ petitioners should have been effected in compliance with such recommendations. I fully agree with the contention of Dr. Hossain. Rule 11, part I of the High Court Original Side Rules governing the procedure for writs under Article 102 of the Constitution which provides that all questions arising for determination of writ petitions shall be decided ordinarily upon affidavits.

339. An affidavit is a declaration sworn or affirmed before a person competent to administer an oath. The only basis on which the affidavit of a living person, not called into witness box, can be acted upon as admissible evidence is that it should be capable of being regarded as a statement in writing complying with the condition prescribed in section 32 of the Evidence Act. The provisions of the Evidence Act are not applicable to the affidavits, yet it is open to a Court on sufficient grounds to permit a fact to be proved by affidavit; the affidavit filed along with the application can be used as evidence of facts alleged therein and it cannot be rejected merely because there has been a verbal denial of allegations by the respondent without any attempt to controvert them by affidavit-in- opposition or without asking for the attendance of the deponent for the cross-examination. Affidavits can be relied upon by the Courts in proof of particular facts under certain circumstances only. It is a practice of Courts in writ matters to require an affidavit in proof of an assertion. Normally, an affidavit-in-opposition by a party controverts the allegations in the affidavit produced by his adversary is a sufficient indication of his intention that he is not prepared to admit the facts set out in the affidavit. In writ proceedings the affidavits, counter-affidavits filed by the parties constitute not merely their pleadings but also partake of the character of evidence in the case and it is from that angle that the statements of facts alleging malafide and corrupt motives of the Executive have to be examined.

340. The learned Assistant Attorney-General does not oppose the appointment of the petitioners but he has opposed the petitioners' appointment from the date they acquired their right to be appointed. The learned Assistant Attorney-General, by citing the example of Mr Justice Khandaker Musa Khaled, submits that Justice Khandaker Musa Khaled did not get seniority although he was senior to some of his batchmates as he subscribed oath as Judge after a few months of taking oaths by his batchmates. All the learned Counsel, on the other hand, contend that the petitioners' case is quite distinguishable from the case of Justice Khandaker Musa Khaled. It is argued that the petitioners have challenged the malafide acts of non-appointment by the Executive despite recommendation of the CJB as unconstitutional. According to the learned Counsel, the then government with a malafide motive did not appoint the petitioners although they had acquired right to be appointed under Article 95(1) of the Constitution and their claim was established from the fact that after the change of the government, the present government did not opt to contest the matters which manifestly proved that the past government arbitrarily did not appoint the petitioners. There are sufficient materials on record for arriving at the conclusion that the CJB had recommended the petitioners for appointment as Judges against permanent vacancies but the then government did not appoint them without intimating anything to the CJB and appointed Judges of their own choice.

341. The petitioners stated that they were humiliated in the eye of the general public who could have thought that they were dropped because of incompetence or other disqualifications but, as a matter of fact, they performed their responsibilities to the satisfaction of the Bar, the CJB and the Executive but most illegally and arbitrarily the Executive refrained from appointing them although they were competent to be appointed. It is further stated that in India 547 Additional Judges were appointed during the period between 1st January 1983 and 10th April 1993 in different High Courts and only 7 persons were dropped but in our country the ratio of dropping Additional Judges during the tenure of the past government is more than 50%. From the above facts, it is claimed that the Executive government acted malafide, arbitrary and unfairly in dealing with the cases of the petitioners.

342. These facts suggested that in the appointment and non-appointment of Judges some sort of politicisation and corrupt motives worked and the last government dropped more than half of the Additional Judges appointed by the past government. Petitioners stated that the new appointments were made in order to support ill political motive with a view to include their own men as Judges in the SCB and accordingly, they did not appoint the petitioners and others and that "such action of the executive was, in fact, a fraud on the Constitution and the Executive exercised its statutory power most arbitrarily and discriminatorily to curtail judicial independence and to control the Higher Judiciary."

343. Mr Hossain submits that failure to implement the recommendation of the CJB and appointment of new Additional Judges by phases is breach of constitutional law, adversely impacts on the independence of the Judiciary, is discriminatory, arbitrary and malafide. Mr Hossain argues, the Executive according to its sweet will appointed Judges whom they liked and did not appoint the petitioners as they did not show allegiance to their ideology -this exercise of power is malicious. Mr Hossain has referred the case of Express Newspaper Pvt. Ltd. vs Union of India, AIR 1986 SC 872. It was observed in that case as under:

"Fraud on power voids the order if it is not exercised bona fide for the end design. There is a distinction between exercise of power in good faith and misuse in bad faith. The former arises when an authority misuses its power in breach of law, say, by taking into account bona fide, and with best of intentions, some extraneous matters or by ignoring relevant matters. That would render the impugned act or order ultra vires. It would be a case of fraud on powers. The misuse in bad faith arises when the power is exercised for an improper motive, say to satisfy a private or personal grudge or for wreaking vengeance of a Minister as in S. Partap Singh vs State of Punjab, (1964) 4 SCSR 733: (AIR. 1964 SC 773). A power is exercised maliciously if its repository is motivated by personal animosity towards those who are directly affected by its exercise. Use of a power for an alien purpose other than the one for which the power is conferred is malafide use of the power. Same is the position when an order is made for a purpose other than that which finds place in the order."

344. Mr Hossain has also referred a passage of Warrington, CJ, in Short vs Poole Corporation, (1926)1 Ch 66 that:

"No public body can be regarded as having statutory authority to act in bad faith or from corrupt motives, and any action purporting to be of that body, but proved to be committed in bad faith or from corrupt motives, would certainly be held to be inoperative."

<u>345. Admittedly, during the tenure of the last government 45 Additional Judges were appointed while the petitioners along with five other Additional Judges were not appointed despite recommendation of the CJB. Ten Additional Judges of this Court stated on oath that in the matter of appointment and non appointment of Judges in the highest Court of the country were made with malafide motive of appointing persons of their own choice. Having regard to the high status and dignity of a Judge, it is fair that when the government is discontinuing the right of such Judges in the HCD, they should be told the reasons which have weighed with the government in discontinuing them. It has to be borne in mind that the nature of allegations were never even anticipated before and there are several glaring instances of corrupt motives in the matter of appointing Judges in the higher Judiciary by men in authority and position. These are phenomenon of which this Court is bound to take judicial notice. Therefore, the allegations of malafide and corrupt motives in the non-appointment of the petitioners have been established in the absence of denial of facts.</u>

346. The government exceeded all norms in the matter of non-appointment of the petitioners as well as in the matter of new appointments.
