full_judgment:
These Rules call in question the legality and propriety of the judgment and order dated 18-2-2003 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Second Court, Noakhali, allowing Miscellaneous Appeal No.60 of 2001 and dismissing Miscellaneous Appeal No.51 of 2001, heard analogously with Miscellaneous Appeal No.58 of 2001 by setting aside those of the dated 15-5-2001 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Begumganj, Noakhali, allowing pre-emption in Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1999. These Rules having arisen out of a common judgment, have been heard together and are being disposed of by this judgment.

2. Short facts leading to these Rules are that on 1-4-1999 opposite party Nos. 5-6 as preemptors claiming as holding lands contiguous to the land transferred instituted Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1999 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (briefly as Act) in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Begumgonj, Noakhali, impleading the co-sharers tenants including the petitioner for pre-emption of 0.36 acre of land out of 0.72 acre described in the schedule of the application for pre-emption, transferred by Syed Noor Nabi as vendor in favour of opposite party Nos. 1-4 as pre-emptees by a registered kabala dated 26-10-1997 at a consideration of Taka one lac. Subsequently the opposite party No.23 of the application for pre-emption, claiming as co-sharer by inheritance in the holding, was transposed as co-preemptor.

3. The pre-emptor's case, put in a nutshell, is that opposite party No.5 Syed Noor Nabi having owned and possessed the land under pre-emption (briefly as land) transferred the land to pre-emptees by registered kabala deed dated 26-10-1997 and the same was entered into the book on 3-12-1998, no notice was served upon them and the pre-emptees are the strangers of the land under pre-emption. The pre-emptors are the co-sharer tenants, holding lands contiguous to the land transferred who came to know about such transfer in the last part of Falgoon, 1405 BS. Thereafter they instituted Miscellaneous case by depositing the consideration money for Taka one lac along with statutory compensation at the rate of Taka 10% thereupon for pre-emption of the land transferred. The opposite party No.23 (herein petitioner) was transposed as co-pre-emptor claiming as a co-sharer by inheritance in the holding.

4. The pre-emptees contested the case by filing joint written objection denying all the material allegations made in the application for pre-emption contending, inter alia, that the land was transferred within the knowledge of the pre-emptors by a registered kabala deed dated 26-10-1997. Before transfer the vendor approached to all co-sharer tenants and the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred to purchase but all of them had expressed their inability to purchase the land. The pre-emptees purchased the land for the purpose of ,construction a dwelling house therein. After purchase an improvement work has been made on the land at a cost of Taka 1,25,000. Hence the preemptors are not entitled to pre-empt the land transferred.

5. On the pleadings different issues were settled including the issue of maintainability, and the pre-emptors are entitled to get an order of preemption.

6. In course of trial the original pre-emptors examined four witnesses, co-pre-emptor examined two witnesses and pre-emptees examined three witnesses in support of their respective cases.

7. After hearing the learned Judge of the trial Court allowed the pre-emption to the effect that out of 0.36 acre of land original pre-emptors will get 0.18 acre of land and co-pre-emptor will get rest 0.18 acre of land. Against which the co-pre-emptor as appellant preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.51 of 2001, pre-emptees as appellants preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.58 of 2001 and original pre-emptors as appellants preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.60 of 2001, in the Court of District Judge, Noakhali, ultimately all the appeals were heard analogously by the learned District Judge, Noakhali, who by the judgment and order dated 18- 2-2003 allowed the Miscellaneous Appeal No.60 of 2001 and dismissed other two appeals holding that the application for transposition as co-pre-emptor filed by the opposite party No.23 of the pre-emption case was barred by limitation.

8. Feeling aggrieved, the co-pre-emptor preferred the instant applications and obtained the present Rules.

9. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr. Faruque Ahmed, Advocate for the co-pre-emptor petitioner seeks to impeach the impugned judgment and order on the two-fold arguments. Firstly, the summons of the preemption case was not duly served upon the co-preemptor and on his behalf his brother Nurul Huda (opposite party No.21) received the summons who was not the recognised agent of the co-pre-emptor. Secondly, the summons shown to have served cannot be treated as good service, so according to him the application under section 96(4) of the Act was filed by a the pre-emptor within time and considering such facts the learned Judge of the trial Court allowed pre-emption. In support of his contentions, the learned Counsel refers the case of Abdur Rahman vs Shamsunnahar Begum reported in 7 BLT (AD) 125 wherein at paragraph No.6 it has been observed:

"The High Court Division rightly held that in the instant case there is no evidence that the husband of the pre-emptee respondent was the recognised agent of hers. Therefore, the summons was not duly served upon the pre-emptee respondent. Limitation will start from the date of knowledge which is 8-8-1986 and the pre-emptee respondent filed Miscellaneous Case No.4 of 1986 on 11-8-1986 well within the period of limitation as prescribed by Article 164 of the First Schedule to the Limitation Act."

10. The learned Counsel further refers the case of Md Ismail vs Province of East Pakistan through the Chief Secretary, Govt. of East Pakistan reported in 16 DLR (AD) 438 wherein it has been held:

"Notice served on a third person not good notice."

11. The learned Counsel lastly submits that the learned Judge of the Court of appeal below without reversing the finding of facts as to the service of summons upon the co-pre-emptor, illegally allowed the appeal, thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

12. Mr. Mihirkanti Majumder, the learned Advocate appearing for the original pre-emptors (herein opposite party Nos. 5-6), opposes the Rules and submits that the kabala under pre-emption was registered on 26-10-1997 and it was entered in the book on 3-12-1998 and the instant case was filed on 1-4-1999, the summons of the opposite parties of the pre-emption case was served on 4-4-1999, so according to him, subsequent application or transposition of the opposite party No.23 as co-pre-emptor dated 7-7-1999 was barred by limitation. He lastly submits that on consideration of the materials on record the Court of appeal below rightly held that the application for transposition of the opposite party No.23 as co-pre-emptor was barred by limitation, accordingly rightly dismissed the Miscellaneous Appeal No.51of 2001 which calls for no interference by this Court.

13. In order to appreciate the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels I have gone through the revisional application, pleadings, evidences, all exhibits, judgments of the Courts below, other materials on record and given my anxious consideration to their submissions.

14. Now the question calls for consideration, whether the learned Judge of the Court of appeal below committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgment and order.

15. On going to the materials on record, it transpires that the original pre-ernptors claiming as the holding lands contiguous to the land transferred prayed for pre-emption of 0.36 acre of land outof0.72 acre described in the schedule of the application for pre-emption impleading all co-sharer ten- ants of the holding. Of them Abul Quashem opposite party No.23 of the preemption case, on 24-6-1999 filed an application to transpose him as co-pre-emptor claiming as co-sharer by inheritance. The said application was rejected as barred by limitation as well as an incomplete application. Again on 7-7-1999 he filed a complete appellation under section 96(4) of the Act narrating his status and cause of delay. For the convenience of understanding section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 it reads as hereunder:

"96(4) When an application has been made under sub-section (1), any of the remaining co- sharer tenants including the transferee, if one of them, and the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred may, within the period referred to in sub-section (1) or within two months of the date of the service of the notice of the appellation under clause (b) of sub-section (3), whichever be earlier, apply to join in the said application; any co-sharer tenant or tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred, who has not applied either under sub-section (1) or under this sub-section, shall not have any further right to purchase under this section."

16. It is pertinent to mention that the kabala under pre-emption was registered on 26-10-1997 and it was entered into the book on 3-12-1998, the Miscellaneous Case for pre-emption was filed on 1-4-1999 Summons were served upon the opposite parties on 4-4-1999. It appears from the report of the process surveyor that opposite party No.1 Nurul Huda received the summons on behalf of the opposite party No.23 Abul Quashem, who did not himself receive any summons and even summons were not approached to his family members and also it was not served at his homestead by hanging. Moreover, on perusal of the record it transpires that co-pre-emptor is a businessman having a grocery shop in Chittagong in the name and style "Alamin Store". He used to stay in Chittagong for his business purpose. These facts furnished corroboration by the nationality certificate dated 14-11-1994(Exhibit 8) issued by Chittagong City Corporation and voter identity card (Exhibit 9) issued by the Commissioner of Ward No.15, Chittagong City Corporation. OPW 1 AKM Golam Mostafa, pre-emptee and OPW 2 Md Safiullah also admitted in their cross-examination that the co-pre-emptor Abul Quashem used to stay at Chittagong. He came to know about such transfer on 20-6-1999 from his brother opposite party No.21 Nurul Huda. On behalf of co-pre-emptor witness -No.2, Abu Taher also deposed to that effect and corroborated such averment regarding knowledge. So, I hold that opposite party No.23 Abul Quashem filed an application to transpose as co-pre-emptor within time as prescribed in section 96(4) of the Act. It is evident that there is no material to show that opposite party No.21 Nurul Huda was the recognised agent of opposite party No.23, Abul Quesherm, so service of summons upon opposite party No.21 who received, the same on behalf of the opposite party No.23, cannot be treated as good service. Therefore, the limitation will start from the date of knowledge which is 20-6-1999 and the application under section 96(4) of the Act was filed within time. The learned Judge of the trial Court rightly held that summons were not duly served upon opposite party No. 23 i.e. co-preemptor. I am also in full agreement with such view of the trial Court. It further transpires to me that it is the discretion of the learned Court to allow the subsequent application for transposition if it feels necessary for the interest of justice and rejection of earlier application is not a bar to file a subsequent fresh application in this regard. It also appears to me that the Court of appeal below without reversing the finding of facts relating to service of summons arrived at by the trial Court most erroneously held that without examining opposite party No. 21 Nurul Huda as to the date of knowledge, the opposite party No. 23 Abul Quashem failed to prove the date of knowledge. This view of the Court of appeal below is absolutely wrong in as much as witness No.2 Abu Taher categorically stated that in his presence on 20-6-1999 opposite party No. 21 Nurul Huda for the first time disclosed about the land transferred to opposite party No. 23 So, in my view this evidence is sufficient to prove the date of knowledge.

17. It transpires that after considering the evidence on record both the Courts below concurrently held that the pre-emptees are the strangers to the land under pre-emption I do not find any misreading on non consideration of the evidence to arrive at in such findings of the Courts below. After appreciating the evidence on record I am also in full agreement with the aforesaid views of the Courts below, that the pre-emptees are the strangers to the land under pre-emption. It further appears that all the issues involved in the suit have rightly been framed, considered and decided by the trial Court with reference to the evidence and materials on record but the impugned judgment and order of the Court of appeal below is not a proper judgment of reversal as it failed to consider the evidence orally and documentary on record and, as such, the Court of appeal below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. On perusal of the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned Court of appeal below, it appears that the learned Judge without reversing the finding of facts arrived at by the trial Court as to the service of summons and limitation allowed the appeal and the same cannot be sustained in the eye of law.

18. In the case of Hajarilal Mondal vs Md. Mozaffor Bepari reported in 8 BLC (AD) 77 wherein it is held:

"It is a settled principle of law that the lower appellate Court being final court of fact will have to discuss and re-assess the evidence on record independently while either reversing or affirming the finding of the trial Court. In a case of reversal it is more incumbent upon the appellate Court to re-assess the evidence on record and to arrive at his own independent finding.in the instant case, the specific findings of the trial Court have not been reversed by the lower appellate Court exercising its power under Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code. Accordingly, the trial Court's judgment and decree are restored."

19. Moreover, the impugned judgment and order of the Court of appeal below in its entirety are not well founded in the facts and circumstances of the case. So, the grounds urged and contentions advanced by the learned Counsel for the petitioner are the correct exposition of law and facts and, as such, the legal pleas taken by him prevail and appear to have a good deal of force. On the contrary, I failed to discover any merit in the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the pre-emptor opposite party Nos. 5-6.

20. Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case and foregoing narrative I am of the view that the impugned judgment and order suffers from legal infirmities which call for interference by this Court. Thus the Rule having merit succeeds.

21. In the result, both the Rules are made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order dated 18-2-2003 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Second Court Noakhali, so far it relates to allowing Miscellaneous Appeal No. 60 of 2001 and dismissing the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 51 of 2001 are hereby set aside and the judgment and order dated 15-5-2001 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Begumganj, Noakhali, in Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1999 is hereby affirmed. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

Office is directed to send down the records of this case at once with a copy of judgment for information and necessary action.

End.

lawyer:
Gazi Mohammad Neamat Hossain, Advocate ------- For the Petitioners. 
Ramzan Ali Sikder Advocate ------- For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Dominous Pizza and others ------- Petitioners
Vs.
Domino's Pizza Inc  ------- Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 5-5-2005 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 7th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No.3 of 2000 rejecting the application for rejection of the plaint should not be set aside or such other or further order or orders passed, as' to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The opposite party as the plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.3 of 2000 in the Court of the learned District Judge, Dhaka impleading the present petitioners as defendant praying for the following reliefs:

(a) A decree may kindly be passed in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendants declaring that the trade mark and business name 'Dominous Pizza', being used by the defendants, amounts to infringement of plaintiffs' trade mark 'Domino's Pizza' and that the defendants has no right, title or claims to use the said trade mark and/or business name of the plaintiff.

(b) A decree for permanent injunction may kindly be passed restraining the defend- ants whether itself or their men/women, employees, agents, partners, share holders or officers from using, preparing, storing, marketing, selling or offering for sale, passing off or attempting to pass off any goods bearing or under the trademark 'Dominous Pizza' or any other trade mark confusingly similar or identical to the trademark 'Domino's Pizza and Logo' of the plaintiff.

(c) A decree directing the defendants to deliver up to the plaintiff for destruction or defacement of all the products, menu cards, bill beaks and any other offending labels/packaging and other promotional! printed materials along with printing blocks, dyes, wrappers, plates, advertising material bearing the imitated trade mark 'Dominous' and any other trademark confusingly similar or identical to the trade mark 'Domino's Pizza & Logo' of the plaintiff.

(d)  A decree directing the defendants to furnish the complete accounts of the profit made during the period of infringement and also to direct the defendants to deposit the profit amount into the Court for the payment to the plaintiff.

3. The plaintiff alleged that, the plaintiff has been carrying on business in its name 'Domino's Pizza' and its business name is Domino's Pizza and its trade mark is also 'Domino's Pizza' accompanied by a logo of its Domino's. According to the plaintiff, it has world-wide business of manufacture and merchant of pizza or pizza-related products. The plaintiff also alleged that it has got 385 registrations in different countries and has filed applications for registration in about 114 different countries including Bangladesh and their applications for registration are pending. The plaintiff made several other statements including that the plaintiffs trademark 'Domino's Pizza' has acquired an excellent reputation and goodwill on account of the extensive use of high quality of the plaintiff's products and extensive advertising in the printing and audio visual media. The plaintiff clearly asserted that the said reputation and goodwill extends to Bangladesh, where like other parts of South Asia, the advertisements are seen by millions of people on satellite TV and on account of purchases made by the customers in respect of the plaintiffs products 'Domino's Pizza' and had also mentioned a list of the countries including the year and the sale price in these years. According to the allegations made in the plaint, the defendant's business was not even in existence when the plaintiff started its business in Bangladesh also with the trade mark 'Domino's Pizza' and again 'Domino's Pizza' accompanied by the logo and the plaintiff applied for registration on 5-3-1998 in class 30. In Bangladesh the plaintiff has two pending applications for registration of trade mark 'Domino's Pizza' under No. 54634 dated March, 5 of 1998 in Class 30 and trade mark 'Domino's Pizza' and logo under No. 54635 dated March 5 of 1998 in Class 30. The plaintiff also asserted that the defendant started producing pizza and pizza-related products by using the plaintiffs trademark 'Dominous Pizza' and thereby earning huge profits and causing irreparable loss to the plaintiff. The plaintiff stated that it has incurred huge loss and its name and reputation is being damaged by the defendant by passing off their service and products as those of the plaintiff, with products below the standard service and products including the quality maintained by the plaintiff resulting in confusion deception amongst customers, who believed that they were customers of products as prepared by the plaintiff though, in fact, those were prepared by the defendants. The plaintiff made several other statements which are materials for proving their case during trial.

4. The suit was filed some time in 2000. The defendants duly entered appearance and filed written statement denying all the averments made in the plaint and contending that the plaintiff has no registered trade mark in respect of 'Domino's Pizza' and pizza-related products and that the defendants also applied for registration of the trade mark 'Dominous Pizza' on 5-7-1998 which is pending disposal by the Registrar of Trade Marks. The defendants filed an additional written statement some time in 2003. In the additional written statement the defendant stated that the defendants' partnership had been controverted into a Private Limited Company on 19-9-2001. The suit was fixed for steps under section 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure and then a date was fixed for preemptory hearing. Ultimately, on 26-6-2003 the hearing of the suit commenced when PW 1 was examined in part and further hearing was fixed on 4-3-2004. On 4-3-2004 the defendant filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint alleging, inter alia, that the plaintiffs suit was not maintainable before the learned District Judge as it was barred under section 73 of the Trade Marks Act. The application was filed under Order VII, rule II read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and also under section 10(3), 20(1) and 20(2) of the Trade Marks Act, 1940 for rejection of the plaint. In the said application, the defendant asserted that the defendants are partners of the partnership firm under the name and style Ms Dominous Pizza of 7 Sena Kallyan Complex, Mohakhali, Dhaka, Bangladesh and have been carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling of food products, namely, pizza, pizza combo, paste combo, etc by establishing a restaurant under the above name since the year 1998. Since then the said business concerned under the name and style Ms Dominous Pizza, is running continuously without any break and without any objection from any quarter. It is also stated that the defendants have acquired a monopoly right over the said trade mark 'Dominous Pizza' and to protect and safeguard the monopoly Trade Mark the defendants filed two trademark applications before the Registrar of Trade Marks Dhaka and the Trade Marks Registry, Dhaka, which allotted serial Nos. 56056 in Class 30 and 60801 in Class 29 and after provisional acceptance by the Trade Marks Registry. Dhaka, the said trademarks were duly advertised in the Trade Marks Journal No. 251 at pages 480 and 575 respectively. It is also alleged that after having noticed such applications, the plaintiff lodged notice of opposition giving rise to Opposition Case No. 1964/02 and 1965/02 respectively and the said opposition cases are now pending. The defendants further admitted in paragraph No.5 of their application that the plaintiff also filed two applications for registration of their alleged trade mark 'Domino's Pizza' under application Nos. 54635 and 54636, both in class 30 and the applications after being advertised in the Trade Marks Journal No. 225 and the defendants filed two requests on Form TM 55 for extension of time for filing notice of opposition and the said two TM 55 are now pending for consideration. According to the defendants, the plaintiff made statement in paragraph No. 12 which clearly indicates that the plaint is liable to be rejected. According to paragraph No.7 of the application, standing from the facts stated in paragraph 12 of the plaint, it is apparent that the plaintiff has admitted that the trademark 'Domino's Pizza' has not been registered as yet by the Registrar of Trade Marks, Dhaka, rather it is under consideration for registration. According to the defendant, since registration of trademark 'Domino's Pizza' is still pending for registration, the suit under section 73 of the Trade Marks Act 1940 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka is barred by provisions of section 20 (1) of the Trade Marks Act, 1940 and, as such, the plaint is liable to be rejected. According to the defendants, since trade mark of the plaintiff admittedly is pending registration, the suit instituted before the learned District Judge is barred under section 10(3) of the Trade Marks Act, 1940. The defendants further alleged in paragraph 10 of the application that the plaintiff in paragraphs 32 and 33 of the plaint has alleged that the goods of the defendants are being passed of as the goods of the plaintiff and the plaintiff has sought relief accordingly by the present suit before the learned District Judge, Dhaka under section 73 of the Trade Marks Act, 1940 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) is barred by the provisions of section 20(2) of the Trade Marks Act and, as such, the plaint is liable to be rejected.

5. The plaintiff resisted the prayer for rejection of the plaint by filing written objection and upon denying all the allegations made in the application for rejection of the plaint and asserted that the defendants themselves stated by filing additional written statement that they are no more partners but they formed a company which was registered with Registrar of the Joint Stock Companies but in the application for rectification of the plaint described themselves as the partners of the partnership firm which is not only misleading but also misconceived. It is also stated that the name of the plaintiff is 'Domino's Pizza Inc' and its trading name is 'Domino's Pizza' and its registered trade mark is also 'Domino's Pizza' accompanied by a logo comprising of the image of the domino pizza piece. It is further stated that the plaintiff is a worldwide and reputable business entity from the USA since 1960 and elsewhere as manufacturer and merchants of pizza and pizza-related products and the plaintiff is the true and original adopter, user and owner operator of the trade mark 'Domino's Pizza' which has continuously been used by the plaintiff since early 1960s and has earned tremendous reputation all over the world including Bangladesh, as producer and seller of delicious and good quality Dominos pizza and pizza-related products. Due to advertisement appearing in the international media, the defendants started using the plaintiffs' corporate name, trade name and also the trademark with logo and the reason for adopting the above name and marks by the defendants was to get readymade market and to earn instant profit at the cost of the plaintiffs though the defendants are not entitled to use the trade mark 'Domino's Pizza' which belonged to the plaintiff who is it earlier user, adopter and manufacturer of pizza and pizza-related goods using the trade mark 'Domino's Pizza.' According to the plaintiff, the claim of relief against passing off their goods i.e. pizza and pizza-related products by the defendants as their own goods accompanied by infringement of their trade mark, and thereby the suit is very such entertainable and there is no reason for rejection of the plaint. According to the plaintiff, it is an established and settled principle of law that an action for passing off is maintainable even without having registration of trade mark and their suit under section 73 of the Trade Marks Act which is maintainable before the learned District Judge and the prayer for rejection of the plaint is liable to be rejected.

6. The learned Additional District Judge, 7th Court, Dhaka, heard the prayer for rejection of the plaint and on consideration of the statements made in the plaint and also in the application for rejection of the plaint, came to the conclusion that the statements need evidence during trial of the suit and the plaint cannot be rejected under Order VII, rule II of the Code of Civil Procedure and also under section 10(3) of the Trade Marks Act, 1940 and section 20(2) and section 73 of the Act. Accordingly, by the impugned judgment and order dated 5- 5-2004, the learned Additional District Judge rejected the prayer for rejection of the plaint.

7. Being aggrieved thereby, the defendants, as petitioners, moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

8. Mr Gazi Md Neamat Hossain, the learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioners, has placed the impugned order and submits that the trial Court committed a gross error of law in failing to notice that the plaintiffs trade mark admittedly not being a registered one, the suit for action of passing off is not maintainable under section 73 of the Act. The learned Advocate further submits that the statements made in paragraph No. 12 of the plaint clearly indicate that the plaint, as filed is liable to be rejected as the plaintiff instituted the suit before the learned District Judge, Dhaka, under section 73 of the Trade Marks Act though the said section is not applicable in the facts of the case. The learned Advocate further submits that the suit is barred under section 20(2), section 21 and also under section 10(3) of the Trade Marks Act. According to Mr Hossain, registration of the trademark is not sufficient to attract the provision of section 20(1) of the Trade Marks Act. According to the Trade Marks Act, the trade marks must be registered with the Registrar of Bangladesh and unless it is entered in the Registry of Trade Marks in Bangladesh, it cannot be construed as a trade mark used or proposed to be used in relation to goods for the purpose of indicating or so as to indicate a connection in the course of trade between the goods and some person having the right either as proprietor or as registered user, to use the mark whether with or without any indication of the identity of that person, as defined in section 20( 1) of the Trade Marks Act. In support of his submission, the learned Advocate has relied on the decisions in the cases of Ram Krishna Bhakat vs Firm Haji Janabally and Abdul Jalil reported in AIR 1948 Calcutta 321 and Ranjit Lal Maria vs Vidya Parkash reported in AIR 1951 Simla 176. The learned Advocate, Mr Hossain, has also relied on the decision in the case of PM Swamy vs Sultan Ahmed reported in AIR 1958 Madras 490, in the case of Burmah Eastern Ltd vs Burmah Eastern Employees Union reported in 18 DLR 709.

9. Mr Ramzan Ali Sikder, the learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the plaintiffs opposite party, on the other hand, supports the decision of the trial Court and submits that the proposition of law is by now established that a plaint can be rejected only on a reading of the statements made in the plaint and not traveling beyond the statements made in the plaint. Mr Ali submits that the statements made in the plaint do not attract any provision of Order V II, rule II of section 10(3) or section 20(1) or section 20(2), neither section 73 of the Trade Marks Act, 1940. Mr Sikder submits that a reading of the plaint would show that it is a case of infringement of a trade mark right accompanied by an action of passing off which is entertainable by the learned District Judge under section 73 of the Trade Marks Act. Mr Sikder has invited my attention to the plaintiffs' trade mark 'Domino's Pizza' and 'Domino's Pizza' accompanied by its logo and even if the trade mark is not registered, the suit under section 73 of the Act is very much entertainable by the learned District Judge, as the statements made in the plaint indicated that the suit is one for infringement of the plaintiffs' trade mark right accompanied by passing off action and there is no application of Order VII, rule II of the Code of Civil Procedure nor is the plaint liable to be rejected under section 20(1) or section 10(3) of the Trade Marks Act. In support of his submissions, the learned Advocate has relied on a decision in the case of Ismat Zerin Khan vs World Bank reported in 11 MLR (AD) 58 = 58 DLR (AD) 1 and also in the case of Sunil Kumar Das vs Canon Kabushiki Kaisha reported in 57 DLR 93 and also in the case of Messrs Tabek Restaurant vs Messrs Tabeq Restaurant reported in 1987 SCMR 1090. Mr Sikder has also relied on the case of Universal Pharmaceutical Ltd vs Social Marketing Company reported in 50 DLR 584. Mr Sikder also relied on a decision reported in Universal Pharmaceutical Ltd vs Social Marketing Company reported in 2 MLR (AD) 201 = 50 DLR (AD) 92. This decision upheld the decision reported in 50 DLR 548. Mr Hossain, on the other hand, relied on a decision in support of his submission that a suit for passing off an action is not entertainable by the learned District Judge under section 73 of the Trade Marks Act but may be entertained by any other competent Court but not under the special jurisdiction as provided by section 73 of the Trade Marks Act.

10. I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for both the parties and perused the plaint, the application for rejection of the plaint and the written objection including the impugned judgment. In the application for rejection of the plaint, it appears that the main contention is that the plaintiff has instituted a suit on the passing off action which is to be instituted in the ordinary Civil Court and, as such, the suit cannot be entertained by the learned District Judge under section 73 of the Trade Marks Act. Mr Hossain, the learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioners, candidly submits that a suit for infringement of trade mark accompanied by passing olfaction shall lie before the learned District Judge of the trade mark which is a registered one. According to Mr Hossain, In the present case, admittedly the trade mark 'Domino's Pizza' of the plaintiffs is not registered and therefore passing of action is not entertainable by the learned District Judge under section 73 of the Trade Marks Act which is a special jurisdiction. From the decisions cited by the learned Advocate Mr Hossain as reported in AIR 1948 Calcutta 321 it appears that the suit was filed in the Court of the Special Subordinate Judge of Assam Valley District claiming compensation from the latter on the allegation that they were passing off the biris manufactured by them as the biris of the plaintiff. It was held, 'the defendants, it is said are counterfeiting the name and the label and are passing off their goods as goods of the plaintiff'. In these circumstances, it seems to us that the present case does not come within the purview of section 73 of the Trade Marks Act, 1940 and consequently, the subordinate judge had ample jurisdiction to entertain and dispose of the suit. It was therefore a suit for compensation of the allegation of action of passing off. The decision does not support the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner. The other decision reported in AIR 1951 Simla 176. it was held there, "where the plaintiff alleges that the defendant is passing off his publication as the publication of the defendant and is thereby deceiving the subscribers and advertisers of the plaintiffs' paper, the pith and substance of the plaint is appropriate in a passing off action under section 20(2) and the suit is not hit by section 73 of the Trade Marks Act. In the said decision it has been further held that. "the main question in a passing off case is, whether the defendants is passing off his goods as the goods of the plaintiff, whereas in an infringement action the plaintiff has to prove that he has a proprietary right in the trade mark and having proved that, he has to prove that the defendant is using either the identical mark or similar mark." This is not exactly the point before us. The learned' Advocate for the petitioner, Mr Hossain, also relied on a decision in the case of PM Swamy vs K Sultan Mohideen AIR 1958 Madras 490 where it has been held that where it is apparently a passing off action the plaintiff also alleges an infringement of his registered trade mark and seeks relief on that basis, the suit would still be a suit for the infringement of a trade mark or otherwise relating to any right in a trade mark within the meaning of section 73 and would therefore fall within the scope of the ban imposed by that section. The City Civil Court not being a District Court or a Court superior to a District Court within the meaning of section 73 has no jurisdiction to entertain such a suit taken as a whole. The view expressed in this case is also not exactly the same as in our case where admittedly the trade mark has not been registered. In the Madras case, it has been held that infringement of a registered trade mark along with passing off action is maintainable under section 73 of the Trade Marks Act, 1940. In 18 DLR 709 there was no issue with regard to Trade Marks Act but it was held "from a mere perusal of the plaint itself, it must be held that the suit is prohibited under law. Even if the case does not come within the letter of Order VII, rule II of the Code of Civil Procedure, there is no doubt that it is barred under legal provisions. The Court below should therefore have rejected the plaint in limine. If Order VII, rule II of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be prayed in aid, the inherent power of the Court should be invoked." This is an established principle of law which is not applicable in the facts of the case before us.

<u>11. In 50 DLR 548 it was held, "the registration of the latter company is provisional and it has started marketing and selling its product 'Oral- saline' from the last part of 1994. But the respondent started marketing the selling of its product 'Orsaline' from 1984. So it is a clear case of "passing off." This view, expressed by the High Court Division with regard to applicability of section 73 of the Trade Marks Act was affirmed and maintained by the Appellate Division in 2 MLR (AD) 201 = 50 DLR (AD) 92. The suit arose out of declaration that the Oralsaline and Orsaline are not similar and identical. The Appellate Division construed the provision of section 73 of the Trade Marks Act, 1940 and held "a suit against the infringement of trademarks or copyright lies in the Court of the District Judge having jurisdiction and not in any inferior Court. When any order is passed by the Court of Subordinate Judge, such order cannot be protected in the face of an appropriate order passed by the Court of Additional District Judge." It is not disputed that a suit if filed against infringement of trade mark, it lies before the learned District Judge under section 73 of the Trade Marks Act and it is not denied by the learned Advocate for the defendants' petitioners. The main question which needs consideration is, whether a suit for infringement of trade mark accompanied by a passing off action can be maintained by a party before the learned District Judge, even if the trade mark is not registered. This question was answered by Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Messrs Tabaq Restaurant vs Messrs Tabaq Restaurant reported in 1987 SCMR 1090. In the said decision it has been held, "what is described as a passing off action may be a passing off action simpliciter or a case of infringement of trade mark coupled with passing off trade mark being registered or unregistered". In the said decision, the Supreme Court of Pakistan construed section 73 of the Trade Marks Act, 1940 and held the expression suit otherwise relating to any right in a trade mark. The word "otherwise" is of comprehensive significance and it is cut down in its scope and meaning only when it is followed by a enumeration and when it receives ejusdem generis construction. There being no enumeration therefore no restriction can be imported. Similarly, the words "relating to" brings in comprehensiveness and wider import. In a passing off action, which is based on the infringement of an unregistered trade mark, section 73 would clearly be applicable and it is to such passing off cases that the words "otherwise relating to any right in a trade mark" suggest that the section applies also to actions for passing off. This view taken by the Supreme Court of Pakistan is applicable in the case before us. On a careful perusal of the statements made in the plaint, it appears that the plaintiff sought to make out a case of infringement of trade mark coupled with an action of passing off. It therefore appears that the matter needs evidence to prove the statements made in the plaint and without such proof there is no statement in the plaint suggesting that the plaint is liable to be rejected. The learned District Judge has considered in detail the entire statement made in the plaint and came to the conclusion that the plaint, as stands, cannot be rejected as there is no legal bar in the frame of the suit. As it appears that the suit is one for infringement of trade mark coupled with passing off action, section 73 of the Trade Marks Act is clearly attracted and the suit filed before the learned District Judge was within jurisdiction and the suit was entertain- able and maintainable before the learned District Judge. At this stage, it is not proper to decide this issue before the suit goes to trial for producing evidence by both the parties, both oral and documentary and no conclusion can be drawn whether the suit as filed is entertainable by the learned District Judge or not. Section 10(3) of the Trade Marks Act, 1940 is a matter not of the Court, it is solely of the Registrar as it provides certain prohibition of registration of identical or similar trademarks. Sub-section 3 of section 10 provides that the Registrar of Trade Marks, only is permitted by law to decide which trade mark is identical or nearly resembles each other in respect of the same goods or description of goods. The Registrar may refuse to register any of them until their rights have been determined by a competent Court. This is therefore a matter to be dealt with by the Registrar of Trade Marks and not by the Court and therefore, the plaint cannot be rejected by applying section 10(3) of the Trade Marks Act. Section 20( 1) of the Act relates to institution of any proceedings by any person to prevent or recover damages for the infringement of an unregistered trade mark unless such has been continuously in use since before the 25th day of February, 1937 by such person or by a predecessor in title to his and unless an application for its registration made within five years from the commencement of this Act, has been refused and the Registrar shall on application in the prescribed manner grant a certificate that such application has been refused. This is not the case before us. Section 21 of the Act provides for right conferred by registration and admittedly in the present suit both the plaintiff and defendant do not claim for registration of their trade mark. Section 21(1) of the Act also therefore has no application in the facts of the case before us. I have already noticed that on a plain reading of the statements made in the plaint, it appears to me that it is a suit for infringement to trade mark accompanied by an action for passing off and thus the suit, as filed was entertainable by the learned District Judge and there was no reason for rejection of the plaint as section 73 of the Act is applicable in the facts of the case. The submission of the learned Advocate for the defendant petitioner was that the learned District Judge was not competent to entertain the suit has no substance. The other decision referred to by the learned Advocate for the opposite parties, namely 57 DLR 93 does not call for any consideration as the facts are distinguishable. The learned District Judge has on application of the relevant provision of law correctly rejected the prayer for rejection of plaint. Section 73 of the Act empowers the learned District Judge to entertain a suit relating to infringement of a trade mark or otherwise relating to any right in a trade mark i.e. passing off action. On a perusal of the plaint, I find that the learned District Judge has taken a correct view as the plaint discloses statement of facts relating to infringement of trade mark 'Dominous Pizza' along with an action of passing off. The suit is therefore, liable to be proceeded with and there is no statement in the plaint indicating a bar to maintain the suit or to entertain the suit by the learned District Judge. I have already noticed that section 10(3) has no manner of application in the facts of the case before us.</u>

12. Having given my anxious consideration, I do not find any substance in any of the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

13. In the result this Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The order of stay as granted at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated.

The learned District Judge, Dhaka is directed to dispose of the suit as early as possible, preferably within a period of 6 months from the date of the receipt of this order by the said Court.

The office is directed to send a copy of this Court to the concerned Court positively within a period of 60 days from date.

End.

lawyer:
Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh with Khandaker Rezad Raquib, lmmamul Kabir; Mejbahur Rahman, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners. (In all the writ Petitions).
Md Khurshid Alam Khan, Advocate ----- For the Respondent No.2 (In WP No.4202 of 2009).
AKM Fazlul Hoque Advocate ----- For the Respondents. (In the Writ Petition Nos. 506. 4205 and 4207 of 2009)
parties:
Nur Hossain Miah & others ------ Petitioners
VS
Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Ashfaqul lslam J : Writ petition Nos. 4206, 5067, 4202, 4207 of 2009 are heard together and disposed by a common question of fact and law.

2. In writ Petition No.4206 of 2009 initiation of Tejgaon PS Case No. 53 dated 19-3-2009 under sections 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, sections 420/409/109 of the Penal pending before the Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate, Dhaka has been challenged by the petitioners.

3. Similarly in Writ petition No. 5067 of 2009, Writ petition No. 4202 of 2009 and Writ petition No. 4207 of 2009 petitioners have challenged initiation of Tejgaon Police Station Case No.53 dated 19-3-2009, Tejgaon Police Station Case No.54 dated 19-3-2009 and Tejgaon Police Station Case No.55 dated 19-3-2009 respectively all under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 read with sections 420/409/109 of the Penal Code under different grounds.

4. Facts are almost similar in all the petitions and in all these cases as we have found that right after lodging of the FIR the petitioners moved this Division under Article 102 of the Constitution and obtained the Rules.

5. In all these petitions a common ground has been taken by the petitioners that without approval of the government i.e. sanction of the government FIR was lodged against the petitioners in violation of the provision of section 32(1)(2) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act which cannot be sustained under law. Besides, some other points are also argued. Mr. Sheikh Fazle Noor Taposh, Mr. Khandaker Reza-e-Raquib, MrImranul Kabir, Mr. Mejbahur Rahman, the learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the petitioners in all the petitions.

6. Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan and Mr. AKM Fazlul Hoque, the learned counsels appearing on behalf of the Anti-Corruption Commission, on the other hand, oppose all the Rules. Mr. AKM Fazlul Hoque, the learned counsel filed affidavit in oppositions in writ petition Nos, 4206, 5067 and 4207 of 2009 and submits that leaving aside all the points those are settled by the Appellate Division and this Division, the writ petitions are no maintainable as being pre-mature. In paragraph 24 of the affidavit in opposition tiled in writ petition No. 4206 of 2009 it has been categorically stated that the petitioners are fugitive from justice or law and have no right to seek aid or assistance of any Court and the Court will not pass any order in their aid. This view finds support in the decisions reported in Anti-Corruption Com- mission vs Md Hossain 61 DLR (AD) 17. Anti-Corruption Commission vs Dr HBM Alamgir 15 BLC (AD) 44 and Anti-Corruption Commission vs ATM Nazimullah Chowdhury 62 DLR (AD) 225. It is to be mentioned that the initiation of the cases against the petitioners alleging offences under different sections of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947 and the Penal Code will be followed by subsequent procedure of law governing the same.

7. Mr. Md Khurshid Alam Khan, the learned counsel for the respondent in Writ petition No. 4202 of 2009 submits that right after lodging of the FIR when the investigation had just started the petitioner brought this writ petition which is also not tenable under law since no proceeding as such was pending before any competent Court of jurisdiction and tor this reason interference by this Division at an initial stage of investigation cannot be supported under law. In this regard the decision of Abdul Hoque vs the State reported in 60 DLR (AD) 1 has been relied upon wherein their Lordships of the Appellate Division unanimously held that before taking of cognizance of a case by a competent Court for tribunal a proceeding cannot be said to be pending and accordingly, a proceeding cannot be quashed unless cognizance in respect thereof has been taken and process issued.

8. We have heard the learned counsels for the petitioners and the respondents and considered their submissions. We have also gone through the petitions and the different Annexure and the supplementary affidavits carefully. Since the decision of our apex Court clearly spelt out the provision of section 32 of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act in this context holding no sanction is required before filling a case under the act and also on the point that a case cannot be quashed unless cognizance has been taken by the Court having jurisdiction we are of the view that both the points apply adversely in the instant writ petitions.

9. It has been argued that in violation of section 32(1)(2) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 the FIR was lodged against the petitioner since no sanction was obtained by the Commission as required under that said provision. We hold that this question has been set at rest which is no longer a resintegra. No sanction is required for lodging any FIR in contemplation with section 32(1)(2) of the Anti-Corruption Act 2004 un-amended or amended. This view reached in its finality in a very recent decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Anti-Corruption Commission vs Dr. Mohiuddin Khan Alamgir reported in 62 DLR (AD) 290 wherein his Lordship Mr. Justice ABM Khairul Hoque while construing this point observed: -

"The High-Court Division, however, misinterpreted Section 32 of the Act, the original as well as the amended one, in holding that a sanction by the Commission is required before lodging an FIR. The High Court Division further misconceived the amended section 32 and wrongly held that a further sanction is required to take cognizance Of the offence by the Court in spite of the sanction given earlier under Sub-section (2) of Section 32 of the Act. But as a matter of fact no sanction is required to file a complaint and the unamended as well as the amended section 32 requires only one sanction from the Commission.

His Lordship further observed that:

Under the above amended section, after completion of the investigation, the investigating officer, under sub-section (2) of section 32, on obtaining the sanction from the Commission, would submit the police report before the Court along with a copy of the letter of sanction. The Court under sub-section (1), would take cognizance, only when there is such sanction from the Commission, Both the sub- section (1) and sub-section (2) of the section 32 envisages only one sanction, not two Sub-section (1) does not-spell out or even envisage filling of-any fresh sanction when the sanction to prosecute has already been filed along with the charge sheet of the investigating officer. It only envisages that without such sanction from the Commission as spelt out in sub-section (2), no Court shall take cognizance of the offence under sub-section (1) of section 32"

The second argument of the Learned Counsel for the respondent Mr. Khurshid Alam Khan that right after lodging of the FIR when the investigation had just started the petitioner brought this writ petition for which the same is not tenable under law since no proceeding as such was pending before any competent court of jurisdiction also merits substance. In this regard the decision of Abdul Hoque vs the State 60 DLR (AD) 1 as referred to above can profitable be cited wherein their Lordships of the Appellate Division after discussing pertinent potion of the reported cases of Bangladesh vs Tan Khong Hock 31 DLR (AD) 69. Syed Mohammad Hashem alias Hashim vs State 48 DLR (AD) 87 and N Mahmud vs N Ahmed 36 DLR (AD) 14 unanimously held: All the cases seeking quashing of the proceedings were preferred before taking of cognizance of the offence by the senior Metropolitan Special Judge 	Accordingly, before taking of cognizance of a case by competent court or tribunal a proceeding cannot be said to be pending. And accordingly a proceeding cannot be quashed unless cognizance in respect thereof has been taken process issued and so the instant criminal miscellaneous cases preferred under section 561A the Code of Criminal Procedure are guite premature and so the High Court Division should not enter into the first information report and the charge sheet in order to appreciate whether the facts alleged therein constitute any offence or not.

10. The process that has to be followed after lodging of the FIR cannot be throttled or stifled at an initial stage of the case. The petitioners however will have ample opportunity to argue their cases before the appropriate forum in due course. Therefore, at this moment we are not going to digress into any point touching upon the merit of the respective cases against the petitioners,

<u>11. Moreover, from the perusal of the writ petition No. 4202 of 2009 in paragraph No. 19 as well as the prayer 'd' it appears that the writ petitioners without surrendering before any Court of law filed the writ petition and obtained rule and stay challenging the lodging of Tejgaon PS Case No. 54 dated 19-03-09 under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sections 420/409/109 of the Penal Code, pending before the Court. of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka.</u>

<u>12. The principle of criminal jurisprudence is that a person concerned should submit to the process of justice before he can. claim right of audience provided in law as well as the judicial convention, which is very much effective in the Court of law as the age-old maxim goes that a person who seeks justice from the Court of the law must come before the Court to agitate his grievance and must surrender first to the process of justice, otherwise, he remains to be fugitive from justice and cannot seek aid of assistance of the process of justice in .order to claim right of audience against the process of the Court issued against him. When an FIR lodged he immediately becomes wanted by the Court in order to give effect to the order of the Court. His appearance is ensured by means of a warrant if necessary. If he does not surrender to the process nor his arrest is secured, then dispensation of justice is defeated. He remains a fugitive from justice. In the case Chand Shah vs Crown reported in 8 DLR (FC) 24 it has been held that it was an essential condition of an administration of justice in a case affecting an individual or individuals, that the persons concerned should submit to the process of justice. It has been further held in the Chand Shah's case that the Attorney-General who appeared to secure the interference of the Court on behalf of fugitives, without ensuing that such persons conform to the judicial orders applicable to them, was not acting in accordance with his proper duty to acting furtherance of justice.</u>

13. In ACC vs HBM Iqbal 15 BLC (AD) 44 Justice SK Sinha observed:

" Admittedly the writ petitioner was a fugitive from justice on the date he moved the writ petition. He was away from the country and craved permission of the Court to affirm affidavit on his behalf by one HBM. Shoave Rahman. The permission was given and the learned Judges issued Rule Nisi as above. It is now settled that a fugitive from Justice is not entitled to obtain a judicial order defying the process of the Court. Besides, the Learned Advocates who move applications for the fugitives shall also have to face the consequence of committing contempt of Court. This principle is being followed for over 60 years in this sub-continent References in this connection are Chand Shah vs Crown, 8 DLR (FC) 34. Gul Hasan vs Slate reported in 21 DLR (SC) 109. ACC vi Mahmud Hasan 61 DLR (AD) 17"

14. In a recent decision our Appellate Division held in the case of State vs Zakaria Pintu alias Md Zakaria Pintu reported in 18 BLT (AD) (2010) 491 = 62 DLR (AD) 420 that a bail although may often be a right to an accused but sometimes it is imperative on the part of the Court to refuse if there is serious allegations against him, like murder, rape, violence etc., because the Court just always keep in mind that justice must ultimately be done by ensuring punishment upon the offender otherwise, the offenders will get upper hand and, the sober of section of the society will suffer, which will destroy the fabrics. After all, it is the first and foremost duty of the State to bring the offender to book in order to ensure justice in the society. In the said reported case in paragraph 16 it has been observed:

It may be noted that proper investigation is the precondition for ensuring dispensation of justice. Mainly for that purpose, when there is allegations of serious offence, bail is generally refused, in order to avoid tempering of evidence so that the police may collect evidence from the witnesses, who may otherwise be afraid of reprisals. If the witnesses themselves are afraid of the own life and limb or of their near ones, they will never come forward with, the truth against the marauding offenders, if let loose on obtaining bail from Court. Ultimately, the administration of criminal justice would collapse and no member of the society will be safe. If must also be remembered that the fugitives generally do not come out in the open, out of fear of the police and the public in general but once they are enlarged on bail, instead of feeling shy, they without the fear of the police become doubly emboldened, while the informant and the witnesses take refuge in their hearth and home. The learned Judges would do injustice to their vow to dispense even handed justice if they give a blind eye to this naked truth of the present day situation,"

<u>15. In the instant case the petitioners were fugitive from justice when moved the writ petition and obtained the Rule and stay. In view of the above, at the time of 'motion' hearing this Division wrongly entertained the writ petition and stayed the investigation against the writ petitioners.</u>

16. In view of the discussion as made above, we hold that writ petition is premature and a fugitive has no right to seek any kind of redress as against their grievance, if any.

18. Resultantly, all these Rules are discharged with cost.

19. The order of direction granted earlier by this Division at the time of issuance of the Rules is hereby recalled.

Let a copy of this judgment be transmitted to the Chairman, Anti-Corruption Commission, Dhaka.
